requirements in line with the EU Credit Directives. Going forward, it is recommended that
transparency and disclosure of information in the banking and [ORG] sector should be improved to
foster competition and increase the comparability of financial products and services.
B. Capital [DATE]. [LOCATION]’s capital markets are currently small, but they have the potential to play a more
important role in the country’s future. At present, the capital market in [LOCATION] represents a small
part of the financial system. And while many companies appear to be listed on the two entity-level
stock exchanges resulting from the mass privatization program undertaken in the late-90s, in reality
very few companies or institutions have actually used the securities markets to raise capital to
finance growth and expansion. However, the two entity-level governments have just recently begun
to issue treasury bonds and T-bills to finance their own budgetary needs. Going forward, the
government debt market will hopefully continue to expand and deepen so that it can become a
more meaningful source of funding for the governments’ own needs in both entities.
75. The capital market played a key early role in [LOCATION]’s transition through facilitating
voucher privatization and enhancing transparency. However, the subsequent losses caused by
failed [ORG] ([ORG]) have damaged investor trust and market development.
Having established the two entity-level stock exchanges in the late-90s to support the first stage of
the mass privatization program, the governments of both entities seem committed to using their
respective exchanges to create more transparency within the economy, a feature which distinguishes
[LOCATION] from other, less-transparent emerging markets. However, another key element in the
governments’ privatization strategy has proven less successful, namely, the decision to establish so-
called privatization funds as a means of providing investors with another way of investing their
vouchers, while encouraging the post-privatization restructuring of numerous formerly public sector
enterprises.
76. Although a number of other transition countries also used privatization funds as part
of their voucher programs, in [LOCATION]’s case, most of these funds have failed to achieve any
meaningful restructurings of the firms in their portfolios. As these [ORG] were set-up as closed-
end vehicles, investors today are unable to realize the little value that still remains in these funds.
This negative experience has been suffered by a very large number of [ORG] investors and has caused
severe damage to investor trust and confidence in the capital market generally and the fund
management sector in particular. Considerable thought has already been given to this issue in both
Entities, but so far no substantive progress has been made.
77. Importantly, the legal and regulatory framework for the capital market is basically
sound, but the regulators lack the resources necessary for effective implementation. The two
capital markets in [LOCATION] are regulated at the entity-level by two separate securities commissions,
each with its own set of broadly similar laws and regulations. The respective regulators have begun
the process of adopting various [ORG] directives and protocols into their own legislation, with the result
being a fairly sound and improving legal framework, though a lot of further work still lies ahead.
Both regulators have only a small number of staff and thus lack the resources necessary to supervise
the very large number of firms whose shares are presently listed on the two exchanges or to
effectively implement many of the rules and regulations that are already in place. Currently there are
no formal organizations in place for this kind of cooperation, but going forward, it will be important
for the regulators to work more closely together to share the burden of developing new legislation
and new instruments, etc.
78. Although the government could use the stock market to privatize and recapitalize
some remaining large public sector companies, the privatization process in both entities is
currently stalled. In many advanced and emerging countries around the world, governments have
used the domestic capital markets to facilitate the privatization of large public sector firms and to
raise substantial amounts of capital in so these firms can continue to expand and prosper. Although
to date, both Entity-level governments still have a number of large and profitable SOEs, significant
sums could be raised on the domestic stock markets, positively impacting capital market
development. It would be advisable for both entity governments to consider engaging qualified
financial and legal advisors to develop a strategy for privatizing and recapitalizing some of these
large, strategic SOEs using either the domestic and/or global capital markets.
79. For the capital market to develop in the medium term, much closer cooperation
between the entity-level regulators and the two stock exchanges will be essential. Given
[LOCATION]’s small population and the rather small size of its capital markets, there is a compelling case
for combining the two markets into a single, unified marketplace, but [LOCATION]’s current constitutional
framework would not allow this. As an alternative, [LOCATION] could follow a model similar to what has
been done in the [LOCATION] - and is currently working well. In the [LOCATION], efforts were made to link-up national
exchanges and harmonize legislation and regulation across the entire region, but without requiring
any country to give up their national stock exchanges or their rights to regulate their home markets.
Instead, a so-called ‘passporting’ framework has been put in place that allows for issuers, investors
and market intermediaries to operate in each other’s national market, thereby creating a vastly
larger ‘common’ market, without sacrificing any institutions or independence.
80. As the two entities already share the same currency and are adopting the same [ORG]
Directives, it should be fairly straightforward to create an electronic link between the two
entity-level exchanges. However, for more complex regulatory matters that affect both entities, it
would be preferable to consider forming an association, similar to what [LOCATION] has done in
establishing the [ORG], which brings together the provincial and
territorial securities regulators from all 14 of [LOCATION]’s provinces and territories.

D. [ORG] Governance
90. The [ORG] and the [ORG] have equity or debt in their respective domestically-owned
banking sectors. The [ORG] owns the [ORG]nt of the [ORG] ([ORG]) owns a majority stake in [ORG] and preferred, convertible shares in two other
commercial banks, [ORG] and [ORG]. Additionally, the [ORG] also holds subordinated
debt in [ORG]. The [ORG] holdings are managed by the [ORG].
Governance processes reveal a number of common practices and concerns
91. Banks’ supervisory boards are not performing their intended leadership role.
Supervisory boards provide little strategic direction (in terms of business approach and risk
appetite), seemingly focused on conducting high level compliance activities rather than holding
bank management accountable for executing its strategy, the prudent operation of the bank or
establishing strong systems and controls. As a result, the management board is de facto placed in a
stronger leadership and decision making position, resulting in an important blurring of lines of
accountability and operational management.
92. Despite the existence of a structured recruitment process for banks’ supervisory board
members, overall the boards lack the experience, skills and independence to effectively guide
their institutions. Selection criteria are rather basic (university degree and five years of professional
experience). As a result, many board members do not have important sector specific skills needed to
direct and oversee a bank. The government recruitment committee does not communicate with
existing board members to determine the skills needed to construct a board with relevant
experiences and qualifications. The laws are silent regarding independence requirements of
supervisory board members and do not limit the number of civil servants in the supervisory boards
of state banks.
93. The internal audit functions of state banks are not fulfilling their mandates in practice
nor does the audit board structure promote effective monitoring of the banks’ control
environment. The audit board operates as a separate corporate body rather than as subcommittee
of the board. This arrangement has the effect of diffusing responsibility and accountability for
internal audit oversight and effectiveness.28 As a result, the supervisory board is not fully apprised of
the quality of performance of the internal audit function. Moreover, banks’ internal audit
departments suffer from understaffing and cannot comprehensively cover bank operations with a
high level of quality.
94. The risk management function in the state banking sector is a nascent. Banks report
that the functions typically support the credit approval process (which involves them in the business
line), determine credit classification according to regulation, and periodically perform portfolio
monitoring. However, the head of the functions are accountable to senior management and are
currently not independent.

qualitative performance of these financial institution investments. Given the specific types of credit,

Scope and Approach
A [ORG] mission visited the [LOCATION] from [DATE]-20, 2019 to update the findings of the 2010 [ORG].
This was a two-step full FSAP with the [ORG] mission and the joint [ORG] Core Principles (BCP)
for Effective Banking Supervision assessment mission taking place during June-July, 2019, prior to
the [ORG] missions. In addition, the [ORG] mission and the joint [ORG] assessment mission
predated the outbreak of the global COVID-19 pandemic. The [ORG] Technical Notes and the BCP
Detailed Assessment of Observance have not been updated, but the [ORG] reflects the relevant policy
reforms undertaken since the [ORG] mission, and the findings and recommendations remain pertinent
in light of the COVID-19 developments.
As part of this mission, selected [ORG] Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation were
assessed and are the subject of the separate Technical Note on Capital Markets Regulation and
Supervision.
This Technical Note was prepared to determine potential reforms or initiatives that would provide
further impetus towards the development of capital markets. It provides an overview of the
government securities market and then delves into the corporate bond and equity markets. Greater
emphasis has been placed on an analysis of the latter two markets as both the [ORG] and the [ORG]
have identified the key challenges in the government securities market and have been working with
the key regulators and issuer. Consequently, this note reviews the current state of the capital
markets, provides an overview of the reforms and market developments since 2010 and provides
several recommendations for the relevant regulators and SROs.
The note is organized as follows: Section I provides a broad overview of the debt and equity
markets; Section II provides a macroeconomic overview; Section III deals with government securities
markets; Section IV with corporate debt; and, Section V with equities.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1. The [LOCATION] corporate debt and equity markets will need to grow to provide
alternative financing sources to support the strongly growing economy and emphasis on
infrastructure spend. Capital markets deepening will be an essential pre-requisite for the country’s
continued economic development. The [LOCATION] capital markets lag regional peers in terms of size
and liquidity. In addition, sound macroeconomic fundamentals and recent strong economic growth
are not reflected in the growth of the capital markets. The emphasis on infrastructure spend through
the “Build, Build, Build” approach2, will require diverse funding sources to be nurtured,
2. Well-functioning capital markets ensure the optimal allocation and pricing of capital.
This enables retail and wholesale pools of capital to be efficiently deployed in a manner that maximizes
returns for such owners of capital against their risk profile. Ultimately, capital should be priced
according to the risks (creditworthiness) of its users and borrowers and becomes the source of
expansion financing for companies and investment returns for investors. Policy reforms following the
Asian Financial Crisis accompanied the growth of domestic markets in [LOCATION]. The [LOCATION] was
not one of the worst affected countries from the Crisis and therefore focused more on developing its
banking sector.
3. Although structural constraints exist on both the supply side (pipeline for issuance) and
demand side (investor base), there are a number of initiatives that could be undertaken to grow
issuance and investment. While, the conglomerate structure of the economy that provides sufficient
liquidity to large groups; the service sector orientation of the economy, and high liquidity particularly
in the banking sector have restricted capital markets development, other potential issuers such as
sub-national entities could consider using the capital markets. The introduction of new products
could be facilitated by improving market infrastructure. On the investor side, the domestic
institutional investor base could be diversified and developed through needed pension reform and a
streamlining of the many mutual fund structures. Technical and procedural barriers for foreign
investors, particularly in the debt markets, could be streamlined and reduced.
4. Furthermore, there are a number of technical and operational issues that could be
addressed, that could significantly improve the enabling environment for and functioning of

the capital markets. The result of these factors has been a lack of focus in policy development and
implementation that has hampered capital market development. Key issues include:
• a lack of commitment to reform from key stakeholders that has impeded the development of
markets and market infrastructure;
• an onerous tax environment that has deterred issuance and investment;
• a continuing need to improve investor confidence by strengthening the quality of supervision
and enforcement for market intermediaries and market operators;
• cumbersome regulatory requirements and processes around issuance, particularly debt
issuance; and
• outdated and inefficient trading and post-trading infrastructure, and governance concerns
regarding market operators.
5. In order to effect meaningful change, a capital markets champion is required. The latter
will be required to traverse multiple government departments, regulatory bodies, and vested
interests. This champion should be cognizant of the relevance of capital markets to the country and
possess the will and vision to drive legislative, regulatory and tax reforms. In addition, a commitment
to initiate a change in the ownership and governance of key exchanges and enforce policy against
entrenched interests will provide considerable impetus for development.

II. MACROECONOMIC OVERVIEW
13. Capital markets have not grown in step with strong GDP growth and sound
macroeconomic fundamentals. Capital market funding will be needed to support the growing
economy and infrastructure spend. GDP growth was at 6.2 percent in 2018, down from 6.7 percent in
2017 as global headwinds in relation to trade and manufacturing caused a slowing down of net
exports. Import growth outpaced exports driven by robust public investment activity. Private
consumption growth experienced its slowest pace since 2014, affected by high inflation, weaker
consumer sentiment and a reduction in remittances from [ORG] ([ORG]). However,
public consumption growth accelerated by double digits for the first time since 2012 due to the
government’s expansionary fiscal stance, characterized by its ‘Build, Build, Build’ policy.
14. An increase in public investment spending was the principal driver of economic growth
in 2018. This in turn led to a surge in imports driven by capital investment goods, raw materials and
intermediate goods. Exports, particularly in the services sector which accounts for 56 percent of
GDP, also fell due to a softening in global growth and trade.
15. Inflation rose steadily throughout most of 2018, prompting the [ORG] to tighten its key
policy rate. Headline inflation rate rose from 2.9 percent, year-on-year, in 2017 to 5.2 percent in 2018
driven by rising food, energy, and transport prices and the impact of natural disasters. The rise in
inflation caused the [ORG] to tighten its key policy rate by 175 basis points to 4.75 percent in [DATE]. This directly impacted secondary market trading in GS as banks pulled back from trading and
marking-to-market legacy portfolios of sovereign debt10.
16. The fiscal deficit exceeded its programmed target and reached 3.2 percent of GDP in
2018, as the government increased public spending in line with its expansionary fiscal policy.
In 2018, the country’s public expenditure effort reached its highest level since 1983. A significant
increase in spending on infrastructure and personnel services was the primary driver of the overall
acceleration in public spending. Despite robust revenue growth, driven partially by tax policy and
administration reforms, which saw the tax ratio reach 14.7 percent of GDP in 2018, expenditures
outpaced revenues. The financing of persistent fiscal deficits will require sustained issuance of GS.
17. The [ORG] baseline forecast projects real GDP growth at 6.4 percent in 2019 and
6.5 percent in both 2020 and 2021. The country’s growth outlook remains strong, and economic
growth is expected to recover in 2019, driven by higher private consumption amid a projected decline
in inflation from lower expected oil prices. The growth forecast also assumes further ramping up of
public spending causing the fiscal deficit to sustain and financed primarily by domestic borrowing.

III. GOVERNMENT DEBT
18. Efforts in recent years have been focused on developing the money and GS markets and
have been effective in setting appropriate pricing benchmarks for corporate securities.
Significant progress has been achieved from 2016 to date in developing the short-end of the yield
curve through increased issuance, initiating a predictable and transparent issuance policy, enhancing
the primary dealer network and adopting a new valuation methodology and trading platform for
benchmark bonds. Emphasis has also been placed on stimulating secondary markets by developing
repo markets for GS. The new initiatives undertaken represent a prudent and well-structured
approach towards developing capital markets which should be continued.
A. Money [DATE]. Several significant measures have been taken from [PHONE] to improve the functioning
of money markets and provide more reliable pricing benchmarks at the short end of the yield
curve. To better manage liquidity and provide more consistent pricing benchmarks, the [ORG] shifted
to the interest rate corridor (IRC) in June 201611. Post the IRC’s implementation, there is an overnight
lending rate, an overnight deposit facility, 2 auction-based term deposit facilities, and an overnight
reverse repo facility (which is aligned with the [ORG]’s policy rate)12. Previously, Special Deposit Accounts
and foreign currency swaps were used as the primary monetary policy instruments to withdraw excess
liquidity from the banking system. After the IRC’s introduction, money market yields such as T-bill
rates and the interbank call loan rates have entered the corridor and moved in line with changes in

27. There have been concerted efforts to broaden and deepen the GS market. These
initiatives have focused on:
• Increasing the Issuance of T-bills. As of [DATE], T-bills only comprise 12 percent of total
domestic GS stock, which has a duration of 10 years. While the supply of T-bills has increased,
almost a third of outstanding stock is held by funds managed by the [ORG] and the [ORG].
Consequently, there is still considerable room to raise issuance, reducing duration slightly
without incurring any significant refinancing risk. A sufficient supply of T-bills will further
develop the short-end of the yield curve and increase the correlation between T-bill yields
and key [ORG] policy rates, strengthening the monetary transmission mechanism. The increased
supply will also provide enhanced benchmarks for further sovereign and corporate issuance.
• Issuance of the [ORG]’s Own Instruments. [ORG]’s new charter enables it to issue its own
domestic debt instruments. This will add to the supply of short-dated instruments, provide
further collateral to develop the nascent repo markets and enable the [ORG] to more effectively
manage liquidity. While an important step in the development of money markets in the
[LOCATION], this will require close co-ordination between the [ORG] and [ORG] to ensure that the
size, timing, duration and type of instruments adhere to national borrowing targets and any
competition for investors is avoided.
• Predictable and Transparent Issuance Policy. A publicized and transparent debt issuance
program placed within the context of long-term borrowing needs and the concomitant
strategy will reduce uncertainty in both primary and secondary markets. In [DATE], the
[ORG] adopted a new issuance strategy and it is important that this is now closely coordinated
with the [ORG]’s expected issuance plan. The combined issuance strategy should be disclosed
to the market as part of the MTDS.
• Pricing of Benchmark GS. In [DATE], the traditional system of bond price referencing
that based reference rates for all bonds on the average rates of eight designated benchmark
tenors instead of individual traded bond prices was eschewed in favor of a Bloomberg-based
valuation model (BVAL) and trading platform. Transitioning to an improved valuation
methodology has enhanced the pricing of benchmark issues and smoothened the yield curve
appreciably.
• Primary Dealer Framework. A network of primary dealers comprising 35 financial
institutions is in place and is supported by 10 banks that act as designated market makers. In

[DATE], the Enhanced GSEDs Program was launched to further stimulate secondary
markets. Under the enhanced framework, current GSEDs are evaluated based on their primary

• Developing a Derivatives Market. In the first stage of developing capital markets the onus

should remain on deepening primary issuance markets and stimulating secondary markets
through the above-mentioned measures

• Enhancing the Repo Program. There are 4 primary issues that continue to affect the repo
market:
o Firstly, documentation in relation to the GMRA where foreign banks would prefer the
agreement to be governed by English rather than [LOCATION] law. This issue should

shortfalls for dealers rather than enabling it to be used effectively for liquidity management

more accommodative policy to enable the development of the repo market.

the use of buybacks and exchanges for GS that are the most widely traded. As was explained in

issues depending on their tradability. This mechanism would ensure that untradeable issues
would be removed from the market and replaced with more liquid instruments. It may also allow
dealers to swap illiquid issues with more liquid instruments on a scheduled basis.

A. Supply Side Issues
32. Some of the supply-side issues that affect corporate bond issuance are structural and
related to the conglomerate control of the economy that restricts the number of firms that are
able to come to market. The ownership of the country’s largest banks by these family businesses is
also a source of cheap liquidity that prevents greater issuance. In addition, businesses tend to be
under-levered, while the service-oriented structure of the economy is not highly capital-intensive.
There are also specific issues in relation to a penal taxation regime and a protracted regulatory
approval process that limit supply and increase transaction costs. All the above-mentioned points are
further elaborated in paragraphs 33-41.
33. Easy access to bank financing for prospective issuers. The dominance of business groups
in the economy who are also the most frequent issuers, provides most of these entities with access to
cheap bank financing. 7 out of the 10 largest banks (that includes two state-owned banks) are owned
by conglomerates and this, combined with the relatively liquid balance sheet of banks, provides a
ready source of competitive funding for corporates. The [ORG]’s decision to lower the statutory cash
reserve requirement from the current 17 to 16 percent by [DATE] will further increase banks’
liquidity. SBLs are also set at 25 percent of a bank’s net worth to an entity22. For the large banks, this
translates into significant credit exposure limits for each subsidiary of a business group as lending to
such entities is not consolidated unless the holding company also becomes a borrower.

light of increased public investment spending that has resulted in a higher than targeted fiscal deficit
and the desire to achieve tax neutrality, many transaction taxes may not be repealed and may continue
in diminished form.
37. In relation to all debt instruments, regardless of issuer, there is currently a final
withholding tax (FWT) on interest income and a documentary stamp tax (DST) on initial
issuance. The FWT is 20 percent on interest income for domestic institutional investors, which
increases to 30 percent for foreign corporations. The tax reform package recommends that this be

percent on the initial issuance of debt instruments . It has been proposed that this may be increased
to 0.75 percent to unify it with DST applicable to equity issuances. In addition, debt instruments are
also subject to a 0.1 percent transaction tax on trading while debt instruments of greater than 5 years
remain exempt from capital gains tax. The new tax regime proposes to maintain the tax-exempt status
of tradable debt instruments but imposes a 15 percent final tax on non-traded instruments. The
estimate of potential tax collected from debt instruments is presented below24:

has previously gone to market. In order to expedite approval, the [ORG] introduced shelf registrations
for 3 years in the IRR where total issuance amounts can be approved and then issued in tranches over
the defined period27.

B. Demand Side Issues
42. The investor base for recent issues of corporate bonds has been focused on retail bank
customers of the underwriting banks or investment houses. Approximately 60-70 percent of
issues have been directly placed with these investors recently inclusive of the larger bank issues of
PHP 25-30 billion with typical face values of PHP 50,000. The balance of the issues has been primarily
placed with institutional investors comprising asset management ([ORG], [ORG] and mutual funds) and
pension funds. The concentration of issuers may have resulted in both banks and funds reaching their
per party exposure limits and turned the focus towards a more retail investor base.
43. Increased focus on retail investors could limit the long-term capacity of domestic
markets in terms of size and tenor as bonds are a wholesale rather than retail product28. This
distribution is also heavily skewed towards ‘buy-and-hold’ investors which will not further the
development of active secondary markets. In addition, direct selling of this nature, while increasing
financial literacy and diversifying the investor base, potentially raises portfolio concentration risk for
investors. It is important that suitability requirements are in place for bank customers. Consequently,
it is imperative that the [ORG] ensure banks’ compliance with all appropriate disclosure, suitability and
investor protection requirements.
44. Foreign participation in debt markets remains minimal due to cumbersome processes
to seek tax-treaty based relief on FWT. There is also currently no system for a one-time registration
of investors, either domestic or foreign, with the [ORG] and the [ORG]. The latter’s registration system
also requires new accounts to be opened for each new bond issuance as the securities are registered
directly in the beneficiary’s name and traded bilaterally.29
45. Potential plans for [ORG] to acquire 49 percent of the [ORG]. The acquisition is
being considered to assume control of [ORG] that functions as the central depository for both debt
and equity securities and to allay potential concerns over the robustness of its clearing system.
However, this may result in a potential conflict of interest whereby a leading market participant
([ORG], which holds almost 10 percent of outstanding stock in [ORG] and is a leading player in
secondary markets) assumes control of the fixed income market’s SRO. The ability of [ORG] to

46. The following measures can be considered to address the supply and demand-side
issues that have been enumerated above. The recommendations encompass all the key
components of capital markets in relation to regulation, market-based reforms, issuers, investors and
underwriters:
• Rationalize the Existing Taxation Regime. The reliance on transaction taxes needs to be
reduced to achieve competitiveness in comparison to regional peers. Ideally, all such taxes
should be removed or minimized to the extent possible and the introduction of any new taxes
resisted. The current regime is distorting pricing in capital markets, deterring issuance and
compares unfavourably with regional peers31. An impact study should be commissioned to
ascertain the effect such taxes have on capital market development. On the supply-side, this will
require a determination of taxation’s effects in increasing the cost of capital and impacting supply
in terms of primary market issuance as transaction costs are raised through the imposition of
DST. On the demand-side, the effect of taxation on reducing investor returns through the
imposition of FWT will require to be assessed. The net effect of both supply and demand-side
factors could be negative and must then be measured against the potential increase in revenue.
Such an exercise requires both issuers and investors to be engaged and the development of an
econometric model that can identify the effects of raising taxes against the potential contraction
of primary and secondary capital markets. At certain levels of taxation, issuers will find alternative
means of finance while investors may prefer to invest away from bonds.
Currently, the analysis on the effects of taxation follows a simple averaging approach that selects
high and low volume points in the issuance and trading of instruments to estimate potential
revenue from a removal or change in applicable taxes. This fails to account for the complexity of
capital markets and the many variables that may affect volumes in both primary and secondary
markets. Finally, an assessment will also be required to be made that if businesses are provided
with greater access to expansion capital, their revenues may rise, increasing corporate income
taxes that may offset any reductions in transaction taxes.
• Streamline the Registration Process. The principle that should inform the process is to ‘register
the instrument and not the issuer’. From current requirements, it appears that an instrument
31 Please see paragraph 38.
[LOCATION]
registration application provides an opportunity to do surveillance on the issuer which results in
excessive documentation requirements. For companies already registered with the [ORG] and
listed, much of the documentation that is requested will already be available. If the focus is
registration of the instrument then a form providing issuance details and certifications that
confirm good standing of the issuer should suffice along with references to other filed reports.
A ‘no-review’ policy may also be considered for companies that are current in filing their reports
and have not been subject to sanctions for misconduct. The onus should be on more effective
utilization of the [ORG]’s resources and improved co-ordination between the regulator and the
[ORG] to minimize the current duplication of tasks.
• Review Bond Issuance Regulation. All current regulation is reverse engineered from rules
pertaining to equity issuance. It would be useful for the [ORG] to tailor its regulation specifically
for bond issuance. Specifically, shelf registrations should be utilized for equity issuance while
MTN programs should be employed for bond issuance. The terms of approval for MTNs need
not change but the tenors can be expanded to 5 years given the typical tenors of most corporate
debt issuances. Since bond issuances also have potentially larger sizes than equities, registration
fees for MTNs may also be reviewed. In addition, consideration could be given to introducing
other fast-track public offer initiatives that provide automatic approvals and initiating hybrid offer
regimes that target QIBs.
• Allow Taps of Existing Issues. The current practice of providing approvals for debt issuances
with greenshoe options should be discontinued as this is a market stabilization technique used
for equity issues. In relation to debt, permission to increase the issue size by a defined amount
and within a specified period could be made part of the initial approval process. The ability to
increase the size of an existing issue under the terms and conditions of the original issue but at
the prevailing market price could result in the issue being priced at a premium or discount in
relation to its coupon payments. Internationally, this is a technique utilized by issuers to access
the market when there are particular windows of opportunity usually caused by favorable interest
rate movements or investor demand. Taps allow issuers to go to market with an updated
prospectus but with minimal new documentation. They therefore reduce transaction costs for
issuers that may not have MTN programs in place and benefit investors with increased supply of
issues that are in demand, deepening both primary and secondary markets. The criteria for
granting an approval to tap existing issues should be decided by the [ORG] according to strict
criteria that include the previous meeting of regulatory requirements. Internationally, the current
practice is to allow taps in the initial regulatory approval for an issue as the technique is based
upon prompt access to the market which may be delayed if further permissions were required at
[LOCATION]
the time of execution, The [ORG] may require a notification from the issuer to keep it informed of
the tap’s execution.
• Increasing the Diversity of Issuers. The ability to introduce new issuers to the market is a
structural issue related to the close conglomerate control of the economy. A potential solution
could be in enabling some of the better managed local governments to access the market.
Funding to local governments is currently provided by the state-owned banks, and these lines
could be used as letters of credit to enhance their credit. Additionally, loans provided by local
governments could also be collateralized as part of the issuance to create asset backed ‘covered
bonds’ that provide recourse to both the issuer and the collateral. Permission to access markets
could also be provided to the better run governments that meet certain governance
requirements.
• Enhancing Market Making Support. A system of market making for corporate bonds could be
considered to attract investors into issuances. The banks acting as underwriters or as joint lead
managers of the issue could be the designated market-makers. In order to stabilize the issue
post issuance and to fulfill their market-making responsibilities, a relaxation in SBLs could be
provided for a defined period from the date of issuance.
• Deepening the institutional investor base. It is critical to address demand-side issues by
diversifying the investor base and creating deeper pools of institutionalized capital. As was
illustrated in Table 3 (Section IC 11), the [LOCATION] currently lags regional peers in terms of the
assets managed by its mutual and pension funds and the total assets of its insurance companies
in proportion to its GDP. Creating a level playing field by eliminating regulatory and tax arbitrage
among its collective investment schemes by passing the Collective Investment Scheme Law
would be a significant step in this direction.
Equally important, is to develop its pension funds sector where reform is imperative. The
state-owned pension funds, [ORG] and [ORG], currently operate on a defined benefit basis and
remain unfunded. While immediate reform here may be difficult to achieve, greater asset
allocations for corporate debt could still be cultivated. The main focus should be on the
development of private pension funds. These would need to be offered by private-sector
corporations and structured on a defined contribution basis to ensure that they were fully funded.
Also, plans should be portable to ensure continuity should an employee change an employer.
Such plans would place the onus on private pension fund managers to provide the requisite
returns to pensioners to ensure the plan’s sustainability and would need regulation as this is
currently an unregulated sector. A potential way forward could be provided by [ORG] that was
first introduced in 2008 to enable [LOCATION] citizens to create individual retirement accounts,
[LOCATION]
offering 5 percent tax credits for contributions up to PHP 100,000 (individuals) and PHP (family).
The revival of [ORG] may require the level of contributions to be enhanced and applicable tax
credits to be significantly increased. Operations could also be simplified as currently unrelated
parties are required to be the product provider, pension administrator and custodian of the
assets.
• Easier Registration Process. A one-time registration with the [ORG] and [ORG] for investors should
be introduced which may require some modifications in the latter’s registration system. This may
make the process of seeking tax relief for tax-exempt investors easier and may also encourage
more foreign participation. An easier investor registration process could also further stimulate
secondary market trading.
• Improving Market Infrastructure. The proposed acquisition of [ORG] by [ORG] appears to
be an attempt to improve market infrastructure by gaining control over the clearing and
settlement system for corporate debt and equities that is managed by [ORG]. While this may be
legitimate cause to pursue the preferred methodology has the potential to be a market disruptive
event which could compromise the [ORG]’s integrity. The proposed acquisition will also require a
relaxation of the [ORG]’s single party ownership rules which will emit the wrong messaging to the
market. Therefore, a market-wide solution to address trading and post-trading concerns should
be developed. If there are concerns around the efficacy of [ORG]’s systems, then a different
acquisition vehicle could be considered or [ORG] convinced to transfer [ORG]’s operations to a
separate operator that can introduce improved technology. The guiding principles for the
proposed transaction should be clarity in the intended objectives along with complete
transparency and compliance with key regulation. Effective communication with the market
would also alleviate many of the existing concerns.
• Increasing Issuer Awareness of Bonds. It is the responsibility of both regulators and market
stakeholders to educate the market and particularly prospective issuers about the benefits of
disintermediation. In bank-centric markets, the distinction between bank loans and bonds must
be clearly made as the latter instrument offers clear advantages to issuers in terms of size, tenor
and non-collateralization. This is an exercise that is a part of improving financial literacy and
facilitating the maturation of capital markets in the [LOCATION].
V. EQUITY [DATE]. Listed companies are substantially owned and controlled by a limited number of family
owned groups. In 2010, it was estimated that 12 family ownership groups controlled 75 percent of
[LOCATION]
the [ORG]’s market capitalization32. Anecdotally, further consolidation has resulted in the top 10
business groups constituting 80 percent of market capitalization and 100 per cent of total corporate
debt outstanding (inclusive of bank issues). Approximately a third of the top 100 companies are listed
on the [ORG] while both listed and unlisted companies remain closely held. This ownership structure
pervades the corporate sector and ultimately limits the number of issuers and the size of issues that
come to market. Most of the conglomerates have listed resulting in reduced sizes in recent IPOs with
only 4 out of the 20 IPOs from 2014-18 being in excess of USD 200 million.
48. Attracting listings from non-family owned businesses has proved challenging. A SME
Board was created in 2003 but has had a total of 4 listings and none since 2015 despite efforts to
explicitly focus on this sector. Such companies are largely filtered out by the regulatory requirements
that specify minimum years and absolute amounts of profitability. In addition, the high transaction
costs and the protracted nature of the listing process act as significant deterrents to new SME listings.
49. The stock market’s investor base is institutionally driven. Foreign investors accounted for
51 percent of total trading volume in 201833, while their participation in primary markets is driven by
the size of the offering that has remained small. The smaller sizes have enabled issues to be pre-
dominantly placed with domestic institutions.
50. Retail participation remains limited. Only 0.8 percent of the population maintains a stock
brokerage account with active accounts reportedly a quarter of that number. The [ORG]’s Consumer
Finance Survey 2014 also revealed that only 0.2 percent of [LOCATION] households owned securities and
investment products. In aggregate, only 3 percent of [LOCATION] adults invest in stocks, bonds or other
collective investment schemes.
51. Legacy issues in relation to prompt, impartial and transparent enforcement actions to
ensure investor protection continue to deter retail investors. Prosecution rates for serious
offences and market misconduct have remained low although the number of cases sanctioned has
increased. The fines associated with market misconduct are paltry and remain insufficient to deter
violations. Consequently, investor protection is weakly perceived which can only be addressed
through consistent and well publicized enforcement actions that increase confidence in the
effectiveness and impartiality of the regulator.
52. The market is also largely illiquid with turnover below regional peers34. In order to
promote greater trading, the [ORG] implemented a new rule in [DATE], doubling the minimum

public float for firms conducting IPOs to 20 percent. However, the new rule may deter family-owned

given to lowering minimum float requirements for smaller-sized companies to encourage more
listings. Trading liquidity is also concentrated in a small number of companies with the 25 most
frequently traded companies accounting for almost a third of total market turnover in 201836.
53. The [ORG] has also not enforced its own rules consistently in terms of industry ownership
limits at the [ORG] that were set at 20 percent post demutualisation. Despite efforts to limit brokers’
ownership to 20 percent, this also remains at 26 percent with a greater amount of board control vested
in the smaller but older brokers. Out of 134 brokers, the top 20 control approximately 80 percent of
the business but do not have equivalent board representation. Disproportionate control by smaller
brokers that do not benefit from the volumes generated by foreign investors incentivizes them to
keep transaction costs high. Many of the smaller brokers also continue to not be in compliance with
minimum capital requirements that have been set at PHP 100 million.
54. The issues that generally affect capital markets in the [LOCATION] and have been
explained in relation to corporate bond issuance, also apply to equity markets. As was pointed
out in paragraphs 49 and 50, the structural composition of the [LOCATION] economy has limited the
size and volume of IPOs and the number of companies that are listed. In addition, an institutional
investor base is dominant where foreign investors have become increasingly prominent in trading (6
of the top 10 brokers are also international) while domestic retail investors are scarce. In the absence
of significant numbers of new listings, meagre retail participation and a lack of new products, equity
markets have remained stagnant. The following analysis highlights some key issues and provides
recommendations that could provide added impetus to market development37.
A. Supply Side Issues
55. High rates of taxation have produced market distortions and do not represent best
practice. The imposition of an IPO tax on a sliding scale that is derived from the size of the public
offering in relation to company’s total shares, can reach 4 percent for offerings up to 25 percent of a
company’s total stock38. In order to avoid such taxes, IPOs have been structured as ‘backdoor listings’
whereby a dormant shell company that has already been listed is acquired. Assets are then transferred
to this company and the subsequent recapitalization announced as a follow-on offering. This is
obviously an inefficient listing process and raises other issues of market transparency and surveillance

56. Broker commissions can vary between 0.25 to 1.5 percent and have been resistant to

already been discussed in Section IVA 40. All companies that apply for a listing are also required

58. The introduction of new products has been problematic. Short-selling remains elusive as
the trading system does not ensure anonymity and is unable to successfully track short positions
especially where custodian accounts are involved. Brokers have also been unable to agree the terms

ETF was introduced but has foundered under the current tax regime, especially the stock transaction
tax which taxes the initial exchange of the underlying basket of securities for the issuance of a new
security and then the sale of the issued ETF. A REIT law was also passed in 2009 but there have been

B. Demand Side Issues
59. The difficulties related to on-boarding clients was commonly cited to the [ORG] team as
a primary impediment to market growth. The requirement to conduct KYC on a ‘face-to-face’ basis
and onerous documentation requirements have also prevented making inroads into the potentially
lucrative market of OFWs41. This problem is compounded by the fact that most broker offices tend to
be Manila-centric.
60. A lack of financial literacy and awareness continue to impede greater retail participation
in capital markets. It is incumbent upon both regulators and market intermediaries to continue
investor education about the benefits of diversifying their investment portfolio through greater
participation in capital markets.
61. The potential recommendations enumerated below must be viewed holistically. Taken
together, they provide a powerful signal to the market that policy makers and key market stakeholders
are committed to developing capital markets:
• Reducing Transaction Costs. This requires concerted and coordinated action between the [ORG],
[ORG] and [ORG]. 3 vital components need to be addressed – reducing transaction taxes, curbing fees
and commissions and improving the regulatory process:
o The first requires a minimization of existing transaction taxes and a resistance to the
imposition of any new taxes. In addition, a study should be commissioned in the
manner explained in Section IVC 46 and for the [ORG] to explain that easier access to
expansion capital will enable business growth. This will allow more taxes to be collected
directly from expanding businesses and a more efficient shift from a transaction-based
taxation system that deducts at gross to progressive taxation that collects from net income.
o The second component focusing on reducing fees and commissions requires the [ORG] to
enforce its rules and regulations more consistently in relation to key stakeholders,
particularly brokers. Resistance to lower fees and product innovation can only be ended if
the [ORG]’s board becomes more representative of all its stakeholders. A possible starting point
could be the uniform enforcement of minimum capital requirements required for brokers and
ensuring that industry ownership limits for all parties are in compliance.

o The third component requires a rationalization of the [ORG]’s approval processes and
potential amendments in the listing requirements related to the minimum profitability
stipulations in tenor and absolute values. The need to review such requirements for SMEs
is more pressing. In addition, the investment company laws require review to allow for
differentiation between various types of capitalisations in relation to corporations and mutual
funds. Greater automation at the [ORG] to reduce the level of physical documentation both in
terms of registration and fulfilling ongoing requirements would also make a significant impact
in expediting approvals42.
• Increasing Investible Instruments by Introducing New Products. New products and
instruments such as ETFs, REITs, forwards and futures, new indices and short-selling are essential
for further market development. While some attempts to introduce these products have been
made in the past, they have foundered in the current tax environment in some cases, while in
other instances, cumbersome regulation or a simple lack of commitment to innovation from the
[ORG] seem to have thwarted progress. Consequently, there needs to be consensus at the [ORG], [ORG]
and [ORG] level as to policy in relation to capital markets and the direction they wish the [ORG] to
take. This should be followed by the constitution of a new, more representative board at the
exchange that proactively looks to drive change and promote product innovation.
• Increasing the Retail Investor Base. Online verification for all potential clients of brokers should
be made possible provided all AML requirements have been met. Existing bank customers could
also be allowed to open brokerage accounts with minimal additional documentation such that
banks can perform ‘one-touch’ KYC at their branches. Concurrently, brokers could be
encouraged to open more offices outside metro [LOCATION].
• Improving Investor Confidence by Enhancing Supervision and Enforcement. It is imperative
that the [ORG] continues to enforce its rules and regulations impartially while enhancing its
processes for market surveillance43 to provide greater protection to investors.
• Increasing Financial Literacy. Programs that target retail investors should be initiated in
partnership with key market stakeholders. A demographic segmentation of the population
would identify the groups that are most likely to participate in capital markets and these should
become the primary points of focus for financial literacy programs.

I. INTRODUCTION
1. This Financial Sector Assessment (FSA) is based on the work of the joint [ORG]
missions' that visited [LOCATION] from [DATE] 1-3 1,2002 and [DATE]-1 7,2002 in the
context of the Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP). The principal objectives of the
missions were to identifiy the strengths, vulnerabilities and development needs in the financial
sector, and to assist the [LOCATION] authorities in designing appropriate policy responses. The
[ORG] findings were discussed with the authorities at wrap-up meetings chaired by the Minister
of [ORG] and the Governor of the
[ORG] at the conclusion of the second [ORG] mission, and during the March, 2003,
[ORG] Article IV mission in which the two [ORG] team leaders participated. The authorities
expressed broad agreement with the conclusions of the assessment, and have taken a number of
measures to implement key recommendations. The final [ORG] Report was delivered to the
authorities in August, 2003.
2. This report summarizes the main findings and policy recommendations of the missions.
11. MACROECONOMCOICNT EXT AND BACKGROUND
3. [LOCATION] has been remarkably successful in achieving rapid growth and substantial
diversification of a formerly mono-agricultural economy. Real output growth over the past
two decades has averaged just below 6 percent per year, leading to an impressive rise in per
capita income, a marked improvement in social indicators, and a narrowing in income disparities.

[LOCATION] has also succeeded in fostering a stable and democratic political system, underpinned
by strong institutions and the rule of law. Sound economic management and a far-sighted
development strategy have permitted the country to diversify its export and productive bases
from a sugar-based economy into one based on four pillars of development: sugar, textiles,
tourism, and financial services.
4. Maintaining the past high rates of growth and employment will pose a major challenge.
The trade preferences on which two of the pillars of the economy are founded are being eroded2,
forcing the the sugar and textile industries to significantly improve their competitiveness or lose
market share to larger, lower-cost producers. Both industries are restructuring and shedding
labor. Since the early 1990s, unemployment (currently about 10%) has been rising despite
continued robust growth, due primarily to labor market rigidities and a mismatch between the
qualifications of the labor force and the skills demanded by the workplace. The erosion of
preferential trade arrangements is likely to lead to a further rise in unemployment.
5. The authorities have embarked on an ambitious program to transform the economy. In
partnership with the private sector, the government is taking decisive measures to build a
knowledge economy based on higher value-added services, notably in information and
communication technologies. They have also adopted programs to modernize and improve
competiveness in the sugar and textile industries, and are investing heavily in education in order
to realign the labor force with the requirements of the new engines of growth. The investments in
education and infrastructure required to implement this reform agenda have contributed to high
and unsustainable fiscal deficits (6 percent of GDP in 2002/03, and 5.5 percent forecast for the
current fiscal year), and it is important that the authorities pursue their announced program to
reduce the deficit to to 3 percent of GDP over the medium-term. Successfully re-engineering the
economy while maintaining macroeconomic stability and social cohesion will represent a
significant challenge, and there are down-side risks which could adversely impact the financial
sector.
111. OVERALALS SESSMENT
6. [LOCATION] has a relatively large and well-developed domestic financial system and a
growing offshore sector. [LOCATION] belongs to a select group of developing countries where
domestic bank assets represent approximately 100 percent of GDP, and contractual savings
exceed 40 percent of GDP. The growing offshore financial sector is also large relative to GDP,
but weakly integrated with the domestic economy. The basic financial sector infrastructure, such
as payment, securities trading and settlement systems, is modern and efficient. Access to
financial services is extremely high, with more than one bank account per capita and widespread
In the sugar industry, most [LOCATION] sugar is sold in the [ORG] ([ORG]) market at the guaranteed
[LOCATION] producer price, which is well above the world market price. This arrangement is currently under legal
challenge at the [ORG]. The expiration of the Multifibre Arrangement at the end of 2004 will expose the export-
oriented textile sector to stiff and uninhibited competition from low-cost producers such as [LOCATION].
-3-
branch banking and ATMs. Unlike in most developing countries, new and small firms do not
face major constraints in accessing financial services and credit.
7. In order to move to the next stage in financial sector development, however, [LOCATION]
needs to further diversify its financial sector. While the financial sector is generally sound
and profitable, the dominance of a few major players and the concentration of risks within a
narrow banking sector pose certain systemic risks and inhibit competition and innovation.
8. Overall, the [LOCATION] financial sector is currently in good health, and the short-term
stability risks are modest. The principal risks facing the domestic financial system are linked to
the structure of the underlying economy. As wealth and economic activity are concentrated in a
few sectors and in a number of large, diversified family-controlled conglomerates, credit
concentration in the banking sector is high. A severe or prolonged downturn in economic
activity in key sectors where bank exposure is significant could potentially threaten bank
solvency, though stress tests indicate the system is resilient to all but very large shocks. A further
risk arises from the short maturity profile of domestic public debt, which exposes the
government to roll-over risk. Finally, there are some reputational risks associated with potential
money laundering in the offshore sector, though recent measures to strengthen the AML regime
should help to mitigate this vulnerability.
9. The strategy for mitigating the potential risks facing the banking system in [LOCATION]
requires a multifaceted approach. This includes: (i) continuing the strengthening of banking
supervision and encouraging banks to reinforce their internal controls; (ii) fostering the
development of alternatives to bank lending to reduce portfolio concentrations and increase
competition; (iii) encouraging sound international risk diversification; (iv) strengthening
provisioning levels so as to enhance the resilience of the system to a downturn in economic
activity; and (v) reducing the government’s implicit contingent liability in the banking system.
10. The assessment of standards and codes found a high level of compliance with
internationally accepted norms and best practices. The authorities have made substantial
progress in this area and are upgrading key financial sector legislation and regulations. The
ongoing implementation of the assessments’ recommendations should help further strengthen the
supervisory and regulatory framework and enhance the resilience of the financial system.
IV. MAINF INDINGS
A. Banking Sector
11. [LOCATION]’ strong economic performance has spurred the development of a large,
profitable and sound banking sector. The domestic banking sector, which constitutes over
two-thirds of the domestic financial system, has grown at an average 13 percent pea.o ver the past
five years. There are 10 banks, though the system is highly concentrated: the two large
domestic banks, [ORG] ([ORG]) and [ORG] ([ORG]),
control roughly 70 percent of system aggregates, and the two largest foreign banks, [ORG] and
[ORG], control a further 22 percent of the market. The system is generally well capitalized,
highly profitable, and liquid. The average capital adequacy ratio of 13.1 percent comfortably
exceeds the regulatory minimum of 10 percent. The return on assets has been consistently above
- 4 -
2 percent, and return on equity over 20 percent during the past five years. The average net
interest margin of 3.5% appears reasonable given the sector’s risk profile, and operating costs are
relatively low. Finally, the system is rather liquid, with liquid assets covering 63 percent of
short-term liabilities.
12. Opportunities for portfolio diversification are constrained by the structure of the small
island economy. With sugar, tourism, and textiles accounting for some 40 percent of bank
credit, the sectoral distribution of credit is probably as diversified as the economy allows.
However, loan portfolios are also concentrated at the level of individual counterparties, and
exposure to related parties is relatively high. Credit to the four largest borrowers in the economy
exceeds the capital base of the system, and large exposures represented, as of [DATE],
225 percent of system capital. While portfolio concentrations are to some degree unavoidable,
the recent tightening of BOM guidelines on large exposures and related-party lending represents
a positive development. In comparison to countries in the [LOCATION] region and similar income
levels, asset quality appears relatively sound, with a ratio of nonperforming loans (NPLs) to total
advances averaging around 8 percent over the last five years. To guard against a deterioration in
the quality of their portfolios, banks have been reducing their exposures to sectors where the risk
is considered highest. Provisioning is relatively low (23 percent of gross NPLs), in part because
banks historically have achieved significant recoveries from collateral. This level of coverage
might, however, prove to be inadequate in the event of a sustained economic downturn, when the
realizable value of collateral is likely to deteriorate.
13. Stress tests indicate the system is resilient to most external shocks. While credit risk is
by far the most important risk facing the banking system, operational risk is also a concern, as
highlighted by the detection of a substantial fraud at [ORG] in February, 2003. While the bank’s
strong underlying profitability enabled it to comfortably absorb the approximate US $3 0 million
loss, the fact that the fraud went on undetected for several years points to a major failure of
internal audit, control and governance systems. The banks face moderate and manageable
liquidity and equity price risks, and negligible direct exchange and interest rate risks due to well-
matched currency books and largely variable rates on loans and deposits.
14. Faced with limited growth opportunities in the domestic market, the two dominant
banks have expanded in the region. While the regional market offers welcome opportunities
for growth and diversification, it has also exposed the banks to riskier, less developed markets.
Thus, expansion needs to be accompanied by enhanced risk management tools and effective
information exchange between domestic and foreign regulators.
15. [LOCATION] has no deposit insurance, but there is a general perception, based on past
government behavior, that there is an implicit blanket guarantee for depositors. In view of
the large size of the deposit base (72 percent of GDP), this implicit contingent liability is quite
high and may be unmanageable. [ORG] and [ORG] are widely considered “too big to fail” by
depositors, and, in past cases of bank resolution involving smaller banks, depositors did not
suffer losses. In at least one case, the [ORG] advanced funds to ensure all depositors were repaid.
While it is to the credit of the [ORG] that insolvent banks have been addressed, in some instances,
it might have been preferable for the authorities to ensure orderly exit rather than preserve weak
banks, thus laying the foundation for future problems. The authorities are considering
establishing formal limited deposit insurance. The introduction of such a scheme should be
- 5 -
contingent upon further strengthening of supervision, the adoption of a more forceful prompt
corrective action plan by the [ORG], and a withdrawal of the government from direct ownership
in depository institutions. Should the policy decision be taken to introduce deposit insurance, it
is important to ensure that the design incorporates best practices in order to obtain the expected
benefits in dealing with problem banks, and to mitigate potential adverse effects.
B. Financial and Capital [DATE]. The short-term money, foreign exchange, and treasury bill markets are relatively
underdeveloped. This makes it difficult for banks and other financial institutions to manage and
allocate risks efficiently. It also impedes the development of more sophisticated financial
instruments that would enable [LOCATION] companies to efficiently hedge risks. The authorities
need to address a number of issues identified in the Treasury bill auction process and pursue
efforts to stimulate more efficient money and foreign exchange markets.
17. The longer-term government and corporate bond markets are also underdeveloped.
This is paradoxical given the strong and rising demand for longer-term assets from contractual
savings institutions, the need for the [ORG] to extend the maturity profile of public debt, and the
excessive risk concentration of the banking sector on a few large corporate borrowers. To
encourage the development of these markets, the government needs to harmonize the tax
treatment of interest income on financial instruments, eliminating the current disincentives to
hold corporate securities, and to establish a yield curve through regular issuance of longer-term
government bonds and a more active secondary market Strict enforcement of recent prudential
requirements for banks regarding large exposures and related party lending should also help to
foster the development of a corporate securities market.
18. While the institutional, legal, and technical infrastructure of the stock exchange ([ORG])
is highly developed, the market is characterized by low volume, poor liquidity and lack of
depth. From 1997 to 2002, market capitalization declined from 43 percent to 19 percent of
GDP; the average price-to-earnings ratio fell from approximately 14 to 6; and average turnover
hovered around 5 percent, indicating that the market is small, even relative to the small
e~onomyM.~a ny of the challenges which face the market fall outside the scope of government
policy, including the small scale of the domestic market, the need for local investors to diversify
internationally, the recent global bear market, and the withdrawal of foreign portfolio investment
from emerging markets. However, the [ORG] can take certain policy measures to promote a more
active capital market. Investor confidence can be enhanced by improved standards of disclosure
and corporate governance, and by more effective regulation and supervision of market
participants, which is particularly critical in a market where there is considerable overlapping
ownership among issuers, traders and investors. Measures to diversify the issuer base, including
privatizations and greater regionalization, should also be pursued. Finally, the government
should review the role of government-sponsored funds, which may create distortions in the
pricing of securities.

C. Insurance
19. The domestic insurance industry is well developed, and the large and medium sized
companies are efficient and financially strong. At 4.1 percent, insurance penetration
(premidGDP) is roughly on a par with [LOCATION], [LOCATION] and [LOCATION]. Life premia represented 61
percent of the total, providing further evidence of the development of sector. Life business has
been favored by generous tax incentives and the high level of development of pensions and
housing finance. The nonlife business is also generally sound, and does not suffer from high loss
ratios or long delays in settlement. There are 22 insurance companies operating in [LOCATION], but
the market is highly concentrated, with the three largest groups controlling 76% of total
insurance assets. Despite this high level of concentration, the industry appears competitive,
efficient, and reasonably profitable. There are, however, a number of smaller companies which
have weak financial ratios, and suffer long delays in settling claims, often forcing their customers
to seek redress in court. Four of them have been intervened recently and remedial action has
been taken. Further consolidation of the industry should be promoted to ensure sound
competition and greater safety. This can be achieved by raising the level of the minimum capital
and introducing risk-based capital requirements.
20. Life insurance companies face considerable reinvestment risk arising from the duration
mismatch of their assets and liabilities, and could suffer losses in the event of a large and
persistent fall in interest rates. This is due to the shortage of long-term assets in the local
market and the prevalence of long duration liabilities on their books. While the risk of
significant losses is mitigated by periodic review clauses in policies which offer guaranteed rates
of return, and the relatively low rates of guaranteed return compared to current interest rates,
caution is nevertheless advisable. With the contractual savings industry’s strong and growing
unsatisfied demand for long duration assets, it is in a position to stimulate the development of a
long-term government and corporate bond market, as well as the equity and venture capital
markets.
D. Pensions
2 1. [LOCATION] has a well-balanced multi-pillar pension system, but the Basic Retirement
Pension (BRP) scheme faces issues of affordability. Due to a rapidly aging population the cost
of an unchanged BRP is projected to double by 2020. The government is considering various
options for containing the cost of this scheme. Increasing the entitlement age to 65 and applying
an affluence test that would exclude high-income people would contain the projected cost to
roughly its current level (3.2 percent of GDP) in 2020.
22. The [ORG] has accumulated substantial resources (17 percent of GDP)
and is well run by the standards of most developing countries. It has high coverage, a low
contribution rate, low operating costs and good investment returns, even by comparison to most
private funds. The recent fraud involving large time deposits placed with the [ORG] underscores
the need for stronger internal controls and for subjecting its operations to external audit by a
reputable international auditing firm. The [ORG] invests heavily in government securities and
needs to diversify its holdings and adopt more professional asset allocation and investment
policies. It also requires considerable upgrading of its operations, creation of an independent
-7-
Board of Trustees, and appointment of full-time executive management. The [ORG] is currently
based on an opaque point system, and consideration should be given to converting the [ORG] to a
more transparent defined contribution scheme, complemented with the offer of real annuities
based on life expectancy on retirement.
23. The occupational pension funds appear to be generally sound, although the civil service
pension scheme is unfunded. Most occupational pension schemes appear to be well managed
with diversified assets, good investment returns, and low operating costs. They generally follow
sound accounting and actuarial practices, and are reasonably well funded. The civil service
pension scheme operates on an unfunded basis and suffers from a growing deficit. The
government faces a critical policy decision regarding the establishment of an appropriate basis
and level of funding in order to protect benefits from future budgetary pressures. One reform
option would be to create a defined-contribution scheme for new recruits, while continuing the
defined-benefit scheme for existing civil servants. A White Paper on Pension Reform, due in
early 2004, is being prepared for public consultation on the main policy options.
E. Other NBFI’s
24. The development of independent non-deposit-taking lenders could increase competition
and lead to greater access to financing at lower rates. Although both small and large firms
seem able to access financing, rates remain relatively high and firms may have difficulties
financing growth due to the widespread bank practice of taking floating liens that include all
current and future business assets of the firm and personal assets of the owner. While leasing is
already well-established in [LOCATION], most companies are reliant on deposits for funding, and
are therefore exposed to risks associated with maturity mismatches. Further development of non-
deposit-taking NBFIs could be facilitated by the removal of tax policies that discourage the
development of the corporate bond market.
25. The establishment of a comprehensive credit information bureau would also promote
greater diversity and competition in the financial sector. The [ORG] has taken the positive
initiative to propose the establishment of a credit information bureau. The current proposal to
include initially only large bank loans will help reduce systemic risk; however, to foster
competition and improve access to credit for smaller firms, the bureau should in time be made
more comprehensive in scope. Amendments to the Banking Act and Bank of Mauritius Act that
would allow the sharing of information are being considered. In accordance with best
international practice, these amendments should allow for future relationships or joint-ventures
with private credit bureaus, and should incorporate modern consumer protection provisions.
Credit information would also be enhanced by standardizing and making electronically available
financial information submitted to the Registrar of Companies.
F. Offshore Financial Sector (Global Business and Category 2 Financial Institutions)
26. [LOCATION]’ offshore financial center has grown rapidly since its inception in 1988, but
remains small compared to the more established jurisdictions. Global businesses are
attracted to [LOCATION] by a very low tax environment supported by 26 double tax avoidance
treaties; modern business-friendly legislation for global business; policies favoring open trade,
capital flows and exchange convertibility; good telecommunications; relatively low wages; a
- 8 -
multilingual workforce; and location. As of June, 2002, the offshore sector included 14 banks, 11
captive and 4 non-captive insurers, 22 1 global funds and approximately 20,000 [ORG] ([ORG]) companies engaged in non-financial services or personal/family trusts. Global
financial activities are large relative to both GDP and similar domestic activities. Category 2
bank assets amounted to 94 percent of GDP, marginally less than the assets of domestic banks;
Category 2 insurance premia were 4.3 percent of GDP in 2001 and comparable to domestic
premia; and the global mutual fund industry, with assets under management of $6.7 billion or
about 1.5 times GDP, was significantly larger than the domestic fund industry. The licensing
process for Category 2 banks and insurance companies appears to be effective, as license holders
are generally subsidiaries or branches of well-established international financial institutions of
high repute and standing, and both sub-sectors appear sound and profitable.
27. Linkages between the offshore financial sector and the domestic economy have to date
been limited. While the industry confers important benefits in terms of global recognition, and
development of world class financial, legal, accounting, and auditing skills, restrictions on
dealings in local currency and the generally wholesale nature of the offshore financial business
have implied a small impact of offshore activities on employment and economic activity. The
sector does not therefore currently represent a systemic risk for the domestic economy, though it
does pose reputational risks associated with money laundering or the financing of terrorism. The
authorities are aware of these risks, and are taking steps to mitigate them4. The authorities have
announced their intention to implement a phased integration of the onshore and offshore sectors,
with the objective of eventually having a single financial center that caters to both domestic and
global business.
28. Changes in tax and regulatory regimes in other jurisdictions could materially affect the
growth of the global business sector. Such developments are possible in [LOCATION] and [LOCATION], the two most important markets for the [LOCATION] global business sector. There have been
legal challenges in [LOCATION] courts essentially related to the argument that [LOCATION] tax vehicles
may be abused by third country residents for tax-advantaged investments in [LOCATION]. While none
have succeeded to date, a significant narrowing or cancellation of the treaty would affect
[LOCATION] adversely’. Similarly, proposals by the [LOCATION] authorities to tax world-wide
income derived from [LOCATION] sources or to further relax exchange controls would
adversely affect [LOCATION] business. [LOCATION] is guarding against these risks by seeking to
enter into treaties that follow good practices in avoiding the encouragement of “tax shopping”;
defending legal challenges effectively; and negotiating treaties and successfully attracting
business with other countries.
The [ORG] ([ORG]) firms constitute the most significant source of potential AMLiCFT risk to
[LOCATION]. These companies have no physical presence in [LOCATION], and are inherently difficult to supervise and
monitor. Many were licensed at the time when [LOCATION] did not have strong customer identification requirements in
place. Stricter licensing requirements are now in effect and monitored, and the [ORG] is vetting existing license
holders.
[LOCATION] has consistently been the greatest source of FDI into [LOCATION], with some $7.5 billion in investment flowing
from [LOCATION] to [LOCATION] between 1991 and 2003. These inflows have decreased sharply in 2003, which may be
related to the ongoing legal challenges and uncertainties on future tax benefits.
