G. Accounting, Auditing and Corporate Governance
29. Recent high profile financial scandals have raised concerns about the quality of
auditing and corporate governance. The Companies Act 2001 has mandated the use of
International Accounting Standards (IAS) and International Standards on Auditing (ISA) for all
companies other than small private companies; however, there appears to be a gap between
standards and practice. The [ORG] has recently conducted an assessment of compliance
with international auditing and accounting standards. The assessment focuses on the need to
strengthen monitoring and enforcement arrangements through the creation of a financial
reporting council, the establishment of a professional body for the audit profession, and
enactment of a new law dealing with accounting, auditing and financial reporting. The
authorities have announced their intention to introduce legislation in line with these
recommendations in the near future.
30. In line with international trends, the authorities are also taking steps to strengthen
corporate governance. The Companies Act 2001 and the listing rules of the stock exchange
have enhanced shareholder protections, and the [ORG] has issued binding Guidelines on
Corporate Governance for the banking sector which are in line with international best practice.
The [ORG] completed an assessment of corporate governance in 2002, and made detailed
recommendations for improvements. In the wake of this assessment, a draft Code of Corporate
Governance has been prepared and presented for public consultations. The draft code provides
guidelines on Board and audit committee composition, and qualifications and roles of company
directors, CEO’s and corporate secretaries. It also provides strict guidelines governing conflicts
of interest, which is a key concern in [LOCATION] given the concentration of corporate ownership.
Once the code is finalized and adopted, listed companies should be required, at a minimum, to
disclose their level of compliance. The [ORG], as a shareholder in numerous companies, should
set an example by strictly adhering to the code.
H. Financial Sector Regulation and Supervision
3 1. The [ORG] [LOCATION] has undertaken a comprehensive program of legal and
regulatory reform over the past three years with a view to developing [LOCATION] as a
competitive international financial center of high standing. This reform process was well
underway, though incomplete, at the time of the [ORG] missions.
32. The government has adopted a prudent and phased approach to integrated regulation
and supervision of the financial sector. The [ORG] ([ORG]) was
established in December, 2001 as the unified regulator for the non-bank financial sector, while
the [ORG] has maintained full responsibility for banking regulation and supervision. It was
decided at the time of the creation of the [ORG] that a review would be conducted in three years to
determine whether to merge the [ORG] and [ORG] into a single unified regulatory authority for the
financial services sector in light of national and international developments. The [ORG] has taken
over the regulatory and supervisory functions of the former [ORG] ([ORG]),
the [ORG], and the [ORG] ([ORG]), and has
also assumed responsibility for financial services that were previously either unregulated or only
partially regulated. With technical assistance from the [ORG], the [ORG] is working to put in
- 10-
place sound prudential and market conduct standards and policies, and has undertaken an
ambitious staff recruitment and training program to enable it to effectively carry out its broad
mandate.
33. Banking supervision is of a good standard, reflecting significant progress made in
building the capacity of the [ORG] in recent years. However, there is scope to further
strengthen the legal framework, develop needed regulations, and enhance implementation. Most
legal deficiencies would be addressed if the current drafts of the new banking bill and Bank of
Mauritius bill were enacted. Prudential guidelines are all of a commendable standard, and the
[ORG]'s capacity to enforce guidelines has substantially increased in recent years. However, there
is a need for additional guidelines to address country and market risks and credit policy. Finally,
banking supervision could benefit from further strengthening, notably in the areas of
consolidated supervision, the supervision of operational risk, and problem bank resolution.'
34. Regulation and supervision of the insurance sector have improved markedly since the
creation of the [ORG], but further strengthening is required. The regulatory framework has
many strong elements, including reliance on solvency monitoring, prudent asset diversification,
and internationaI accounting and actuarial standards. Gaps exist, however, in corporate
governance, internal controls and risk management. Furthermore, solvency ratios are below
international standards, and do not include risk-based capital requirements. These deficiencies
have been addressed in the new draft insurance bills. Supervision needs to place greater
emphasis on risk management and early warning systems. The [ORG] should also establish clear
procedures for early and effective intervention.
35. Enactment of a comprehensive law on occupational pensions would be desirable, and
proactive supervision needs to be developed. While the regulatory framework is extensive and
contains many important provisions to enhance the security of retirement benefits, it is
fragmented and has important gaps, such as the need for safe custody of assets and adequate
asset diversification. The [ORG] is currently finalizing a draft pensions bill, and has commenced
consultations with the industry. The complete absence of supervision represents a major
shortcoming, which needs to be addressed to protect the pensions of participating workers. In
strengthening regulation and supervision, however, care should be taken to avoid disrupting the
good performance of the larger schemes.
36. The regulation and supervision of the securities industry require considerable
strengthening. The [ORG] is currently preparing key legislation with respect to securities,
collective investment schemes (CIS), and market intermediaries. Completion of this legislative
agenda is critical to address existing deficiencies and gaps in the legal and regulatory framework.
One of the most important gaps is the absence of legislation governing CIS, despite the existence
of a sizeable domestic and offshore mutual fund industry. The [ORG] has imposed licensing and
reporting requirements in the absence of legislation, but these requirements need to be backed by
legislation which addresses important issues such as the segregation of funds, disclosure of
investments, calculation of investor interest and net asset value, competency of managers and
directors, and separation of functions within the [ORG] framework. It is also important that the

I. Insolvency and Creditor Rights
37. Banks and financial institutions enjoy strong and enforceable creditor rights, but the
legal framework governing corporate insolvency needs to be updated. Nearly all corporate
lending in [LOCATION] is done on a secured basis. Banks and financial institutions benefit from
strong, preferential rights with respect to security and fixed and floating charges, but
enforcement procedures are often slow and inefficient. The legal framework for corporate
insolvency is outmoded, and is oriented almost exclusively towards liquidation. The authorities
are working on a new law which will address weaknesses and incorporate recommendations of
the assessment of insolvency and creditor rights systems that was recently conducted by the
[ORG].
J. Payment Systems
3 8. [LOCATION] has well-developed, modern, and secure payment systems. Mauritius’
Automated Clearing and Settlement System (MACSS) is a very modern, fully computerized,
web-oriented, real-time-gross-settlement, large-value payment system. Checks are cleared
through a manual, netting system, with three daily settlements through the MACSS. Card
payments are technically well developed, with all ATMs, electronic funds transfers and point-of-
sale transactions integrated in one network. Securities settlement is done on T+3 basis in a
modern, fully computerized system. The assessment of payment systems conducted by the [ORG]
mission concluded that [LOCATION] fully complied with most of the [ORG] ([ORG]) Core Principles.
K. Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT)
39. The legal and institutional framework on anti-money laundering and combating the
financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) in [LOCATION] is broadly in line with [ORG] 40 + 8
Recommendations. The [LOCATION] authorities have demonstrated strong political will and
commitment to meeting international standards, and have made significant progress in
establishing a comprehensive AMLKFT regime in recent years. The [LOCATION] government
passed the Economic Crime and Anti-Money Laundering Act (ECAML) in [DATE]. Further
efforts by the [LOCATION] government to improve the country’s legal and institutional framework
have resulted in the enactment of major legislation, including the Dangerous Drug Act 2000, the
Financial Services Development Act 2001, the Prevention of Corruption Act 2002 , the
Prevention of Terrorism Act 2002, and the Financial Intelligence and the Anti-Money
Laundering Act 2002, which replaced the ECAML. The [ORG] was recently admitted to the
[ORG]. While certain deficiencies in the legal and regulatory framework were noted in
the assessment conducted in December, 2002, the authorities have acted promptly and decisively
to address them. Technical assistance has been provided, and amendments to existing legislation,
as well as new regulations and guidelines have been promulgated to strengthen customer due
diligence requirements, facilitate the exchange of information, and clear certain ambiguities in
the legal framework. Further work is recommended to improve the coordination of law
enforcement efforts, and to expand the scope and focus of AMLICFT reviews during on-site

recommendations, the [ORG] has recently issued new guidelines for supervisors, and the
authorities have formed a task force to strengthen the coordination of law enforcement agencies.

Executive Summary
Public expenditure on household-based social assistance (SA) in [LOCATION] has increased signifi cantly since
2005. From a low base in the early 2000s, [LOCATION]’s aggregate national public expenditures on SA permanently
increased from 2005 after the central government allocated a portion of the savings from fuel subsidy reforms to a
number of SA initiatives. In 2010, national expenditures on SA are estimated at Rp 29,709 billion (US$ 3.3 billion),
equivalent to 2.6 percent of total national expenditures and 0.5 percent of GDP.
[LOCATION]’s strong fi scal position leaves [LOCATION] well placed to further increase SA expenditures. Declining
debt payments and subsidy reductions have opened up fi scal space over the past decade and supported a general
increase in social sector and SA spending. With debt-to-GDP of just 25 percent in 2010, [LOCATION] could further increase
expenditure on both items without raising debt levels.
Nonetheless, current expenditures on SA are dwarfed by spending on regressive energy subsidies which in
some years consume over 20 percent of total national expenditures. Subsidies’ high costs and poor targeting are
well known and the current [ORG] has more than once signaled its intention to reduce energy subsidy
spending, but reform is currently stalled. Progress on subsidy reform would further strengthen [LOCATION]’s fi scal position
and enhance its capacity to increase expenditures on more targeted SA programs.
The increase in spending after 2005 primarily refl ects greater central government investment in programs to
protect poor households from fuel and food shocks as well as large health and education expenses. The central
government is the dominant player in the SA sector, accounting for almost 90 percent of total expenditures. In years when
the government has increased regulated fuel prices (2005-06 and 2008-09), the largest compensatory SA response has
been an unconditional cash transfer program (BLT) to vulnerable households to help cushion them from the infl ationary
shock.
Outside of these years, a rice program for the poor (Raskin) consumes over half of total SA expenditures,
followed by a health insurance program for the poor (Jamkesmas, 18 percent of expenditures), a scholarship
program for poor students (BSM, 14 percent), a conditional cash transfer (PKH, 4 percent) and programs
for especially vulnerable groups (2 percent). Responsibility for executing these programs is shared by six central
institutions, while remaining central SA expenditures are highly fragmented and are distributed across 12 Ministries,
12 programs and 87 activities.
The central government has increased expenditures on many programs with poverty alleviation and social
protection goals like community driven development and social insurance for civil servants. The central
government has also been increasing its expenditures on [LOCATION]’s national poverty reduction program (PNPM), which
promotes community development and funds rural investment projects and other poverty programs which lie outside of
the SA sector. In 2010, the central government also spent at estimated Rp 54,326 billion on social insurance, equivalent
to 7.7 percent of total central government expenditures and 0.8 percent of GDP, mainly to cover the pensions and health
premiums of civil servants. Overall, the central government now spends 1.3 percent of GDP on social protection, of which
around one-third goes to SA and two-thirds to social insurance.
Subnational governments allocate a small amount of SA resources, primarily for staff salaries and general
administration in support of centrally-fi nanced and centrally-designed programs. Local governments account for
just over 10 percent of national SA expenditures, a majority of which is executed by district governments. While little is
known about the composition or impacts of this expenditure, case studies indicate that districts have few discretionary
resources and spend most of their SA budgets on administration and salaries to support central government programs.

1.2 National Expenditure Trends and the Social Assistance
Sector
Growing fi scal space has supported increased social expenditures, although spending on Social Assistance remains
very low when compared to expenditures on untargeted energy subsidies
Public spending priorities have changed dramatically since 2001, a shift helped by declining debt payments.
A decade of political stability, sustained economic growth, and sound fi scal and monetary management have helped
increase public revenues and other public resources. Sustained debt reduction has signifi cantly expanded [LOCATION]’s fi scal
space through declining interest burdens, which have fallen from 25 percent to 9 percent of total expenditures from
2001 to 2010 ( Figure 3). Spending on education, a national priority, now accounts for over 20 percent of total national
expenditures. There have been steady but minor increases in infrastructure (10 percent in 2010) and health (5 percent)
while agriculture has been fl at in relative terms at approximately 1 percent in 2001 and 2010. At the same time, however,
government administration spending has risen as rapidly as education (from 11 percent in 2001 to 19 percent currently)
while energy subsidies still consume a large share of fi scal space (20 percent or more in years when global oil prices have
been elevated). In comparison, the SA “sector” – which includes programs normally classifi ed under education, health and
subsidy expenditures – accounted for 2.9 percent of total national expenditures in 2010, up from 1 percent in 2001.

Continued spending on regressive fuel subsidies far outweighs targeted and progressive [LOCATION] expenditures.
[LOCATION] revised its fuel subsidy system in 2005 following a sustained rise in global oil prices: regulated fuel prices more
than doubled for households and the transportation sector while subsidies for industrial users were eliminated. Additional
adjustments to fuel subsidy regime have been made, including the launch of a kerosene-to-LPG conversion program in
2007 and a temporary increase in fuel prices at the height of another spike in global oil prices in 2008. These reforms
helped reduce the immediate burden of fuel subsidies on the budget, but subsidies remain a major public expense,
especially (and automatically) during periods of heightened global oil prices (F igure 6). At the height of global oil prices
in 2008, [LOCATION]’s annual spending on fuel subsidies reached Rp 139 trillion (US$ 14 billion), equivalent to 2.8 percent
of GDP, and consumed 20 percent of total central government expenditure ( Figure 7). The 2011 budget – which assumes
an oil price of US$ 80 per barrel and further fuel subsidy reform – allocates Rp 96 trillion or 11 percent of total central
government expenditure to fuel subsidies. This large fi scal burden does not necessarily benefi t poor households, as
household survey data indicate that commercial users and wealthier households consume the vast majority of subsidized
fuel, while poor and nearpoor households do not consume signifi cant quantities of fuel. Despite this regressive character,
spending on fuel subsidies was more than 4 times greater than spending on targeted SA programs in 2008 and more than
3 times greater in 2010.2
[LOCATION]’s could further increase SA and other expenditures could by additional subsidy reform. Citing their
large costs and poor targeting, the [ORG] signaled its intention to reduce spending on energy subsidies, particularly fuel
subsidies, primarily by improving their targeting, shortly after taking offi ce in late 2009. However, fuel subsidy reform
has subsequently stalled: in [DATE] and again in [DATE], amidst uncertainty over the future path of oil
prices, the [ORG] and [ORG] abandoned reform plans under consideration in order to resist infl ationary pressure. This
has created renewed uncertainty about the future path of subsidy spending. The [ORG]’s Medium Term Development Plan
(RPJM) has projected a sharp decline in nominal spending on fuel subsidies by 2014, with projected spending totaling
just Rp 211 trillion between 2011 and 2014. However, if reform plans remained stalled, spending could rise by an extra
Rp 250 to Rp 350 trillion over [PHONE] with oil prices at US$ 80 per barrel as assumed in the RPJM plans. However, if
oil prices instead remain around their recent levels of US$ 100 per barrel over the next few years, then spending could
be as much as Rp 500 trillion higher. Such large and unplanned additional spending on fuel subsidies could jeopardize

1.3 Central Government Expenditures on Social Assistance
The central government has increased expenditures on social assistance as well as other poverty alleviation
programs and social protection initiatives.
The fi rst generation of SA programs in [LOCATION] began in the wake of the 1998 Asian Financial Crisis (AFC).3
In response to the crisis, the central government established a broad safety net ([ORG], [ORG]) including
large food subsidies ([ORG], [ORG]). The [ORG] also included temporary, short-term programs including public
works (Padat Karya, PK), scholarships and funding for health services. The purpose of this fi rst generation of SA programs
was to ensure that poor households had access to affordable food, health, and education services during the crisis period.
Of the major [ORG] initiatives, only rice for the poor (renamed Beras untuk Rakyat Miskin or Raskin from 2002) continued to
receive signifi cant, and growing, budget allocations and become a permanent SA program.
[LOCATION]’s second generation of SA programs followed the partial removal of fuel subsidies in 2005. A portion
of the savings from the subsidy cuts were reallocated to three SA programs: an expanded Raskin, health insurance for the
poor (Asuransi Kesehatan Masyarakat Miskin, Askeskin) and a large-scale temporary unconditional cash transfer (Bantuan
Langsung Tunai, BLT) to help over 19 million poor and near-poor households cope with the infl ationary shock caused by
the increase in regulated fuel prices. Today, these programs form the foundation of an emerging, permanent SA system
targeted to poor and near-poor households. Askeskin, re-named Jamkesmas (Jaminan Kesehatan Masyarakat), now covers
over 70 million benefi ciaries, making it the largest social assistance program, in terms of intended coverage, in [LOCATION].
[ORG] continues to distribute rice to millions of families across the country. BLT was temporarily re-launched in [PHONE]
to mitigate the infl ationary impact caused by an additional fuel price adjustment in mid-2008. These programs were joined
by an array of small social welfare programs implemented by [ORG], targeting especially vulnerable groups including
at-risk children, the disabled, and neglected elderly.
More recently, social assistance programs with a focus on breaking the intergenerational transmission of
poverty were introduced. In 2007 the [ORG] began piloting a conditional cash transfer program (Program Keluarga
Harapan, PKH) executed by [ORG]. PKH assistance is transferred only when families obtain preventive basic health and
nutrition services, and send their children to school. The program has to date reached over 800,000 poor households and
is preparing for further expansion. In 2008, the government refocused general scholarship programs towards students
from poor households (Bantuan Siswa Miskin, BSM).

Box 1: Com- [LOCATION] has a long history of linking poverty reduction to community-based organizations
munity-based and community-administered initiatives. These programs – often referred to as “community
driven development” – take advantage of the political-administrative structure that has been central
development
in administering most local-level activities since the early 1970s. The system includes the [ORG] (Rukun
and [ORG]), [ORG] ([ORG]), and village (Desa/Kelurahan), which are political-administrative units
that spatially organize households into consecutively larger self-governing groups. These groups
administer social assistance, deliver public goods, and have historically fulfi lled the state’s need for
information, control and surveillance. This system, which was fi rst introduced during the [LOCATION]
occupation of [LOCATION], has historically been strongest, more visible, and judged to be most effective
on the island of [LOCATION]. Examples of the community administrative system in action include delivery of
the basic health care for children 5 years of age or less (Posyandu), delivery of family planning services,
delivery of basic infrastructure and slum upgrading (Kampung Improvement Program), the Program
for Left Behind Villages (Inpres Desa Tertinggal) and more recently Program Nasional Pemberdayaan
Masyarakat (PNPM).
PNPM, launched in 2006, deserves special attention as it is the operational umbrella for
most of [LOCATION]’s poverty alleviation programs using a community-based approach. PNPM
builds on and consolidates the successful experience and structures of three community-based poverty
alleviation programs: (1) the Kecamatan Development Program (KDP), (2) the Urban Poverty Program
(UPP), and (3) the Program for Left Behind Villages (IDT). [ORG]‘s overarching objective is to alleviate
poverty through both improved socioeconomic conditions, including more and higher quality public
goods, and improved community-level governance. [ORG] provides grants directly to community-
level organizations; these organizations essentially apply for those grants by hosting collaborative
and consultative meetings where members discuss and decide on a proposal for the use of the block
grant monies. [ORG] grants reach every sub-district in [LOCATION] every year, and a competitive process
allocates the grants to community groups with the best proposals.
In urban areas, [ORG] block grants facilitate the achievement of a collaborative community
development plan. Communities also benefi t from support for activities jointly proposed by the
government and funded on a cost-sharing basis. The main poverty alleviation activities that urban areas
have so far chosen to use [ORG] funds for include: infrastructure projects, increased poverty awareness
through social mapping at the community level, elections for community organizations, women’s
empowerment through increased participation in community governance and access to revolving credit,
and disaster recovery in the form of housing reconstruction.
In rural areas [ORG] delivers two types of block grants. The fi rst funds village investment
proposals (as in urban areas) and the second supports the participatory planning process it
self. Besides a limited list of prohibited activities, investment opportunities for communities are open.
Villages can also participate in a number of special pilot programs. These include responses to natural
disasters, community-based post-confl ict reintegration, conditional cash transfers to improve health
and education outcomes, natural resource management and renewable energy initiatives, technical
assistance and fi nancial resources for poor farmers, and other pilots that focus on remote geographic
areas and cultivating localized approaches to poverty alleviation.
[LOCATION] has an impressive record at successfully reducing poverty through community-
based programs. The achievements in poverty reduction through public expenditure in this area are
well documented.4 Some of the most robust evidence comes from recent impact evaluations of PNPM.5
The Cluster II community development approach has the potential to address manifestations and
correlates of household or individual poverty that are related to access to, or the quantity and quality
of, local public goods and locally-produced entitlements (like health and education services) as well as
issues that have to do with community organization and voice and links to local government.
Social insurance expenditures, which mainly fund servant pensions, have also increased and still exceed SA
expenditures although far fewer families and individuals are covered by centrally-funded insurance programs.
In 2004, the central government passed the National Social Security System Act which included the promise of universal
social coverage for all [LOCATION]. This system has not yet been implemented, but public expenditures on social insurance
are still growing quickly in real terms and exceed SA expenditures. In 2010, the central government spent an estimated
Rp 54,326 billion on social insurance, equivalent to 7.7 percent of total central government expenditures and 0.8 percent
of GDP. These funds go almost exclusively to cover civil servant pensions.6 A portion of public funds for social insurance
also goes towards premiums for health insurance services provided through [ORG]; again, this health insurance covers
mainly current and retired civil servants.

1.4 Sub-national Government Expenditures on Social
Assistance
Sub-national governments allocate small budget shares for SA spending; expenditure goes primarily to staff
salaries and general administration.
Sub-national governments have offi cial responsibilities for social welfare; nonetheless it is estimated they
execute just 12 percent of national expenditures on SA, though information and data on programs and
expenditure is extremely limited. Law 32/2004 on local government gives to provinces and districts responsibility
for social welfare of all residents and local authorities are expected to have more comprehensive knowledge regarding
the local nature of poverty and impoverished households. Local governments also have some fl exibility to adjust
implementation of SA programs to refl ect local preferences. However, very little is known about local SA program
expenditure7 while detailed sub-national expenditure data remains diffi cult to access, making analysis challenging
especially for relatively small sectors like SA. This section makes some progress in understanding provincial- and district-
level SA expenditure through analysis of aggregate data and select case studies.
Sub-national social protection expenditures have been rising steadily from a low base; district governments
account for a slight majority of spending. At the subnational level, the functional budget category “social protection”
(SP) is used to approximate aggregate SA expenditures. From a relatively low base, these expenditures have been steadily
rising in real terms but still represent a small share of total sub-national expenditures and a small share of GDP (Figure 12,
Table 6). In 2007, the last year for which actual realized expenditure data is currently available, sub-national expenditures
amounted to Rp 2,200 billion, equivalent to 0.8 percent of total sub-national expenditures and 0.1 percent of GDP. District
governments execute just over 60 percent of this expenditure, with the rest executed by provincial governments.

responsibilities between central and local governments. Partially as a result, Jamkesda schemes have
developed widely different population group coverage, benefi t package, member contribution, and
operational principles while health service providers have been prevented from using Jamkesmas funds
when the use of such funds would confl ict with local-level regulations including on Jamkesda and “free
healthcare” for all residents; see [ORG] (2012) for more detail on the effect of disharmonized
regulations on Jamkesmas implementation.
Jamkesda schemes are not yet required to report coverage, utilization, cost, or other
operational and fi nancial information. However, for the last three years, [ORG] has been
collecting limited budget and expenditure information on a voluntary basis. In 2008 and 2009, 140 to
150 districts submitted reports to [ORG]N]; this was more than double the number that reported in
2007, but still less than 60 percent of districts have managed to send two consecutive yearly reports.
Yearly budgets allocated range widely, from less than Rp 10 million (around US$ 1000) to more than Rp
30 billion (US$ 3 million), which is consistent with the variation mentioned above.
Though Jamkesda schemes can clearly involve large sums of money, generous benefi t packages, and
comprehensive coverage, an absence of registration, fi nancial, and utilization data makes it diffi cult to
estimate their contribution to protecting households from high healthcare costs as well as their impact
on overall health spending.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1. [LOCATION] is facing a dual challenge in the next few years: the first one is to raise employment and
productivity to narrow the income gap and facilitate the convergence with the [LOCATION]. The second one is to
program the forthcoming EU grant funds in a manner that promotes income convergence and ensures
continued macroeconomic stability. To facilitate income convergence with the [LOCATION], efforts to increase
employment and productivity are particularly pressing for [LOCATION], because the country has a declining
working age population. At the same time, the country has the second lowest labor market participation
and the lowest employment rate among [ORG] ([ORG]) countries, with a large share
of employment in unproductive segments of the economy, or in areas where labor productivity is
stagnant. The forthcoming [ORG] structural funds, which are designed to help [LOCATION] achieve income
convergence, provide an unprecedented opportunity for the country to catch up with the [LOCATION] standards of
living, ifu sed wisely. However, given the magnitude of expected resource flows, using them wisely is
also a challenge.
2. This report explores the options available for the [LOCATION] government to use optimally both the
[ORG] grant and [LOCATION]’s own funds in the pursuit of enhanced economic growth and development. The
analysis has selectively focused on four areas-nhancing the skills oft he labor force; agriculture; roads;
and environmental protection. These areas were selected because they will either receive the bulk of
expected [LOCATION] funds or if used wisely, are most likely maximize the longer term positive impact on
productivity and growth. In each area, the report has explored the priorities for funding, and implications
of the forthcoming resource flows. In addition, estimates of [LOCATION] transfers in the first three years of
accession have been prepared, both in terms of net transfers to the country (net impact on the balance
payments), and the magnitude of funds expected to flow annually through the government budget.
I. FINANCIALA ND BUDGETARIMY PACT OF PROJECTED EU FUNDS:
3. The net overalljinancial effect of expected [LOCATION] grant funds is projected to be highly positive on
[LOCATION], about 3.7 percent of annual GDP on average during [PHONE], if the country takes all available
funds. Experience from [IBAN] indicates that, if effectively used, the [ORG] funds can contribute to
economic growth both in the short and long run. In the short run they would create increased domestic
demand. In the long term, ifi nvested in the improvement of the physical and human capital with high
economic returns, they have the potential of making an important contribution to economic growth
through the supply side. However, experience also shows that, if badly used, these resources may have
only a short-term positive demand effect on the economy, and in the long term lead to real appreciation of
the local currency and reduced competitiveness, aid dependency, and undermine the efforts to improve
governance. Funds have proven to be most effective, when put to use under broad and well-defined
strategic programs.
4. Beyond the net overall financial effect, the report shows that [LOCATION]’s fiscal position would
deteriorate by about two percent of GDP on average during [PHONE], if the government absorbed all the
available funds and there was no restructuring of the fiscal framework. The analysis indicates that the
deterioration of the national budget balance would stem from increased expenditures. Taking into
account the already high level of public spending, it would be essential to improve the ability of the
government to substitute existing expenditures with [ORG] funds--that is, to reorganize the budget in the
most efficient way to maximize the absorption of [ORG] funds. The need for restructuring is even more
acute in the light of expanding social spending, related to the rapidly aging population, and high
unemployment.
5. The analysis suggests that there is potentially ample room in the [LOCATION] budget to absorb the
expected sharp increase in transfers from the [ORG] by consolidating and increasing efficiency of existing
expenditures, without adversely affecting economic growth. Since the government would like to cap the
level ofp ublic expenditures as a share of GDP at 40 percent, adding [ORG] funds to the budget without any
expenditure restructuring is not an option. That leaves the government essentially with two choices in
terms of accommodating the expected [ORG] funds. The first choice is to accommodate them through full
fiscal adjustment: through fiscal consolidation equivalent to the projected budgetary impact of [ORG]
funds-that is, about two percentage point of GDP. The numbers suggest that the first choice could be
achieved solely by rationalizing spending on military, security, health, government employment,
subsidies, and social benefits. The second choice is to accommodate the [LOCATION] funds through a mixture of
fiscal adjustment and economic growth. However, from the point of view of increasing the rate of
growth, accommodating the funds fully through fiscal adjustment would be preferable in order to make
room for, say, further reductions in payroll taxes. Also, the second option would be risky to follow since
the government cannot control the rate of growth ofG DP.
11. IMPACT AND UTILIZATION OF PROJECTED EU FUNDSBY SECTORS:
6. A mentioned earlier, a large share oft he forthcoming [LOCATION] grant funds is expected to go to support
education initiatives, upgrading of roads, implementation of the [LOCATION] common apcultural policy,
and environmental standards. In each of these areas, the report analyzed options for utilization of [LOCATION]
funds.
7. Education: There is an urgent need to modernize the [LOCATION] education system to ensure the
country has a highly skilled and productive labor force that can make the catching up with the EU
standards ofl iving a reality. This is critical since while the level of education is steadily increasing in [LOCATION]
countries, the participation rate in higher education has been declining [LOCATION]. The demographic
change and declining age cohorts provide an opportunity to improve the efficiency of public education
spending, and ensure it is spent effectively on improving the quality of education and training and
increase coverage oft he shrinking age cohorts of students.
8. The report recommends that the government does not increase public spending on education as a
share of GDP, but seeks efficiency gains within the existing resource envelope. This is advisable, since
public spending on education, when adjusted for income per capita, is already on a level comparable to
many [LOCATION] countries, and spending per student has been steadily increasing, but education outcomes
remain well below CEE levels. Provided credible reform is taken, maintaining the existing level ofp ublic
spending on education as a share of GDP (including possible [ORG] funds) would be warranted. While
consolidation of spending is recommended in many other sectors, given the importance of education for
promotion ofl abor productivity, a differential treatment is recommended on education, assuming reforms
proceed. Reform of the education system would also build a good base for a more productive use of EU
grant funds, and make human resource development programs presented to the [ORG] for funding more
credible.
9. The reform measures needed would include gradual consolidation of schools, universities, and
vocational colleges in light of declining age cohorts to increase student-teacher ratios and release funds
for upgrading of curriculum, textbooks, and facilities. Reforms need to be guided by a leadership group
that consults regularly, including across ministries ([ORG], [ORG], [ORG]), and that unifies the vision across
ministries with periodic Position Papers that set out not only the vision, but progress to date and the way
forward. This group should also lead in garnering support for the reforms by involving the teachers as
well as the general public. Explaining the potential benefits of such reforms is crucial for successful
implementation. The savings from the reforms should be retained within the sector, and used to finance
other quality improvements. To raise the quality of education, there is a need to undertake a curriculum
reform, develop better teaching materials, improve teacher training, open up university administration to
outside representatives, and establish periodic national student assessments to evaluate the impact of
education. At the upper secondary and university levels, it is critical to establish links with the labor
markets to ensure that their graduates are equipped with skills required in the market. In a global
economy, continuous upgrading of skills of the labor force is increasingly important to stay competitive,
and would need to be encouraged.
10. Based on the experience of [LOCATION], the report presents a series of proposals for possible [ORG]
funding to help reform the sector in the areas of: (i)im proving the quality of education; (ii)m odernizing
the educational infrastructure; (iii)im proving access for all; (iv) reducing inequalities; (v) promoting
social inclusion; (vi) building the capacity ofp ersonnel; and (vii) promoting lifelong learning.
11. Agriculture: As part of preparations for [ORG] accession, [LOCATION] has to gradually adopt an
agricultural policy and institutional framework fully compatible with the Common Agricultural Policy
(CAP) of the [ORG]. In this context, the government will need to make a series of strategrc decisions, which
involve the selection of a payment scheme for direct income support measures, the potential topping up of
area based payments, payment modalities, eligibility criteria, and transfers among modalities. In making
these decisions it should not lose sight of efficiency considerations since only higher productivity and
stronger competitiveness can in the long run ensure strong sustainable improvements in the wellbeing of
the rural sector.
12. Selection of a Payment Scheme: Owing to the complexity of implementing a Single Farm
Payment Scheme (SFPS), it is recommended that [LOCATION] opts for a Single Area Payment Scheme
(SAPS), as was done by almost all new [ORG] member states. It would then have a window oft hree to five
years to prepare for a conversion to SFPS, before penalties for non-conversion hcki n.
13. Topping- Up (Complementary National Direct Payments): Calculations show that the introduction
of SAPS payments to agricultural producers, starting at a level of 25 percent oft he EU15 average in 2007,
would increase average income of agricultural producers by 19.1 percent already in the first year of
accession. This suggests that no top-ups are required to maintain and increase average producer incomes.
However, the impact would be uneven across the producers of various agricultural products. Income
from tobacco production would decline as current direct payments are replaced with those under the CAP.
Producers of dairy would also suffer an initial small loss of income, as would some medium to large-size
farmers (50-100 hectares) due to crop-specific effects rather than size effects. The latter, however, would
only be a short-term impact, and turn into income increases in the first year after accession. It, therefore,
does not justify top-ups. Topping up is expensive, competes with other more productive programs, and
establishes a sense of entitlement which makes it politically difficult to remove it later. Given the
arguments in this report on keeping the size oft he state in check and on focusing all new expenditures on
improving productivity, topping-up is not the way forward. A different mechanism of support should be
sought ifi t is necessary for political reasons, perhaps best done through the financing potentially available
under Pillar 2.
14. Payment Modalities: If nevertheless topping-up is chosen, evidence suggests that the application
of specific, coupled CNDPs to limited sub-sectors (tobacco) should be favored over the implementation
of broad, sector-spanning top-ups. Moreover, such support should have a sunset clause. Also, since
support to specific products introduces distortions into production patterns, the form of CNDPs chosen
...
should be as simple as possible. Support to particular regions or sub-sectors would best be addressed
under Pillar 2 as part of general rural development of a specific region. This would also fit better into
strategic considerations ofi nternal convergence among [LOCATION]’s regions, and with the expected strategy
for rural development in the [LOCATION] in general.
15. Eligibility Criteria: According to [LOCATION] rules, the minimum parcel size for which payments may be
requested under SAPS is 0.3 ha, and the minimum holding size eligible for support under SAPS is 1. O ha.
[LOCATION] can decide to set the minimum size of eligible area per holding at a level higher than 0.3 ha, as
long as it does not exceed one hectare. Fixing the eligibility threshold at the 1.0 hectare level would
exclude about 76 percent of all farms, but only 6.6 percent of agricultural land in [LOCATION]. Some
preference was noted in the [ORG] for a mixed threshold model of 0.3 ha for intensive
farming and one ha for all others. This is possible, although this report has argued for a single eligibility
criterion ofo ne hectare. In making this decisions the authorities will have to weigh carefully the benefits
of structural change that would be promoted through consolidation of farms into larger more efficient
units, and the reduction of costs stemming from not having to administer the SAPS for very small farms
versus the adjustment costs for the farmers that would retire.
16. Transfers among Budgetary Allocations: If [LOCATION] decides to top up, there are two ways to do
it. It can top up the direct payments coming from the [ORG] from its own resources, or it can top them up by
using up to 20 percent oft he monies available under Pillar 2, but it must provide counterpart-financing of
these diversions from Pillar 2 funding from its own resources. The Pillar 2 route is obviously fiscally less
demanding, but it would take funds away from activities that potentially have a much larger impact on the
competitiveness ofB ulgaria’s agnculture than direct payments to farmers.
17. Efficiency Considerations: Direct payment schemes such as SAPS can provide some level of
income stability, and help mitigate farmers’ exposure to income risk by guaranteeing a minimum income
from farming. Direct support schemes, however, cannot substitute for the need to raise the productivity
and improve the competitiveness of [LOCATION] agriculture. Productivity growth and improved
competitiveness remain the only sustainable solution to agricultural income problems. Agricultural
support schemes targeting specific sectoral adjustment needs, such as farm consolidation, productivity or
competitiveness-enhancing farm-level investments, and diversification to off-farm activities is the way
forward. These can be tailored to the specific needs oft he different regions, and it can all be done under
Pillar 2.
18. In addition, direct income support payments may reduce the incentives for farmers to restructure,
consolidate, and modernize. Direct income payments may reduce incentives for consolidation, because
they guarantee a minimum income from farming, and therefore reduce the incentive for unprofitable or
older farmers to sell or lease their assets to more productive entrepreneurs. SAPS payments and their
effects on land prices or land rental rates may also make land consolidation more difficult, in particular in
a farming environment in which agricultural credit is not well developed. Evidence from [ORG] member
states indicates that support payments granted on a per hectare basis lead to significant increases in prices
for buying and especially leasing agricultural land. This will significantly disfavor tenants, slow the
consolidation toward more viable farm sizes, and would in effect support land owners rather than farmers.
These trade-offs between direct income support payments, and the need for higher productivity and
competitiveness point to the need to clearly separate rural social measures (such as measures to reduce
social tensions and provide social protection in the rural areas) from the major instruments ofa gricultural
income support.
19. Road network: Recent surveys have shown that only one-third of the [LOCATION] national road
network is in a good condition, and the road capacity around the larger urban centers is not sufficient to
satisfy the growing traffic demand. Furthermore, a considerable portion oft he core national road network
iv
still needs to be upgraded to [LOCATION] technical and safety standards. [LOCATION] has committed to
completing the upgrade of its main road network to [LOCATION] standards by 2014, with a number of roads
upgraded by 2008.
20. The Government would need to give high priority to the rehabilitation and maintenance of the
national road network, while at the same time continuing to construct select motorways and other high
capacity roads. All proposed investments will be subject to the minimum (five percent) economic return
criterion of the [ORG]. The maintenance oft he existing road assets, including clearing the large backlog of
road rehabilitation and repair ofc ritical bridges, could be largely financed from [LOCATION]’s own resources.
These investments generally have high economic returns. Rehabilitation of the core network would also
encompass improving the bearing capacity of road pavements together with improvements to road
geometry and riding quality in order to align these with [LOCATION] standards. The measures would be expected
to lead to lower transport costs and higher road safety standards in [LOCATION]. Financing of motonvays,
however, would go beyond the currently planned budget envelopes for road transport to the tune of 1-2
percent ofG DP per year.
21. The report provides four different scenarios for optimization and financing of investments in
additional class Ir oads and motorways. The scenarios suggest how to maximize the use of available [ORG]
Cohesion funds, which could be utilized either for construction ofn ew motonvays, or for improvements
to Class Ir oads that form part oft he TEN-T corridor. Previous economic analyses have indicated that the
Trakia and Struma proposed motonvay projects would have the highest economic rate of return among
motonvay projects. These two motonvays are also assessed to have the highest potential for PPP
financing. However, since PPP financing would generate long term contingent liabilities for the
government if state guarantees are required, some scenarios presented include and some exclude the PPP
as an option.
22. Environment: Meeting the environmental part of the acquis communautaire will increase
demands on budgetary resources in [LOCATION] over the next decade, and total spending on environmental
protection is projected to increase by about 50 percent in [PHONE]. The spending plans for the water
and waste sectors are, however, inconsistent with the overall budget envelope for environment, and
significantly exceed the expected budget allocations. Also, there are several problems with the details of
water and wastewater sector financing plans that would need to be addressed. Perhaps the most serious is
the unrealistic nature ofa ssumptions regarding municipal financing. These are predicated on increases in
tariffs that are overly optimistic. In case the tariff increases are not realized, programs will either fall
behind their schedule, or the state will have to make up the shortfall. This would cause expenditure in
this category of the consolidated budget to go over its planned limit.
23. It is also quite likely that the level of funds anticipated from the [ORG] will not be forthcoming in
full. Although [ORG] has increased its pipeline ofp repared projects for such funding, and these should
be sufficient to absorb at least the [PHONE] funds, the pipeline will have to be substantially increased
for further expected amounts to be absorbed. As a result, the commitment made by the government to the
[ORG] over the medium term may not be realized, and there is a need to prioritize the undertaking of
investments.
24. In sum, though undesirable, one can expect some delay in [LOCATION] in the implementation of
environmental programs agreed with the [ORG]. However, [LOCATION], [LOCATION], [LOCATION], and the recent new [ORG]
member states have also implemented their environmental programs on a delayed schedule, owing to
large financing requirements.
V
1. [LOCATION]’S EU ACCESSION AND AVAILABILITY OF EU
FINANCING
1.1 [LOCATION] is close to joining the [ORG]. With accession there could be a potentially
large net transfer of grant resources from the EU to [LOCATION]. The aim of these transfers will be to
facilitate [LOCATION]’s income convergence with the rest of the [LOCATION]. Given the much lower standard of
living in [LOCATION], the [ORG] has committed a considerable amount of assistance to the country after its
expected accession in 2007.’ In 2004, the [ORG] committed EUR 4.6 billion in 2004 prices to [LOCATION] for
the period [PHONE]. Since then the figure has been increased to reflect increased funding for rural
development.
1.2 It is an opportunity that does not come along too often for a country. Hence, it is natural that the
[LOCATION] government is focusing on how to optimize the use of the projected grant transfers from the
[ORG]. The government wishes to do that in the context of optimizing all its public expenditures, since,
while the [ORG] grant funds themselves may well be optimally used, they may provide room for other
expenditures from [LOCATION]’s own resources to be allocated sub-optimally. Hence, the problem is one of
optimizing the entire public expenditure envelope, regardless oft he source oft he funds.
1.3 The opportunity of extra funds from the [ORG] comes with a huge challenge: namely, to ensure that
the [ORG] grant funds together with own funds are used in a manner that helped [LOCATION] converge to the [LOCATION]
standard of living. At roughly 30 percent of the average GDP per capita for [LOCATION]25 (in PPP terms),
[LOCATION]’s starting position is not enviable. It also faces a demographic challenge. [LOCATION]’s population
is declining at almost one percent per year, its labor participation rate of 5 1 percent and its employment
rate of 46 percent are among the lowest in [LOCATION],’ and the productivity of its labor force is low.
Analysis in the recent Country Economic Memorandum on [LOCATION] ([ORG] 2005) shows that
assuming a rise of its participation rate from 50 to 70 percent by 2015 and that GDP per capita can be
made to grow at 5.5 percent per year for the next twenty years, [LOCATION] will reach two thirds oft he EU25
average GDP by 2025. The problem is that while there are many countries that manage to grow at those
rates for a decade, the number that achieves that for two consecutive decades drops off precipitously, and
three decades ofs uch rapid growth in a row is a rare event. In the face of such odds, errors will be costly.
Hence the huge challenge.
1.4 The magnitude of the remaining challenge may well sound as a discouraging message after
[LOCATION] has done so well in the past few years. As Table 1.1 shows, GDP growth has been in the 4-5
percent per year range for the past 7 years. Its pace has moved into the 5-6 percent range in 2004, and
seems to have kept up so far during 2005. The unemployment rate has been falling, and as ofN ovember
2005 was approaching ten percent, although this should be tempered by the realization that this is in the
context of very low labor participation and employment rates. Private investment has been growing
strongly, in part driven by foreign direct investment. The budget is in balance, the underlying structural
budget is also in a good shape, primary budget is strongly positive, reserves are strong, and public debt
has fallen precipitously relative to GDP and is now well within the Maastricht bounds. As a result,
[LOCATION]’s sovereign debt ratings have strengthened to investment grade. Perhaps the one dark cloud on
the immediate horizon is the current account deficit, which is currently running at over 14 percent ofG DP
on an annual basis. This could present a problem, if foreign direct investment inflows were to slow down
sharply. For this reason the authorities need to continue to be vigilant to protect the growth momentum
that has been achieved through prudent fiscal policy.

1.5 The huge challenge faced by [LOCATION] is thus one of sustaining rapid growth for some decades
into the future in the face of a difficult demographic, labor participation and labor productivity situation.
To get a perspective on the magnitude of the challenge, one need to consider the fact that there were on
average about four Bulgarians supported by each employee under a labor contract in the private sector in
2004, or, put another way; 1.37 million employees under contract in the private sector were supporting
7.76 million Bulgarians. The group supported includes all the children, some 740,000 workers in the
public sector (of whom 467,000 were employed in the general government), pensioners, and about half of
the working age population that is not formally employed for one reason or another. Even adding the
employees employed in public enterprises to those in the private sector would not change the picture
substantially. This lopsidedness shows how weak the private sector is in [LOCATION]. Hence, it is essential
that strong measures are taken and sustained to help the employment in the private sector grow, and that
the productivity of all workers, private and public, is raised rapidly and continuously for many years to

I. OBJECTIVE OF THE REPORT
1.6 This report aims to assist the [LOCATION] government in exploring their options for the optimal use
of both expected EU grants and [LOCATION]’s own funds in the pursuit of enhanced economic growth and
development. The analysis focuses on the [ORG] commitments to [LOCATION] in the first three years of
accession, estimates the projected net [ORG] grant flows to the country and the budget, and highlights
options to accommodate them into the budget (Chapters 1-2). In addition, the report explores the
priorities for funding, and implications of the forthcoming resource flows in four areasdnhancing the
skills oft he labor force; agriculture; roads; and environmental protection (Chapter 3-6). These areas were
selected because they will either receive the bulk of forthcoming [ORG] funds or, if used wisely, are most
likely to maximize the longer term positive impact on productivity growth.

1.8 The projected [ORG] grant funds have two distinct effects: first, there is the overall effect on the
balance ofp ayments oft he country; and second, there is the effect on the national budget. The distinction
between net flows to the country and net flows to the budget is significant. Flows to the country could
potentially have an impact on the country akin to those of the so called Dutch disease. Macroeconomic
policy must therefore manage them in a way that does not add to inflationary pressures. If they can be
channeled to activities that develop the supply side of the economy, they will help speed up convergence
of [LOCATION] to the [LOCATION]25 GDP per capita, which is the key objective. Net transfers to the budget are part
of these overall net flows to the country. If added to the budget without any expenditure restructuring,
they would by definition increase the level of public expenditures and worsen the budget balance by the
amount of the net transfer. However, if absorbed in the budget through restructuring of existing
expenditures, concerns on macroeconomic policy management would lessen and there might be other
potentially beneficial effects, as will be discussed later in the report.
1.9 The calculation of net transfers to the country is straightforward, although with some initial
complexities because the direct payments to farmers are made retroactively. By contrast, the estimation
. of the budgetary impact on a cash basis has to make allowances for the way the different [ORG] funds are
incorporated (or not) into the budget. In the calculation oft he net budgetary effect, several considerations
were taken into account: (i)B ulgaria’s contributions to the [ORG] budget; (ii)c o-financing requirements,
assuming that all scheduled payments will actually be made; (iii)re quirement for pre-financing of the
Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)-related direct payments to the agricultural producers3; (iv) the fact
that there is no additionality requirement for the [ORG]; and (v) potential savings from
agricultural subsidies paid prior to accession, if there is no topping-up of the CAP direct payments. To
capture the macroeconomic implications, pre-financing of CAP direct payments to agricultural producers
and structural actions are included in the calculation of the net effect on the national b~dget.I~t is
worthwhile noting, however, that when determining the formal compliance with the Maastricht budget
criteria, pre-financing of CAP direct payments will not be taken into account in the budget deficit

the budget on a cash basis is softened considerably by a budget advance from the [ORG] (reflected in the

111. EFFECTIVE USE OF [ORG] GRANTF UNDSL:E SSOFNRSO M EU COUNTRIES
1.16 Experience of [ORG] shows that structural and cohesion funds can play an important role in
accelerating the catch-up process (see Meth-Cohn and Shields (2005)), although success depends on a
number of factors. Meth-Coh and Shields offer four lessons on how to use the [ORG] funds effectively:
a. Develop a clear strategic vision at all levels. In this respect the development of the
National Development Plan aims at the alignment of strategies at national, regional, and
local levels to ensure that funds have a cumulative and long-term impact on growth, rather
that being allocated on one-off projects.
b. Encourage public-private partnerships to ensure high-quality and commercially viable
projects that at the same time promote public sector goals. Cooperation between the private
sector and the public bodies allows the public sector to overcome its budget constraints and
focus more on the profitability and viability oft he projects. Private companies, at the same
time, gain possibilities to share risk and take on more business.
c. Obtain involvement in theprojects at the municipal level. The [ORG] may expect a simpler,
more transparent and decentralized system from 2007 onwards. Higher participation of
local governments is considered crucial for management oft he projects, and municipalities
could get actively involved in seeking private funds to co-finance [ORG] funds.
d. Take into account the inherent inflexibility of [ORG] funds. EU regulations and national
authorities impose tight restrictions on the use of funds under the structural actions. With
the exception of the grants available for small and medium-size enterprises, private
companies generally benefit from [ORG] funds only indirectly, for example through public-
private partnerships.
1.17 In the context of these four recommendations, [LOCATION] faces important challenges related to
effective utilization of the EU funds. These are related to the improvement of the budget procedures,
restructuring of public spending to accommodate EU-related expenditures, and enhancing of the
institutional capacity in the country:
1.18 First, at the national level, there is an acute need for reform of budget procedures to maximize the
absorption capacity for the [ORG] funds. The ongoing introduction of a program budgeting approach is a
positive step in this direction. However, significant further efforts would need to be made to make the use
of EU funds as efficient as possible.
1.19 Second, Table 1.2 indicates that the deterioration oft he national budget balance would stem from
increased expenditures, rather than from lowered revenues. Taking into account the already high share of
the government in the economy (government expenditures-to-GDP ratio amounted to 40 percent in 2004,
as will be discussed in Chapter 2), it is essential to improve the ability of the government to substitute
existing expenditures with [ORG] unds. Fiscal space needs to be made (i)fo r expanding EU-related capital
expenditures (and the national co-financing of these expenditures), (ii)f or liquidity reasons (like pre-
financing of direct payments to farmers in the first year of accession) and (iii)f or the national
contribution to the [ORG] budget. The need for restructuring is even more acute in the light of expanding
social spending, related to the rapidly aging population, and high unemployment.
1.20 Third, actual [ORG] transfers to the national budget depend on the absorption and institutional
capacity, that is, on the extent to which a member-state is capable of spending the structural fund
resources allocated to it in an efficient and effective way. As stated in the [ORG]’s “Assessment of the
Municipal and District Capacities for Absorption of the EU Structural and Cohesion Funds’’ (2004),
absorption capacity has three main dimensions: macroeconomic situation (the overall level of
development), co-financing capability, and administrative capacity. Preliminary assessments reveal an
institutional capacity that varies significantly among the [LOCATION] line ministries. If the shlls of their
personnel are not upgraded, the absorption off unds might suffer.
1.2 1 Unfortunately, since experience ofn ew [ORG] member states with [ORG] funds is so recent, there is not

Funds that flow more or less “automatically”, such as advance payments under the structural and rural

1.22 If effectively used, [ORG] funds should contribute to economic growth both in the short and in the
long run. In the short run they would create higher domestic demand. In the long term, if invested in the
physical and human capital improvements in the country, they have the potential ofm aking an important
contribution to economic growth from the supply side. This demand vs. supply side impact distinction
may be particularly important in the case of funds for agriculture. Pillar 1 spending in agriculture (market
support measures and direct payments to farmers) has its impact mainly on the demand side. Pillar 2
spending in agriculture (rural development) has the potential of making a permanent contribution of
strengthening the supply side oft he economy.
1.23 [ORG] funds have proven to be most effective when put to use under broad, well-defined strategic
programs. Perhaps the biggest task facing [LOCATION] today is to develop such a program (for example in
the form of the National Development Plan), and then back it with real money through a well-thought out
Medium Term Fiscal Framework (MTFF) for 2007-09 and the corresponding annual budgets that reflect
the MTFF. Moreover, the MTFF would need to focus on the [ORG] funds that could engender growth-
oriented activities, while containing and, if possible, reducing the public expenditure envelope relative to
GDP over time.
1.24 The next chapter will explore the fiscal challenge [LOCATION] is facing, and options to make space in
the national budget for the expected transfers from the [ORG].
2. POLICIES FOR GROWTH AND FISCAL SUSTAINABILITY
2.1 The government has three choices to accommodate the expected EU grant funds. The first one
would be to add the funds to the budget without any fiscal adjustment, and let public expenditures
increase as a share ofG DP. This would initially worsen the budget balance. The second option would be
to accommodate them through full fiscal adjustment equivalent to the projected budgetary impact of [LOCATION]
funds-that is, about two percentage points of GDP. The third option would be to accommodate the [LOCATION]
funds over time through a mixture of fiscal adjustment and economic growth.
2.2 Of these options, accommodating the expected [LOCATION] funds to the budget through full fiscal
adjustment would be recommended both from the point ofv iew of increasing growth in the long run and
to make space for, say, further reductions in payroll taxes. The first option is ruled out, since the
[LOCATION] government has expressed a clear intent to keep their public expenditures at their current level
of4 0 percent of GDP or below. Following the third option would be risky, since GDP growth cannot be
controlled by the government, and budget plans should be made on the basis of prudent assumptions
about revenue growth.
2.3 This chapter explores the fiscal challenge presented by the second option: whether full fiscal
adjustment would be feasible. It also begins to explore options to make space in the national budget for
the expected [ORG] funds. The chapter, after presenting the main outlines of [LOCATION]’s national budget (by
sector/function), goes on to analyze what the appropriate size ofB [LOCATION]’s government might be given its
level of development, and where the savings to reduce the size ofg overnment might be found.

2.6 When viewed through the lens of “dependency” ratios mentioned in Chapter 1--each employee in
the formal private sector supporting at least three other Bulgarians--it becomes clear why the public sector
needs to be made more efficient and probably smaller relative to GDP than it is now. A restrained public
sector would reduce the burden on the private sector and thus help make it stronger. At the moment,
public expenditures in [LOCATION] are about 40 percent of GDP. It is a level that the [LOCATION] authorities
would like to sustain and preferably reduce, while keeping the budget in balance. This would allow them
to retain some fiscal flexibility in the face ofp otential negative shocks, the most threatening of which in
the short run may well come from the side of the current account, although pressures from politically
powerful sectors for increased expenditures could also play their part.
2.7 Public spending at 40 percent of GDP implies a heavy tax burden on households and private
business, as high taxes and contributions are practically unavoidable at such a spending level. This is a
concern because high taxes generally distort economic incentives and transfer resources from the private
sector to the public sector, which is typically less efficient, and thereby reduce the growth potential of a
country.’ While some studies of relatively advanced economies have found no impact of taxation on
growth, most find a negative effect and no study has shown positive growth effects ofh igh taxation.*
2.8 Not all taxes have equally distortionary effects, however. High marginal tax rates on income and
profit are more distortionary than proportional taxes on consumption such as the value-added tax. For
this reason tax reforms often aim to increase economic efficiency by broadening the tax base, while
lowering marginal rates on consumption and saving, or by replacing income taxes with proportional sales
taxes.

2.10 Ultimately, the determination of the size of government boils down to estimating the marginal
cost of raising the necessary public funds, and comparing it with the social return of each particular
project financed with public funds. Ifa project does not yield a social return greater than the marginal
cost of funds, it is not worth raising the taxes to finance it. The problem is that it is practically impossible
to calculate the social rate ofr eturn ofa ll projects that are to be financed, and estimating the marginal cost
of funds is fraught with problems. Nevertheless, evidence from various studies suggests that the marginal
cost of funds tends to be greater, the higher the existing level of tax revenue, the greater the use of
corporate and personal taxes to raise revenue, the higher the administrative costs of raising the revenue,
the higher the taxes on exports, and the larger the informal sector in the economy (Warlters and [PERSON]
2005). With tax revenues in [LOCATION] at levels about 40 percent of GDP, and given its relatively small
formal private sector and a large informal sector, marginal cost of funds is likely to be high and above
social returns for a whole range of programs or projects that are currently funded by the public sector.
[PERSON] and [PERSON] (2000), in fact, argue that state spending need be no more than one-third of
nominal GDP in order to achieve the most important social and political objective^.^

2.14 The question now becomes which public expenditures can be reduced without reducing growth.
There are the classic core functions of the public sector, such as law and order, protection of property,
sound money, defense, or public health. These services have the common property that they would be
provided in less than desired quantities for the country as a whole, if they were left to the individuals to
provide them. There are a variety of reasons why such market failures would occur, and it is important
that the reasons for failure of under-provision of any one good or service be understood before action is
taken. The country might, for example, believe that it needs many university graduates, and that the
poorer but talented students may not be able to attend the university or some technical school. This,
however, does not imply that such training should be free for all, or even for a substantial portion of the
relevant population, or that it has to be provided by a public institution. Since much of the benefit of
higher education is typically appropriated by the students in the form of higher salaries, part of the

2.15 Every program in the public budget should be subjected to a scrutiny with the intent that what
cannot assuredly be done best, in the sense of “in sufficient amount and efficiently”, through the public
sector, should be left to the private sector. This is much easier said than done in part because publicly
provided or financed goods and services have a range of outcomes that are hard to weigh against each
other, and hence makmg choices among them becomes an intensely political matter. Yet public funds are
limited and trade-offs must be made. It is, however, unclear how one can sensibly trade off
improvements that promote different sorts of well being (mortality, morbidity, clean air, clean water, or
security) with those that contribute more directly to growth (roads or marketable skills). Nothing
definitive is known in this area, other than that a whole array ofg oods and services will be needed and/or
desired by the population.
2.16 One way of tackling the problem is to examine public expenditures by sector and look for
inefficiencies. Some countries have organized their public expenditures into programs aimed at achieving
certain measurable results. Those that have done it for some years have a track record of being able to
relate the input costs of these programs (expenditures) with the outputs and outcomes, and they can then
compare these results with other countries that have attempted to do the same so as to see whether they
are spending their money effectively. [LOCATION] is just moving in the direction of program-based and
results-oriented budget management, and thus it will be some time before the above approach can be
applied.
2.17 Another way oft ackling the problem is to look at the share ofG DP that is being spent in a certain
sector, and compare it to other countries. If similar amounts ofm oney are achieving very different results
or similar outcomes are the result of rather different levels of expenditures, then there are presumably
grounds for an examination oft he causes oft his discrepancy, and thus a basis for a correction.

IV. CONCLUSION
2.33 This section has tried to establish that there is ample room for [LOCATION] to reduce the size of its
government, and thus accommodate the likely level of [ORG] transfers that will come after the expected
accession without having to reduce growth. [LOCATION]’s public expenditures in the aggregate seem to be
between 3 and 8 percent of GDP higher than would be necessary to keep pace with the growth of a
sample of rapidly growing countries, while improving many of the outcomes. The fact that the private
sector is still weak and is carrying a large tax burden also argues for a smaller state. Finally, an
examination ofp ublic expenditures in terms off unctional and economic classifications suggests that there
should be room for expenditure reductions relative to GDP in health, social benefits, and size oft he civil
service, defense, and security. The envelope for education may be about right at the moment, but like in
other sectors, there is a need for pressing on with the reforms to improve outcomes. As will be argued in
the next chapter, reforms in education, because of its relevance to long-term rapid growth, are crucial to
the successful (growth-promoting) absorption oft he [ORG] funds.
2.34 Reductions will take political resolve. Change means losses for some of the vested interests, so
there is bound to be resistance. The challenge is to be able to convince people that a large majority will
gain from well designed changes. [LOCATION]’s government has gone through difficult changes in the past
15 years and in the past few years has finally seen some fruits of these efforts. It would be important not
to lose the unique opportunity of substantial grants from the [ORG] to help it weather further reforms. This
chapter suggested some areas where greater efficiency in the use off unds could help [LOCATION] maintain its
momentum. It is crucial that the same discipline that has been suggested for the various categories of
expenditure also be applied to the funds that will be coming from the [ORG]. The areas that are likely to
receive the most funds are agriculture, transport, human resource development, and environment. For this
reason the remaining chapters (Chapters 3-6) of this report focus on how the expenditures in these areas
could best be targeted on programs that would help raise productivity and sustain the convergence of
[LOCATION]’s GDP per capita to that ofE U25.

3.11 There is a need to eliminate inefficiencies in the education system, and raise the quality of
education and school participation rates. Measures needed include the consolidation of schools and
higher education institutions” in light of rapidly declining student cohorts to increase the student-teacher

graduates with needed skills are produced. Unwieldy bureaucracy continues to be a feature oft he system
and administrative reforms have been difficult to achieve. Also, there is need to consider of further
engaging the private sector in the delivery ofe ducation at different levels.
3.12 Unless determined moves are undertaken to address such inefficiencies in the outdated

the system. The [LOCATION] system has been through a great deal oft ravail over the past fifteen years. It is
a relatively short time-span to absorb so much change and meet so many new demands. It may well be
that the stage is now being reached when reform measures can be undertaken with greater confidence for
success than was hitherto the case.
