be catalysts for regional development. In [LOCATION], the scheme of [ORG] proved to
be a great success in early 1970s, and the colleges are now called [ORG]. They have
benefited from [ORG] and from the [ORG], and regarded by the [ORG] as one of the
[ORG] success stones in education.
3.32 Rationalization of Universities: [LOCATION] has a large number of universities set up during the
Communist era, which are now incommensurate with the needs of a declining population and with the
type of university education required. Though rationalization of universities to enhance quality and
efficiency has been planned for years, little progress has been made. Yet it is imperative that this issue is
tackled before any further investments are made in the university system. Rationalization is likely to be
costly in the short run, but the long-term benefits can be expected to outweigh the costs. It is important
that [LOCATION] engages in serious planning for university rationalization so that [ORG] could be enlisted to
support this move. Such funds could provide the needed “lubrication” for the change.
3.33 Improving University Infrastructure: In the context ofu niversity rationalization, [ORG] support
could be solicited for infrastructure improvements in universities. There is a great need to build up library
holdings, upgrade science laboratories, and improve ICT equipment. However, a proposal for
infrastructure investment would only have credibility if it supplemented rationalization of universities.
B. Improving the Quality of Basic and Secondary Education
3.34 There are seven ideas for projects to improve quality oft he education system under [ORG]:
3.35 Curriculum Reform: Curriculum Reform continues to be a major policy concern. While
progress has been made and reforms are in place up to the fourth school year, there is a need to speed up
the reform and sequence the vocational elements better with general education. There is also a need to
strengthen the staff expertise involved in the design ofn ew syllabi. The new [ORG], which
is a representative advisory body, plays a useful role in fostering a sense of ownership of curricula
changes. Proposals in this area would need to spell out the objectives, degree of progress, agencies
involved, significance for reform, and costing.
3.36 Assessment Reform: There would be a need to reform the education assessment and evaluation
system. Lack of external assessment oft he school system is a long standing problem, and little progress
has been made owing to tradition, old practices, and some social opposition. The [ORG] was established in [DATE] as a service centre for MES, but would benefit fi-om further expertise
to achieve its aims. An external exam may now be taken at the end oft he fourth year (Stage ofP rimary),
but the exam is not mandatory. There is also discussion about an external assessment at the end of the
next stage of schooling, either at the end of the seventh or eight year, but it is unclear whether this exam
would be made mandatory. The assessment situation at the end of secondary schooling is most
problematic. An external Matura examination was to be introduced in 2003, but that has not happened
yet. According to the law, the exam needs to be operative from the school year 2006 onwards, but also
that seems uncertain. Introduction oft he Matura exam would, however, be ofp ivotal importance for the
quality oft he education system, and it should cover generic pupil competencies as well as specific subject
competencies. Depending on the quality of national policy on the matter, [ORG] support for assessment
reform, and particularly for the implementation oft he Matura test would be well targeted.
3.37 Support for Modern Language Teaching in Schools: Precedents exist for seeking [ORG] funding
for the extension of modern language teaching at various levels of the education system. With the brain
drain ofy oung language teachers out of the school system, there may also be justification to temporarily
provide modem language courses for in-career teachers.
3.38 Training of Trainers (T.O.T .): Initial Teacher Education: Weaknesses in the existing initial
and in service teacher education were identified by [ORG] as a major constraint to the transformation of
the [LOCATION] school system ([ORG] 2004). Since then a law on the reform of initial teacher education
has been prepared, and is due for implementation early in 2006. The content oft he law is consistent with
the [ORG] recommendations, and emphasizes practical experience of student teachers and the use of
internships. Resources to finance the reform would be needed.
3.39 [ORG] established a [ORG] in
2005, which is to have a major role in in-career teacher development. The center will have a network of
regional branches, and there are precedents for [ORG] support for such an entity. The
integration of ICT within teaching and learning in the schools is at the moment the priority. The in-career
work should also be seen to be in support of the curriculum and pedagogic reforms. Also, school based
in-service education for school staff, in particular in vocational education schools, would be needed.
3.40 Staff Development for the Inspectorate: There is also a need to reform the regional school
inspectorate, and shift its role to promoting quality teaching and curriculum reform. It would also be
desirable to equip the inspectorate so that it can engage in whole school evaluations based on best
international practice.
3.41 Retraining of School Directors: In line with the policy decision to devolve more responsibility
and discretion to school directors, it is important that directors get re-training. School directors are key
for improving teaching, learning, and assessment in schools. In addition to extended professional
responsibilities, 660 school directors already manage a devolved school budget, and the plan is to extend
this to further schools in the years ahead. Budget management calls for financial management skills and
improved administration, though. Training courses in these areas have been supported by [ORG] funds in
other countries.
C. Improving Quality in Higher Education
3.42 Six proposals to improve quality ofh igher education under [ORG] would be as follows:
3.43 Career Guidance Services: The Employment Strategy [PHONE] emphasizes the importance of
career guidance in secondary education, but EU support could also be elicited for career guidance
provision at higher education. At present, there is a great imbalance in the subjects taken by students at
university. For example, of the students engaged in Bachelor and Masters Courses in 2002, 57.2 percent
were studying the social sciences, economic management and administration, and technical sciences, but
only 5.9 percent were studying the natural, physical, or mathematical sciences and informatics. There is a
need to develop good information on employment/career prospects for students, and guidance on where
their aptitudes might best be suited. This would need to be linked to data on labor market trends and
needs. A career guidance service could be ofm ajor benefit to students, but also to the labor market in the
longer term, Career guidance services would be most relevant in multi-faculty universities and, over
time, guidance personnel in a number of such institutions could build up a valuable data base. Such
services are likely to be viewed favorably by [ORG].
3.44 Graduate Conversion Courses: Owing to mismatch between the courses offered and the needs
of a changing labor market, [LOCATION] pioneered a scheme of conversion courses for graduates, which
obtained [ORG] support. It permitted graduates in fields such as the social sciences and humanities to
engage in one or two-year courses called Advanced Technological Skills, which allowed them qualify in
subject areas of technological competence (for example, I.T. qualifications). Such an approach could be
beneficial also to [LOCATION].
3.45 Quality Assurance: The [ORG] ([ORG]) issued in 2005
a new policy document on quality assurance, which provides a framework for action in this area. The
framework is supported by the university rectors, and [ORG] has established links with the [ORG] ([ORG]). The [ORG] policy and procedures are in line with good international
practice. [ORG] has made good progress on Institutional Accreditation and Program Evaluation, and
procedures exist for the publication ofN [ORG] reviews. However, the agency would need further financial
and staffing support to engage international experts in its review panels to promote transparency.
3.46 Staff Development for Teaching Staff in Higher Education: Universities in most countries have
recognized the importance of staff development programs, and built these into their quality improvement
policies. Staff development is particularly important when past practices are to be changed. When a
system is also suffering from a brain drain of bright young academic staff, staff development programs
gain further importance to help staff to cope with new curricula, new styles oft eaching and learning, and
new forms of assessment. Without such programs, the quality assessment process would unlikely yield
the desired outcomes, and hence using structural funds for this purpose would be valuable.
3.47 Staff Development for University Leadership: Improving the quality of university leadership,
both for academic and administrative purposes, would also be needed. At present, Rectors are chosen
through elections by their academic colleagues, and may have limited leadership and administrative
experience. They would benefit from being exposed to appropriate courses and experiences among peers,
such as those organized by [ORG] and [ORG]. Since
universities enjoy considerable autonomy, unless their leaders are exposed to new management styles and
best practice in modem universities, reforms in higher education will be further delayed. External
stakeholder representation in university governing bodies would be needed, and university leaders would
need to develop the skills to liaise with external bodies, including the solicitation of external funding.
3.48 A Distance Education Service: Distance education is still not well developed in [LOCATION].
Working in conjunction with the EU-PHARE program for distance education ([PHONE]), the [ORG], involving an association of 20 [LOCATION] universities, was set up within
the [ORG]. With the termination of the PHARE project, funding for the center also
disappeared, though. In [DATE] the [ORG] issued a decree on the Organization of
Distance Learning in Higher Schools, by which distance education can deliver all the traditional degrees
of a university to distance education students. Up to 30 percent of the courses will involve personal
attendance for tutorial purposes. The standards of provision are set by [ORG]. Even though the [ORG] is
less enthusiastic about distance education than before, the government may want to seek [ORG] support for
it.
D. Social Inclusion and Equal Opportunity
3.49 To promote social inclusion and equal opportunity, the following five proposals could be
considered for [ORG] support:
3.50 Program for School Drop-outs: In 2005, [ORG] instituted a new program for unemployed youth
who had dropped out of school. Also in 2005, a survey was undertaken on the reasons for drop-out.
Currently, less than 70 percent of age cohort completes secondary education, but detailed analysis of
attendance figures suggests that the share may be lower than the official statistics indicate. The problem
is most acute in areas of significant socio-economic disadvantage, and there is a risk that the drop-outs, by
falling on social safety nets, will become a drain on the society. The Employment Strategy [PHONE]
expresses a serious concern, and suggests a range of interventions to ameliorate it. Social inclusion is
also an [ORG] policy concern, and [ORG] would be geared to assist national initiatives of this type. The
government would need to prepare a program building on the initiatives underway.
3.51 School Completion Program: A school completion program is designed to prevent drop-outs
before they happen, focusing on pupils at risk of dropping out. A number of actions can be taken to
prevent dropping out, including counseling, provision ofe xtra resources and facilities such breakfast, free
books, organized study time, and extra curricular activities, which help the vulnerable pupil view the
school in a more positive light. [ORG] is already implementing programs that provide a glass ofm ilk and
breakfast at school, and textbooks, school aids, and accessories for specific categories of children. In
[LOCATION], [ORG] supported a School Completion Program.
3.52 Career Counseling and Guidance for Youth: The Employment Strategy indicates that “Centers
for Information and Career Development” for youth are planned, which is supported by the PHARE
program, “Clearing the Pathway to Employment for Youth”. A provision for such career guidance is
essential to reach youth and long-term unemployment. If based on existing initiatives in this area, the
[ORG] support could legitimately be sought.
3.53 Second Chance and Back-to-Education Initiatives: Second chance and back to education
initiatives are directed to the long-term unemployed, whose education levels are often low. [ORG] has
initiated schemes to encourage employers to engage unemployed, and to provide and/or facilitate training
for them. In [LOCATION], the Vocational Training Opportunity Scheme was designed to attract unemployed
people back to education and training. It began as a pilot scheme in 1989, and continues to operate with
the support of [ORG]. The scheme provides courses up to two years, focusing on vocational skills along
with enterprise training, personal development, job search, skills and general studies. Course delivery is
integrative and flexible, with a strong emphasis on core skills-literacy, numeracy, communication and
new technology. Experience built up over sixteen years of its existence could be helpful for [LOCATION].
Funds could also be available to assist general adult literacy schemes.
3.54 Assistance Schemes for Certain Categories of Students: [ORG] support could be obtained to assist
a range of student schemes, including: (i)s chemes for students with disabilities to participate in higher
education; (ii)a ssistance to disadvantaged students to gain access to higher education courses through
special provision made between schools in severely disadvantaged areas and universities; (iii)s tudent
hardship funds which are used when students encounter unexpected hardship through bereavement,
accidents, or loss of employment by parents; (iv) education and training programs for groups such as
’
Roma children. [LOCATION] government is planning to launch a new national training program for Roma
on literacy and vocational training in 2006. In [LOCATION], a roughly equivalent social group is known as
Travelers, and [ORG] has supported programs designed with their needs in mind and which, hopefully, lead
to engagement in mainstream education.
E. Addressing Skills Needs and Vocational Training
3.55 In order to promote lifelong learning and strengthen vocational training, the following ideas
might be considered for support under [ORG]:
3.56 Training of Trainers: Vocational education and training (VET) in [LOCATION] has benefited from a
variety of [ORG] schemes. Yet, there is still a need for the in-career training of teaching staff, linked to the
continuing reform of VET curricula and pedagogic practice. The inclusion of practical, apprenticeship
style experience should form part ofs uch reform. A structured three-year program might be appropriate.
3.57 Lifelong Learning (Continuing Vocational Training): An inter-ministerial group developed in
2005 a “National Strategy for Continuing Vocational Training, [PHONE]”. This is a major step to
promote lifelong learning, and consistent with the [ORG] policy, though successkl implementation of the
strategy will take time and effort. Elements of the program could be packaged in line with common
priorities of [LOCATION] and [LOCATION] policy to be eligible for [ORG] support.
3.58 A National Qualification Framework: According to the [ORG] policy, in the wake of the
[LOCATION] objectives, a framework of national qualifications is to be developed to set out a level of
award, in relation to other qualifications, for all accredited courses available to the population. This
framework would facilitate recognition for various forms of work and academic experience. Such a
framework would bring clarity and coordination to diverse features of an education system. It is a
particularly useful mechanism for the promotion of a lifelong learning policy. The National
Qualifications Framework ofI reland, whose establishment benefited from [ORG] Structural Funds could be a
useful model to follow.
3.59 Quality Assurance in VET: The [ORG]
([ORG]) has made good progress in establishing standards and setting up licensing procedures for adult
vocational training centers. [ORG] operates on a tripartite partnership between [ORG], [ORG], and the
employers. It has successfully liaised with relevant international agencies such as the [ORG], and played a crucial role in ensuring quality and standards in VET. Inclusion of further
partners, and development of a monitoring system of vocational education centers would be welcome,
though. The injection of EU funding to an Agency which is already progressing well would likely yield
returns.
3.60 Improving Data on Labor Market Needs: Data on labor market needs is inadequate in [LOCATION].
In 2005, a new program was planned, with bilateral support from [LOCATION], to establish a comprehensive
survey of employers about their labor market needs, which hopefully will provide information to the
National Statistics Office. The [LOCATION] government could seek support for the establishment of a
standing [ORG] to continuously monitor the changing employment needs of the labor
market and feed these into policy agencies. Such an [ORG], working in association with the
[ORG], which reports on competitiveness issues for the [LOCATION] economy, has
proved to be highly beneficial in the case ofI reland.
F. Research, Technology, Innovation
3.61 MES and the [ORG] prepared a Position Paper entitled “Towards a Science,
Technology and Innovation Policy for Bulgaria” in 2002. While the paper contained valuable
recommendations, it was never implemented. On research funding, the paper proposed a peer review
structure by mixed teams ofB ulgarian and foreign researchers, with a shift from input to output financing.
The [ORG] has agreed that funding for basic research will be provided, while maintaining
a balance with other priorities and activities in the research area. The [ORG]] [ORG] may want to
seek [ORG] support for the setting up of a competitive funding scheme for promotion of research and
innovation, perhaps along the lines of the Irish Program for Research in Third Level Institutions. This
would be consistent with the 2002 Position Paper, and lay the basis for a new tradition of research
funding, in line with aims for the [ORG].
V. CONCLUSIONS
3.62 There is an urgent need to modernize the [LOCATION] education system to ensure the country has a
highly skilled and productive labor force that can make the catching up with the EU standards ofl iving a
reality. This is critical since while the level of education is steadily increasing in [LOCATION] countries,
participation in higher education and education outcomes have been declining [LOCATION].
3.63 The forthcoming [ORG] accession provides an unprecedented opportunity for the [LOCATION]
government to move the planned education reforms forward, by providing incentives and leverage for
change as well as external finding. At the same time, the demographic change and declining age cohorts
provide an opportunity to improve the efficiency of public education spending, and ensure it is spent
effectively on improving the quality of education and training of reduced numbers of students. The
government would need to take advantage oft he period prior to accession to make this happen.
3.64 The government would be well-advised not to increase public spending on education as a share of
GDP, but rather to seek efficiency gains within the existing resource envelope. This is important, since
public spending on education is already on a level comparable to many CEE countries, and spending per
student has been steadily increasing, yet education outcomes remain well below CEE levels. Provided
credible reform is taken, maintaining the existing level of public spending on education as a share of
GDP, including possible [ORG] funds, would be warranted.*' While consolidation of spending is
recommended in many other sectors (see chapter 2), given the importance of education for promotion of
labor productivity a differential treatment is recommended on education, assuming reforms proceed.
3.65 The reform measures needed would include gradual consolidation of schools, universities, and
vocational colleges in light of declining age cohorts to increase student-teacher ratios and release funds
for upgrading of curriculum, textbooks, and facilities. The savings from school consolidation should be
retained within the sector, and used to finance quality improvements. To raise the quality of education,
there is a need to undertake a curriculum reform, develop better teaching materials, improve teacher
training, open University administration to outside representatives, and establish periodic national student
assessments to evaluate the impact of education. At the upper secondary and university levels, it is
critical to establish links with the labor markets to ensure students are equipped with skills required in the
market. In a global economy, continuous upgrading of labor skills is increasingly important to stay
competitive, and hence would need to be encouraged. Further engaging the private sector in education
delivery could also be very important.
3.66 The proposals for projects presented in this chapter for possible [ORG] funding, even though, tilted
towards the interface between the education system and the market, form a broad education and human
development reform package consistent with the [LOCATION] education policy. The concerns underpinning the
proposals relate to key policy concerns of the [LOCATION] authorities, such as: (i)im proving the quality of
education; (ii)m odernizing the educational infi-astructure; (iii)i mproving access for all; (iv) reducing
inequalities; (v) promoting social inclusion; (vi) building the capacity of personnel; and (vii) promoting
lifelong learning.
3.67 With careful planning and strong leadership [LOCATION] can achieve its human resource
development goals. The potential is there, but it will not be realized without a great deal of effort. There
is a lot at stake for current and future generations ofB ulgarians.
2o It is important to note that above considerations mainly apply to education, and not the wider field of human
resources development. In light of the present labor market situation with low activity and employment rates
particularly for low or unskilled labor, and excess demand for skilled labor, resolute action would need to be taken
to raise the low level ofp articipation in life long learning, which may require additional funding.

4.8 The 2003 CAP reform contains a Single Farm Payment Scheme (SFPS) to be introduced in the
[LOCATION] starting in 2005. SFPS is based on direct payments that [ORG] farmers had been receiving under
certain support programs during a reference period (2000 to 2002). As [LOCATION] (like most new member
states) did not operate CAP-conforming direct payments during the reference period, and due to the high
administrative requirements for implementing direct payments on an SFPS basis, [LOCATION], like all new
[ORG] member states, has been given the option to choose the Single Area Payment Scheme (SAPS)
insteadz6. However, using the SAPS rather than the new SFPS approach is limited to the first three years
of membership, with the possibility of two one-year extensions. Before the new member states can
change over to SFPS, they must demonstrate that they have the management and control systems in place
to do so. If they do not have these systems in place by 2008 (201 1 for [LOCATION]), they will continue under
SAPS, but their aid percentage will be frozen at 50 percent oft he [ORG] level.

payment funds2' available in the calendar year, divided by the eligible utilized agricultural areazs.

11. ANALYSISO F THE IMPACTS OF INTRODUCING THE CAP IN [LOCATION]
4.14 As outlined in the previous section, CAP implementation in [LOCATION] raises a chain of important
strategic decisions to be evaluated and taken by the Government. A simple but powerful model of the
[LOCATION] agncultural sector has been used to simulate the impact of these potential decisions on the
financial situation of producers and on the state budget.
4.15 The scenarios evaluated reflect the strategic choices to be made by the government, based on the
options negotiated and confirmed in the Act of Accession. The simulations assess the impact of all
relevant combinations of the listed options (see Table 4.3)35. The impact of the various scenarios is
measured against a baseline scenario represented by the pre-accession support environment. The analysis
is performed in both a short-term and a medium-term perspective. Eleven major agncultural products are
considered in the model, namely wheat, barley, grain maize, sunflower, tobacco, potatoes, milk, beef,
pork, poultry, and sheep and goat. These products account for about 70 percent of the value of gross
agricultural production.
4.16 In the model, farmers’ income is determined by the difference between revenues from the sale of
agricultural produce and tradable input costs and by any non-price-related direct monetary transfers
provided to farmers (for example, per-hectare payments to crops or per-head payments to livestock). Any
change in agricultural policies that affects input prices, output prices, or direct monetary transfers (such as
CAP direct payments) translates into changes in the value-added of agricultural production (that is,
farmers’ income). In the medium to long term, the level of production of the various commodities is
responsive to the level of profitability of each commodity. Therefore, changes in value-added will also
lead to changes in total output, further compounding the initial changes in farmers’ income. For each
commodity the extent of the medium- to long-term supply response is refle~ted.~~

Efficiency Considerations of SAPS Payments: Important Caveats
4.33 Without underestimating the social dimension ofe xclusion from direct income support payments,
the role of direct payments in solving agricultural income problems must not be overestimated. Direct
payment schemes such as the SAPS can provide some level ofi ncome stability and help mitigate farmers’
exposure to income risk by guaranteeing a minimum income from farming. They cannot, however,
substitute for the need to raise the productivity and improve the competitiveness ofB ulgarian agriculture.
Increasing productivity and competitiveness remains the only long-term and sustainable solution to
raising agricultural income. Agricultural support schemes targeting specific sectoral adjustment needs,
such as farm consolidation, productivity, or competitiveness-enhancing farm-level investments, would be
better addressed under the CAP Pillar 2 umbrella. Similarly, the application of a direct income support
scheme cannot substitute for the implementation of Pillar 2 measures, such as an (early) retirement
scheme for the agricultural sector.
4.34 In addition, direct income support payments may reduce the incentives for farmers to restructure,
consolidate, and modernize. They may lower incentives for consolidation, because they guarantee a
minimum income from farming, reducing the incentive for unprofitable or elderly farmers to sell or lease

their assets to more productive entrepreneurs. SAPS payments and their effects on land prices or land
rental rates may also make land consolidation more difficult, in particular in a farming environment in
which agricultural credit is not well developed. Evidence from [ORG] member states indicates that support
payments granted on a per hectare basis lead to significant increases in prices for buying, and especially
leasing agricultural land. This will significantly disfavor tenants, slow any consolidation toward more
viable farm sizes, and in effect support to landowners rather than farmers. These tradeoffs between direct
income support payments, and the need for higher productivity and competitiveness point to the need to
clearly separate rural social measures (such as measures to reduce social tensions and provide social
protection in the rural areas) from the major instruments ofa gricultural income support.
4.35 Direct payments may boost the financial sector, and increase the attractiveness of the agriculture
to the banking sector. Experience from the new [ORG] member states shows that banks are assisting farmers
in applying for direct payments and crediting their activities against the guarantee of the secured direct
payment. Though such assistance may lead to a small outflow of funds out of agriculture, it will
strengthen the relationships between the banking sector and agricultural producers, and create necessary
conditions for increased investments in agricultural assets and efficient use oft he direct support.
Targeting Income Disparities through CAP Pillar 2 Funds
4.36 [LOCATION]’s rural sector requires restructuring to make it competitive and efficient. Many of the
new [ORG] member states required such restructuring, but the need is even more pronounced in [LOCATION],
where half of all holdings are less than 0.5 hectare, and another 26 percent are between 0.5 and 1.0
hectares. A recent poverty study found that rural poverty in [LOCATION] had declined. One of the
hypotheses for this somewhat surprising result was that many rural farming households supplement their
fixed pension income with transfers from relatives (mostly their own children) working in towns or
abroad, from household plots, and from renting out part of their land. However, rural/agricultural credit
remains a major problem in [LOCATION]--with important implications for co-financing of investment
proposals. Other issues implied in the rules for state support or access to financial sources (for example,
to document several years of experience in the business, the need to have been active in the specific
activity, the need of some residency status, etc.) have complicated applications of small and starting
companies for investments and state support, and have been sometimes prohibitive for proposals of new
enterprises. However, measures need to be adopted that allow inefficient farms to close down (through
effective early retirement schemes, for example), and obstacles to the expansion of new and more
efficient farming units to be removed.
4.37 Although direct income support measures can maintain or increase sectoral income at pre-

4.49 Topping-Up (Complementary National Direct Payments): Calculations show that the
introduction of SAPS payments to agricultural producers, starting at a level of 25 percent of the EU15
average in 2007, would increase average income of agricultural producers by 19.1 percent already in the
first year ofa ccession. This would suggest that no top-ups are required to maintain and increase average
producer incomes. However, the impact would be uneven across the producers of various agricultural
products. Income from tobacco production would even decline as current direct payments are replaced
with those under CAP. Producers of dairy would also suffer an initial small loss of income, as would
some medium to large-size farmers (50-100 hectares) due to crop-specific effects rather than size effects.
The latter, however, would only be a short-term impact, and turn into income increases in the first year
after accession. It, therefore, does not justify top-ups. Topping up is expensive, competes with other
more productive programs, and establishes a sense of entitlement which makes it politically difficult to
remove it later. Given the arguments in this report on keeping the size of the state in check and on
focusing all new expenditures on improving productivity, topping-up is not the way forward. A different
mechanism of support should be sought if it is necessary for political reasons, perhaps best done through
the financing potentially available under Pillar 2.
4.50 Payment Modalities: If, nevertheless, topping-up is chosen, simulations carried out for this
report suggest that the application of a specific, coupled CNDPs to limited sub-sectors (tobacco) should
be favored over the implementation of broad, sector-spanning top-ups. Moreover, such support should
have a sunset clause. Also, since support to specific products introduces distortions into production
patterns, the form ofC NDPs chosen should be as simple as possible. Support to particular regions or sub-
sectors would best be addressed under Pillar 2 as part of general rural development of a specific region.
This would also fit better into strategic considerations of internal convergence among [LOCATION]’s regions,
and with the expected strategy for rural development in the [LOCATION] in general.
4.5 1 Eligibility Criteria: According to [LOCATION] rules, the minimum parcel size for which payments may
be requested under SAPS is 0.3 ha, and the minimum holding size eligible for support under SAPS is 1.0
ha. [LOCATION] can decide to set the minimum size of eligible area per holding at a level higher than 0.3 ha,
as long as it does not exceed one hectare. Fixing the eligibility threshold at the 1.0 hectare level would
exclude about 76 percent of all farms, but only 6.6 percent of agricultural land in [LOCATION]. Some
preference was noted in the [ORG] for a mixed threshold model of 0.3 ha for intensive
farming and one ha for all others. This is possible, although this report has argued for a single eligibility
criterion of one hectare. In making this decisions the authorities will have to weigh carefully the benefits
of structural change that would be promoted through consolidation of farms into larger more efficient
units, and the reduction of costs stemming from not having to administer the SAPS for very small farms
versus the adjustment costs for the farmers that would retire.
4.52 Transfers among Budgetary Allocations: If [LOCATION] decides to top up, there are two ways to
do it. It can top up the direct payments coming from the [ORG] fi-om its own resources, or it can top them up
by using up to 20 percent oft he monies available under Pillar 2, but it must provide counterpart-financing
of these diversions from Pillar 2 funding from its own resources. The Pillar 2 route is obviously fiscally
less demanding, but it would take funds away from activities that potentially have a much larger impact
on the competitiveness ofB [LOCATION]’s agriculture than direct payments to farmers. Detailed calculations of
the various options are provided in the previous section.
4.53 Efficiency Considerations: Direct payment schemes such as SAPS can provide some level of
income stability, and help mitigate farmers’ exposure to income risk by guaranteeing a minimum income
from farming. Direct support schemes, however, cannot substitute for the need to raise the productivity
and improve the competitiveness of [LOCATION] agriculture. Productivity growth and improved
competitiveness remain the only sustainable solution to agricultural income problems. Agricultural
support schemes targeting specific sectoral adjustment needs, such as farm consolidation, productivity or
competitiveness-enhancing farm-level investments, and diversification to off-farm activities is the way
forward. These can be tailored to the specific needs of the different regions, and it can all be done under
Pillar 2.
4.54 In addition, direct income support payments may reduce the incentives for farmers to restructure,
consolidate, and modernize. Direct income payments may reduce incentives for consolidation, because
they guarantee a minimum income from farming, and therefore reduce the incentive for unprofitable or
older farmers to sell or lease their assets to more productive entrepreneurs. SAPS payments and their
effects on land prices or land rental rates may also make land consolidation more difficult, in particular in
a farming environment in which agricultural credit is not well developed. Evidence from [ORG] member
states indicates that support payments granted on a per hectare basis lead to significant increases in prices
for buying and especially leasing agricultural land. This will significantly disfavor tenants, slow the
consolidation toward more viable farm sizes, and would in effect support land owners rather than farmers.
These trade-offs between direct income support payments, and the need for higher productivity and
competitiveness point to the need to clearly separate rural social measures (such as measures to reduce
social tensions and provide social protection in the rural areas) from the major instruments of agricultural
income support.

Opportunities
5.14 [LOCATION]’s geographic location gives special importance to road transport. Over 70 percent oft he
population of 7.7 million lives in urban areas. The capital [LOCATION] has about 15 percent of the total

another 15 percent. The rest oft he urban population lives mainly in small and medium sized towns. The
density of the population is low compared to other [LOCATION] countries about 71.1 people per square km.
This spatial distribution of the population tends to increase the demand for transport, especially roads.
Over half ofB [LOCATION]’s territory is also sparsely populated hilly or mountainous terrain, which makes the
cost ofc onstructing transport infrastructure higher than in countries with mostly flat terrain.
5.15 [LOCATION]’s increasing links with the [LOCATION] will have an impact on the directions of trade flows and
create new opportunities for road transport. [LOCATION]’s trade flows were previously dominated by the
[LOCATION] because of its links with the CIS, and these flows were served by maritime transport in
the [LOCATION] and by rail. Today, the [LOCATION] is the main trade partner, which is expected to further intensify

transport infrastructure potentially attractive for transit transport to and fi-om other counties. However,
[LOCATION]’s transport infrastructure, particularly roads, was not planned to satisfy such demand.
5.16 The growth of [LOCATION]’s economy will continue to shape transport demand and favor road
transport. Foreign trade has been expanding at a rapid rate and is now growing at close to 15 percent per
year in dollar terms. As a result, freight transport measured in terms oft on-kms increased between 2000
and 2003 by an average 5.5 percent per year for national transport, and by 10.4 percent for international
transport. Most of this increase was carried by road transport, which grew by 14.4 percent per year, while
rail freight decreased by an average 1.6 percent per year. The market share for road transport has
therefore increased to 55 percent ofn ational transport, and to about two thirds for all freight transported in
[LOCATION], including international transport (Table 5.3). The dominance ofr oad transport is still below the
EU15 average where modal shares are 85 percent for road transport and 15 percent for rail. The
proportion of imports and exports handled by road has also increased in the past five years and is
currently at about 15 percent for exports and 22 percent for exports measured in terms oft onnage.
5.17 In countries with levels ofv ehicle ownership similar to that of [LOCATION] (about 270 cars per 1,000
people), the rate of growth of road traffic can be much higher than GDP (the elasticity of demand with
respect to GDP is greater than one-sometimes as high as about 2.0 for car traffic52). Recent trends in
[LOCATION] would suggest an elasticity of about 1.0 because traffic and GDP have grown at a similar pace.
Nevertheless, in the future, international experience would suggest a higher elasticity, particularly as
disposable income increases.
5.18 The deregulation ofr oad freight together with the transformation of the [LOCATION] economy has
had an impact on the modal split in the country. The economy is becoming less dependent on heavy
industries and agriculture. Consequently, the movements ofh eavy and low value cargo, and ofb ulk raw
materials that were mostly carried by rail and water transport, are being reduced and substituted by the
transport of compact high value goods, carried mainly by road transport. The effect of this trend is
important because it has many impacts on the modal split in a competitive market where rail and water
transport mainly cany long-haul heavy “cheap” freight or multi-modal container traffic. As an
illustration, international freight transported by road almost doubled in 2004, although it is not certain if

decreased by about 7 percent since 1992, and it is estimated that by 2010, the population might further
decrease by another 7 percent. At the same time, the population is ageing, with an increase in the group

income. Vehicle ownership is increasing, albeit from a low base with car ownership at 0.27 per capita,

effects of economic growth over the past five years. Intermediate traffic counts carried out since the last

others have an increase. There is no obvious overall increase despite the increase in vehicle ownership-
possibly because many cars are being used mainly for travel within cities, and therefore contribute little to
inter-urban traffic volumes. Regardless of the actual growth oft he economy and income in the past five
years, the standard of living in [LOCATION] has remained low. The income per capita of the population (in
terms ofp urchasing power parity) in [LOCATION] is currently roughly 30 percent oft he [LOCATION] average.
5.21 [LOCATION] has made significant achievements in the past ten years to attain fiscal discipline, and to
keep the size of the state in check. It is unlikely that under these circumstances national resources
committed to public investment in infrastructure can increase by much as a share of GDP. [LOCATION] will
need to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of public expenditures, particularly in road management,
where investments tend to be large. In a situation where the country is faced with significant need for
basic public infrastructure combined with the challenge of improving competitiveness, the Government
will need to be highly selective in choosing road investments with high economic impacts.

[ORG] which is administered by [ORG].
5.47 EU grant funds-Cohesion Fund: Following [LOCATION] accession, [LOCATION] will be eligible for [LOCATION]

percent of the Community average. All projects proposed for [LOCATION] grant funding need to undergo a

2009, the [ORG] has indicated that €2.3 billion will be available for structural and

allocation is assumed to be available for road investment projects (i.e. about €600 million). This will

the entire program). However, co-financing requirements may be higher where total project costs exceed
eligible costs for [ORG] financing, such as sizeable land acquisition. Unlike [ORG] structural funds,
the [ORG] is not subject to the principle of additionality, and therefore can substitute national

5.48 [ORG] grant funds-European [ORG] Fund (ERDF): [LOCATION] grants would also be
available for projects that foster regional competitiveness and employment within the [LOCATION] (objective 2 of

(objective 3). These initiatives include investments in regional economic and social development, such as

Investments in class 11, I11 and N roads are eligible for funding under the [ORG], if they fulfill these
objectives. This is the case for the class 11, I11 and IVr oads that [LOCATION] committed to upgrade to be able
to carry [LOCATION] axle load standards of 11.5 tons per axle. Upgrading these roads will allow heavy trucks to
pass through [LOCATION], facilitating transit traffic and trans-[LOCATION] trade flows. In addition, none of the.
required upgrades on class 11, I11 and N roads would be eligible for financing from the [ORG].
For this reason, it is recommended to seek financing for these investments under the [ORG]. Unlike the

5.49 Sovereign borrowing: Given its prudent fiscal management and low Debt / GDP ratio, [LOCATION]
has flexibility for additional sovereign borrowing for their road sector investments, while still meeting the
required Debt / GDP limit of 60 percent under the EU Stability and Growth Pact. However, like all
Sources of financing, it carries with it costs. [LOCATION] could also finance part ofi ts needs in road transport
from domestic capital markets.
5 SO PPP financing: Where economically justified and financially feasible, private participation in
[LOCATION]’s road investment program should be considered. Public-private partnerships bring significant
advantages, as they (i)p rovide access to incremental financing to resource-constraint governments; (ii)
create efficiency gains due to economies of scale, improved risk allocation and improved quality of
service; (iii)a llow for earlier implementation of infrastructure projects, as government expenditures can
be phased over time rather than requiring significant upfront investments; and (iv) can be recorded off-
balance sheet as long as the construction risk and either the availability or demand risk is shifted to the
private sector ([ORG] guidelines). PPPs should only be entered into if they provide value for money.
This should be evaluated using the framework of a public sector comparator. In general, PPPs provide
value as long as efficiency gains outweigh increased financing costs and risks retained by the government.
Adequate risk sharing is therefore paramount to avoid unnecessary burdens on the government budget. In
addition, PPPs require a stable and transparent legal framework and competitive bidding to ensure value
for money and avoid overspending by government. The Government has a choice of structuring PPPs in
the road sector as toll roads, shadow tolls, or availability payment schemes. Toll roads require sufficient
traffic to generate adequate financial returns for private sector participation, and a free parallel road which
can create significant traffic diversion. In addition, [ORG]OCATION] regulations forbid the concurrent charging of
direct tolls and vignettes particularly for heavy trucks (greater than 12 tomes). Given these risks and the
potential need for considerable government support, toll roads may not be feasible for most roads in
[LOCATION] due to the relatively low traffic flows. The government should therefore consider alternative
options. Shadow tolls avoid traffic diversion at the cost of fluctuating government support. Availability
payments based on performance criteria have proven a successful model for PPPs in the road sector in
other [LOCATION] countries such as [LOCATION]. Availability payments also have the benefit of
predictable government obligations, which would need to be recorded on the government’s balance sheet.
Given their limited size relative to total project costs, however, the costs of government obligations could
be outweighed by the benefits ofa ccess to private financing and early project realization.

IV. CONCLUSION
5.56 Road infrastructure assets were negatively affected by the sharp decline in public investments
during the period [PHONE]. This led to severe backlogs in road asset maintenance and rehabilitation,
which in turn has adversely affected the movement of goods and people in [LOCATION], and added extra costs
to the [LOCATION] economy.
5.57 To clear the maintenance and rehabilitation backlog and to bring existing infrastructure to [LOCATION]
technical and safety standards, [LOCATION] would have to use all of its current 1.1 percent of GDP road
budget envelope (about EUR 250) on priority interventions with the highest economic returns, including
maintenance programs, rehabilitation, upgrading and improvement of critical links as well as bypasses
and bridges.
5.58 [LOCATION] grants for the road sector are estimated to be about 0.5 percent of GDP per year, and it is
suggested that these funds should be used for interventions that meet the economic return criterion, and
are critical for economic growth and [LOCATION] accession. Available data on traffic and construction costs
suggest that rehabilitation and improvement of Class I roads on [LOCATION] corridors would yield the
highest economic returns. Previous economic analyses have indicated that the Trakia and Struma
proposed motonvay projects would have the required minimum economic rate of return. However, the
estimated construction cost of these two motonvays is close to twice the estimated amount of [ORG]OCATION]
cohesion grants expected to be made available to [LOCATION]’s road sector over the period [PHONE]. The
government will therefore need to decide on the utilization of the Cohesion grants either for the Class I
roads, or for the two motonvays, or a combination of these roads. As soon as new traffic data becomes
available, [ORG] would be well advised to update the economic analyses and fine-tune the investment
strategy, since other Class Ir oads and motonvays on the TEN-T corridors may then be included ift hey
pass the economic test.
5.59 In addition, the Government also has a program to construct over 1,000 kilometers of other
motonvays with an estimated total cost ofm ore than Euro 3 billion excluding taxes. Implementing such a
program over a 10-15 year period using public funds would consume an additional 1.0 to 1.5 percent of
GDP annually running the risk ofc rowding out investment in other sectors. Therefore, the government is
exploring the potential for involving private investors in the program implementation. However, given
the significant cost of the proposed program, the uncertainty oft he demand for this type ofi nfrastructure,
and the willingness and ability to pay for them by [LOCATION] motorists, there is likely to be a call for
government support. Experience in the region has shown that for PPP financing to be successful, some
form of government support (such as minimum traffic guarantees, or availability payments) has been
necessary. The resulting long term contingent liabilities would therefore need to be factored into the
budget by the government. Hence, it is recommended to carry out a careful feasibility study of every
single motonvay project to ensure public funds, if at all available, are used efficiently.

6. ENVIRONMENTAL ISSUES
6.1 The [ORG] concluded the accession negotiations for the environmental chapter
with the [ORG] in 2004. During the negotiations the government made several commitments to
meet a number of directives, the most demanding ofw hich in budgetary terms are those relating to water
and wastewater and to solid waste5’. The programs have been worked out at varying levels of detail, and
in all cases there are still some open questions.
6.2 This section reviews the current government plans relating to the directives dealing with water
and solid waste, as well as all anticipated environmental expenditures fiom state sources, paying special
attention to the budgetary implications oft hese plans. The realism oft hese plans, in particular in terms of
the projected financing, will be assessed.

6.6 The plans include annual financial contributions from the municipalities ofa bout 30 percent over

6.7 Government's plans leave open possible involvement of the private sector, and there is some
interest from potential investors in this sector in [LOCATION]. [LOCATION] already has a concession involving a
public-private partnership operating the water and wastewater system for the city (although there are

however, a significant role for the private sector is unlikely in the short to medium term for the following
reasons:
6.8 The government still has to address the issue oft he ownership ofm unicipal assets. Of the 50 or
so water companies, 13 are entirely owned by the state, 20 are owned by the municipalities, 16 are jointly
owned, and one isj ointly owned by a municipality and private investor ([LOCATION] is excluded from this list as
it has special status of a PPP). Where ownership is shared with the municipalities, what assets belong to
whom is unclear. The question of what will be transferred to any new operators/owners of the water
companies needs to be resolved. In [DATE], a Water Management Law was submitted for
coordination to the [ORG]. The draft envisages changes to the ownership of assets that will
address the questions raised here about the transfer of some of the assets, and to clarify questions of
ownership, but these are still waiting Parliament approval.
6.9 As noted above any private sector involvement would require significant increases in tariffs6'
The body responsible for the regulation ofw ater charges has been established under the Water Regulation
Services Act, its administrative structure is being set up, and it should be operational by 2006. It mirrors
in many respects the energy sector regulator with whom it shares an overall regulatory structure. With
this body in place some increase in tariffs is inevitable, notwithstanding the low political will for such
increases. Furthermore, ift he energy regulator is any guide, the increases could be substantial. This
suggests that municipal financing of water-related investments may be possible some time in the future,
possibly under a number of PPPs. However, given the time lag between setting up the institutions,
announcing any increases in tariffs, and getting to the stage at which tariffs meet private sector
expectations, serious private sector involvement for water and sewerage will take some time to be
realized.
6.10 To attract the private sector, there would also need to be clarity about the responsibility for
management of the sector between [ORG] and [ORG]. At present the division of responsibilities is
not clear, and as a result there is lack ofc larity ofp olicy and actions.

V. CONCLUSIONS
6.23 The meeting of the environmental part of the acquis communautaire will increase demands on
budgetary resources in [LOCATION] over the next decade, and total spending on environmental protection is
expected to increase by about 50 percent in [PHONE] (while environment related capital expenditures
are expected to increase three-fold, the current expenditures are expected to decline). At the same time,
adequate waste water and waste management will help to facilitate growth by making rural areas (80
percent of the country’s territory) attractive for business and local population, and the system construction
might also spur new entrepreneurship.
6.24 The spending plans for the water and waste sectors are, however, inconsistent with the overall
budget envelope for environment, and significantly exceed the projected medium-term budget allocations.
Reconciliation ofp lans is required to stay within the available budget envelope.
6.25 Also, there are several problems with the detailsof water and wastewater sector financing plans
that would need to be addressed. Perhaps the most serious is the unrealistic nature of assumptions
regarding municipal financing. These are predicated on increases in tariffs that are overly optimistic. In
case these tariff increases are not realized, programs will either fall behind their schedule, or the state will
have to make up the shortfall. This would cause expenditure in this category of the consolidated budget
to go over its planned limit. Also, the ownership of water utility companies’ assets would need to be
clarified to entice private sector participation in the sector.
6.26 It is also quite likely that the level of funds anticipated from the [ORG] will not be forthcoming in
full. Although [ORG] has increased its pipeline ofp repared projects for such funding, and these should
be sufficient to absorb the funds assigned for [PHONE], the pipeline will have to be substantially further
increased to absorb future allocations. As a result, the commitment made by the government to the [ORG]
over the medium term may not be realized, and it would be critical to prioritize the undertaking
committed investments to ensure the most important ones get completed. Further, [ORG], and [ORG]
estimates of financing flows differ, and would need to be reconciled. This may be due to different dates
at which they were prepared.
6.27 In sum, though undesirable, one can expect some delay in [LOCATION] in the implementation of
environmental programs agreed with the [ORG]. However, the [ORG] ([LOCATION], [LOCATION]
and [LOCATION]), and the recent new [ORG] member states have also implemented their environmental programs
on a delayed schedule, owing to large and unaffordable financing requirements. Figure 1 shows the
actual and anticipated expenditures for [LOCATION], from 200 1 onwards. The sharp divergence between actual
and anticipated spending is notable, and is currently being in~estigated~A~l.t hough [LOCATION] hopefully
will not experience such a large difference between actual and planned expenditures, some downward
adjustment in the former may be expected.

Abstract
In crisis times, depositors get anxious, can run on banks, and
withdraw their deposits. Correlated withdrawals of bank deposits
could be mitigated if bank deposits are more diversified, that is,
held by more individuals. This paper examines the link between
the broader access to bank deposits prior to the 2008 crisis and the
dynamics of bank deposit growth during the crisis, while
controlling for relevant covariates. Employing proxies for access to
deposits and the use of bank deposits, the authors find that greater
access to bank deposits can make the deposit funding base of
banks more resilient in times of financial stress. Policy efforts to
enhance financial stability should thus not only focus on
macroprudential regulation, but also recognize the positive effect
of broader access to bank deposits on financial stability.

Banking Sector Resilience, Global Financial Crisis.

1. Introduction
Private decisions in finance confront tradeoffs, most notably that of risk and return. Policy
decision making in the area of financial development is faced with similar tradeoffs, notably that
between financial development and financial stability.1 However, not only tradeoffs exist in
financial policy making. While prudential limits exist in extending access to credit, because not
everyone is creditworthy or can handle credit responsibly—as we have learned most recently
from the global financial crisis—a prudential limit may not exist for advancing access to deposits
or insurance (Cull et al., 2012). Hence, synergies can also be found and exploited. Financial
policy reforms may thus focus on synergies first, i.e. advancing financial development and
improving financial sector resilience at the same time. We study one such possible synergy in
this paper; namely, the positive effect that greater financial inclusion in deposits can have on
greater reliability of bank deposit funding in times of stress.
From 2006 to 2009, growth of bank deposits dropped by over 12 percentage points
globally. The most affected by the 2008 global crisis were upper middle income countries that
experienced a drop of 15 percentage points on average. Individual countries such as [LOCATION],
[LOCATION], [LOCATION], and [LOCATION] switched from deposit growth of 58 percent, 31 percent, 57
percent, and 94 percent in 2007 to deposit declines (or a complete stop in deposit growth) of -2
percent, 1 percent, -1 percent, -8 percent in 2009, respectively.
In times of financial stress or crises, depositors get anxious, can run on banks, and
withdraw their deposits (Diamond and Dybvig, 1983; Shin, 2009). Large depositors are usually
the first ones to run (Huang and Ratnovski, 2011). By the law of large numbers, correlated
deposit withdrawals could be mitigated if bank deposits are more diversified. Greater
diversification of deposits could be achieved by enabling a broader access to and use of bank
deposits, i.e. involving a greater share of adult population in the use of bank deposits (financial
inclusion). Based on this assumption, broader financial inclusion in bank deposits could
significantly improve resilience of banking sector funding and thus overall financial stability
(Cull et al., 2012).
This paper investigates the implications of a broader access to deposits for the dynamics
of bank deposits during the global financial crisis. Namely, we analyze whether access to bank
deposits by a larger share of a country’s population can help explain differences in the drop of
deposit growth over [PHONE] across our sample of 95 countries. We also separately estimate
the differences in the relationship between the drop in deposit growth and access to deposits for
low-income (LIC), middle-income (MIC), and high-income (HIC) countries. The employed
proxies for access to and use of deposits are based on [PERSON] (2008) and [PERSON] and

We find that a broader access to and use of bank deposits can significantly mitigate bank
deposit withdrawals or growth slowdowns in times of financial stress (Figure 1). While this
finding holds for the entire sample of HICs, MICs, and LICs, it could be particularly strong in
MICs, where a large share of population still lacks access to bank deposits, trust in banks is yet
to be firmly established, and the integration in global financial flows is growing. In addition to
the access and use of deposits, bank stability—measured by the aggregate z-score, and the
dummy for the occurrence of banking crises are the most significant explanatory variables in our
regressions. The results hold even when accounting for the possible leverage effects of outliers.
The main message is that countries should recognize that policies to promote a broader
use of bank deposits could improve resilience of bank funding. Such policies can thus enhance
overall financial stability and complement the mainstream macroprudential policies to foster
stability of the financial system.
Our paper responds to an existing gap in the empirical literature linking greater access to
deposits with greater financial (banking sector) stability. While the literature postulates that an
inclusive financial sector will have a more diversified, stable retail deposit base that can increase
systemic stability, empirical research confirming existence of such a relationship, especially at
the level of the financial system, is largely absent in the literature (GPFI, 2012; Cull et al., 2012;
[PERSON], 2010).
At the individual and household level, savings support stability and, given their very
large numbers, small savers potentially contribute to stability at the financial system level (Cull
et al., 2012). Low income savers tend to maintain steady financial behavior through the business
cycle. Hence, during crises, deposits from low income clients typically act as a continued source
of funds even when other sources of bank financing dry up or become difficult to roll over. Small
customers thus provide big opportunities to mobilize stable deposits ([PERSON], 2011). Greater
financial inclusion, including access to savings, can also enhance financial stability indirectly, by
providing individuals, households, and small firms with greater access to financial risk-managing
tools. This greater access can enhance resilience and stability of the real economy and thus also
the financial system that serves it ([ORG], 2012; [PERSON] et al., 2012; [PERSON], 2011).
At the bank level, focusing on retail deposit generation can produce a more diversified
and stable funding base that is less sensitive to changes in market interest rates and a bank’s
financial condition. In stress times, insured depositors have proven to be a bank’s most reliable
funding source and, therefore, play an integral role in mitigating liquidity risk ([ORG], 2012). The
global crisis demonstrated that stable retail sources of funding, in contrast with reliance on
borrowed funds, can greatly enhance the soundness and resilience of financial institutions and
reduce volatility of earnings ([PERSON], 2011). Diversified funding base of financial institutions has
played a role in cushioning the impact of a global credit (wholesale funding) crunch on domestic
financial intermediation ([PERSON] and [PERSON], 2010).
At the country level, financial inclusion can boost efficiency of financial intermediation,
through intermediation of greater amounts of domestic savings, and thus improve soundness of
investment financing and investment cycles. Provided that quality financial infrastructure and
competent supervision are implemented, such improvement will, in turn, produce both greater
economic and financial stability ([PERSON], 2010; [PERSON] et al., 2012).
The paper proceeds as follows. Section two discusses some stylized facts. Section three
explains the employed regression model and estimation approaches. Section four describes the
data used for estimation of the regression model. Section five discusses the baseline regression
results for the entire sample of 95 countries, along with a robustness analysis using the robust
regression approach, and an alternative access to deposit proxy together with a GMM estimator.
Section six presents and discusses differences in the model’s estimates across HICs, MICs, and
LICs, and reports related robustness tests. Section seven concludes and offers some policy
implications.
2. Some Stylized Facts
In this section, we preview some stylized facts about the main variables of interest, i.e. bank
deposit growth around the 2008 global financial crisis and access to bank deposits before the
crisis. The preview motivates some choices that we make for our regression analysis, and further
illustrates the extent of heterogeneity in deposit growth and access to deposits across country
income groups.

3. Regression Model
To formally analyze the link between access to bank deposits prior to the 2008 crisis and the
deposit dynamics in the crisis, we use a regression model of the following form:

stability (z-score), the ratio of liquid assets to deposits and short term funding as a measure of the
banking sector liquidity position (liquidity), and the share of the three largest banks’ assets in the
total banking sector assets as a measure of banking sector concentration (concen); deposits to
