Contents
Executive Summary
The main objective of this report is to identify policy reforms and measures to help the [ORG] ([ORG]) improve the corporate governance of commercial and non-commercial [ORG]
([ORG]) at the national level and reduce the fiscal risks and costs of the [ORG] portfolio. By doing so, this
report seeks to also inform and support the [ORG]’s fiscal consolidation efforts. The assessment is guided
by the modules “Fiscal Implications” and “Corporate Governance and Accountability Mechanisms” of the
[ORG]’s new integrated State-Owned Enterprises framework (iSOEF).
[LOCATION]’s commercial [ORG] sector, measured in terms of revenue as share of GDP, is with 3.5 percent of
GDP1 in FY2019/20 smaller compared to other [LOCATION] (SSA) countries (average 14 percent
of GDP), however, SC[ORG] remain key to the socio-economic development in the country and are the

Government has partially implemented reforms outlined in the Presidential Taskforce Report (2013)

benefit from a sequenced reform approach that allows to build capacities and confidence over time to

1. Introduction
Methodology
This report applies the new [ORG] integrated State-Owned Enterprises Framework (iSOEF). In
particular, it covers the overall landscape of the state-owned enterprises (SOEs) portfolio, including
financial performance and risk analysis, and provides an analysis based on two iSOEF modules capturing
key aspects of SOE[ORG], namely “Fiscal Implications of SOEs”, (iSOEF Module 2), which offers an assessment
of the main fiscal costs and risks from the SOE sector in [LOCATION]; and the underlying “Corporate Governance
and Accountability Mechanisms” (iSOEF Module 4). A particular focus was put on financial rather than
operational performance and impact on household welfare (i.e., iSOEF Module 3: Distributional Impact of
SOE Reform). Since market-related adverse effects of [ORG] were assessed as part
of the Kenya Systematic Country Diagnostic 2020, this report provides limited discussion of [ORG]’ role in the market (iSOEF Module 1) and only insofar it is relevant to the scope of this
assessment.
SOE[ORG] and parastatals can take a diverse range of legal and organizational forms, and the terminology
used by countries to define such entities varies significantly. This report uses the [LOCATION] terminology of
“State Corporations”, which refers to both commercial and non-commercial entities where the
government controls the majority or all of the shares. While section 2.2. provides a detailed discussion of
the de jure and de facto definitions and classifications used in the [LOCATION] context, this report uses the
definition of the Consolidated National Government Investment Report FY2019/20, prepared by the
[ORG] ([ORG]), and
differentiates between commercial and non-commercial SC[ORG] accordingly:2
i) Commercial [ORG] include entities that (i) generally operate on commercial principles to

[ORG].
ii) Non-commercial SC[ORG] are also distinct legal entities that are operationally autonomous from
Government, however, they are expected to operate on a cost recovery basis and largely
depend on monies appropriated by [ORG], levies and fees. They include regulatory
agencies and statutory boards, research institutions, institutions of higher learning and
referral hospitals. Non-commercial SC[ORG] deliver services on behalf of line Ministries and are
funded mainly through the National [ORG] in form of grants or loans from the Government
(Consolidated National Government Investment Report 2019/20).

2. State Corporation Landscape in [LOCATION]
2.1. Context and Development of State Corporations in [LOCATION]
Since independence, the [ORG] ([ORG]) has acknowledged the importance of [ORG] for
development with a view to accelerate economic and social development, redress regional economic
imbalances, and increase [LOCATION] citizens’ participation in the economy (GoK 1965). It marked the
beginning of government investments in manufacturing, agriculture and other sectors. The role of [ORG] in
[LOCATION] has expanded significantly during the post-independence period, with state corporations
diversifying in economic sectors ranging from key strategic sectors, such as infrastructure, to non-strategic
ones, such as textiles, sugar, pharmaceuticals, radios, batteries, alcohol, vehicles, and shoes, among
others. By the 1980s, the proliferation of [ORG] in [LOCATION] had become a significant drain on
the exchequer, becoming a principal cause of long-term fiscal problems. The Government acknowledged
that [ORG] had exceeded their mandates (Sessional Paper No. 1 of 1986) and hence, the
1980s and 1990s were characterized by several reform measures that included substantive divestitures
and privatizations. However, [ORG] today are still the primary vehicle for overseeing,
delivering, and implementing large-scale projects and services. Under the government’s Vision 2030, [ORG] remain strategic to the socio-economic development of the country and the government
intends to use [ORG] to achieve the objectives of transforming [LOCATION] into a "newly industrializing, middle-
income country providing a high quality of life to all its citizens by 2030 in a clean and secure
environment."
2.2. De Jure vs. De Facto Definition and Classifications of [ORG]
The State Corporations Act, Cap 446, 1986, is the overarching governing law on the establishment,
fiduciary oversight on management and governance, and financial control of [ORG]. It is
complemented by additional provisions of the Public Financial Management (PFM) Act 2012, Public Audit
Act, Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, as well as various laws establishing [ORG].
[ORG] as defined in the legal framework is relatively broad and captures what are
commonly known as “public enterprises” or also referred to as “parastatals” (see Box 1). Although no
commonly accepted definition of an [ORG] or public enterprise or state corporation exists ([ORG] 2013; [ORG] 2014; [ORG] 2015), there are some shared elements: (a) the entity has its own,
separate legal personality; (b) the state exercises ownership of the entity; and (c) the entity engages
predominantly in commercial or economic activities. The [LOCATION] definition comprises commercial
enterprises, regulatory bodies, services, universities, training institutions and research institutions.
Moreover, the PFM Act and regulations (2015) outline a relatively granular classification of national and
county government entities, creating a basis for a more differentiated and effective oversight regime that
takes into account the heterogeneity of [ORG].

4. Corporate Governance and Accountability
Good corporate governance is the foundation for stable, financially healthy SC[ORG] and the key to
sustainably limiting the fiscal risks and costs emanating from SC[ORG]. Following the iSOEF methodology, this
section assesses the key dimensions of [LOCATION] [ORG]’ corporate governance: legal and institutional
framework, oversight functions, performance monitoring, boards, and controls and transparency.
4.1. Role, Establishment and Dissolution of State Corporations
Procedures for the establishment and dissolution of [ORG] are provided for in various laws
and have evolved in terms of incorporating good practices. Various laws assign the President or the
responsible Cabinet Secretary with powers to create [ORG]. The PFM Act (section 86) and
PFM Regulations (214, 215 and 216) also provide for: (a) the guiding principles for the establishment and
dissolution of [ORG] (b) Cabinet approval process and (c) the role of the [ORG] in
providing recommendations on any of these decisions. In practice (in as far as establishment of SC[ORG]), a
cabinet memo is prepared by the line Ministry with key inputs from [ORG], the State Law Office and the [ORG].
However, failures to adhere to a systematic process of establishing SC[ORG] in the past, coupled with the
fluid and ambiguous definition, has led to a proliferation of SC[ORG] over the years, which entail rigidities in
resource allocation that impede effective prioritization. At the same time, the existence of various pieces
of legislation on dissolution makes dissolving a [ORG] more difficult, which is exacerbated by the fact that,
once established, SC[ORG] often become politicized – a common challenge worldwide.
There are currently several SCs, particularly non-commercial ones, with overlapping mandates and
duplicative functions, for example, in the education and agriculture sectors, and the six regional
development authorities, the mandates of which cut across many other SCs’ mandates. Especially in
light of increasing amounts of [ORG] grants and subsidies to non-commercial SCs – with an average annual
growth rate of 18.5 percent between FY2015/16 and FY2019/20– and the resulting mounting fiscal costs,
rationalization of SC functions could support the [ORG]’s fiscal consolidation efforts.
The [ORG] Systematic Country Diagnostic (SCD) 2020 highlights that the large presence of
commercial SCs presents a major constraint to productivity gains in [LOCATION], as they are still crowding
out the private sector, particularly new investors, while also generating a significant fiscal burden.
[LOCATION] businesses face high levels of government intervention and direct competition from public entities
in areas where there is active private sector participation –such as retail, accommodations,
manufacturing, banking, insurance, and agri-processing– and where government service provision should
therefore be unnecessary. [LOCATION] has a higher degree of state intervention than the [ORG] average and
other middle-income countries (see Kenya SCD 2020). Given the declining profitability and increasing
financial risks of commercial SC[ORG], exacerbated by COVID-19, and the increasing government lending and
debt guarantees to commercial SCs in recent years, accelerating the commercial SC[ORG] rationalization
agenda could help plug losses to the exchequer, release physical and human capital resources, stimulate
competition and private investment, and increase overall economic efficiency.
The Presidential Taskforce Report 2013 stressed the necessity to review and rationalize commercial and
non-commercial SCs with a view to consolidate functions, remove overlaps and duplications, and
improve efficiency and service delivery. The recently published report by the [ORG] (2020) underlines this need and supports taking actions to this end, including the
separation of commercial activities from the non-commercial roles of policymaking and regulation and
service delivery.
4.2. Ownership and Oversight Functions
While the [ORG] is the legal owner of [ORG] shares held by the national government, the key responsibilities
of the [ORG] ownership function are decentralized, with oversight responsibilities fragmented over a
multitude of institutions. This includes the appointment of boards, provision of strategic direction,
monitoring, and reporting. Key oversight entities include:
• The [ORG]: The [ORG], through the Government Investment and Public
Enterprises Department ([ORG]), coordinates the overall management of public enterprises,
develops the strategic objectives and policies relating to the financial oversight and management
of [ORG], and manages the restructuring of [ORG] and overall reforms, amongst others.
• [ORG]: The President through executive orders assigns ministerial responsibility
over SC[ORG]. Line ministries are in charge of sector policies and provide directives to SC[ORG].
• The [ORG]: The [ORG], currently domiciled under the
Presidency, monitors quarterly SC performance and conducts special investigations and audits.
• The State Corporations Advisory Committee ([ORG]): [ORG] is an advisory body to the President,
overseeing corporate governance and [ORG] administration and advising on the reorganization or
dissolution of [ORG].
While a number of laws clearly describe the oversight roles played by various institutions, how these
institutions interact in carrying out their various roles and responsibilities is not clear. The Presidential
Taskforce Report (2013) highlights that often the role and responsibilities of different Government
departments and entities in relation to [ORG] are not clearly delineated, resulting in confusion. For instance,
while the State Corporations Act (section 27) provides that [ORG] plays a role in examining proposals by
[ORG] to acquire interests, enter joint ventures or expand their scope of business, other Acts, such as the
Kenya Airports Authority Act and the Universities Act, provide that the approval to borrow, invest surplus
funds and invest in securities is provided by [ORG] solely. While in practice institutions such as the [ORG] would be involved in providing recommendations on the fiscal implications of investments, and
the State Law Office on aspects of legality, this is not expressly provided for in the various laws, and has
evolved as a matter of practice. Another example is that while the State Corporations Act provides for
investigative powers of the [ORG] (section 19), the PFM Act also assigns
powers to [ORG] to enter, access and inspect [ORG] systems and records for the same purpose.
The lack of clarity of how the different oversight institutions interface in carrying out their roles has a
serious impact when it comes to the acquisition, management and disposal of assets. For instance,
whereas the State Corporations Act (section 13(2)) anticipates the collaboration between the responsible
[ORG], [ORG] and the [ORG] on advising on the acquisition and disposal of assets for [ORG], other
laws, e.g., the National Social Security Fund Act, only make reference to the responsible [ORG] Secretary
and the Board (with no reference to the [ORG]). While [ORG] are established as corporate
bodies with powers to acquire and dispose of assets, the Cabinet Secretary to the Treasury (Incorporation)
Act also establishes the office of the [ORG] as a corporation which exercises residual
ownership responsibilities of all assets on behalf of the [ORG].
Centralized ownership and oversight arrangements are increasingly viewed as a good practice ([ORG] 2014). They can bring greater professionalism to the state’s ownership role by pooling specialized
capabilities and scarce resources, and achieve greater transparency and accountability through better
oversight and performance monitoring. For example, under a centralized ownership model, such as [LOCATION] and [LOCATION], a specialized government department or ownership entity serves as the shareholder
representative with oversight responsibility for public corporations. In [LOCATION], the single ownership
entity ([ORG]) owns the [ORG] shares on behalf of the state and appoints boards, develops key systems
and controls (such as governance, risk management, and internal audit), and monitors performance
([ORG] 2014). The adoption of a centralized model in [LOCATION] has led to increased growth in state
enterprises’ tax contributions, net profits and shareholder returns.
The [ORG] has made some significant reform efforts in the past years to move towards a centralized
model. For example, the Government Owned Entity Bill 2014 proposed a far-reaching reform toward a
centralized ownership model, including the rationalization of oversight agencies and the establishment of
a holding company over commercial [ORG]ORG]. However, it has not been adopted yet for various reasons, as
outlined in Box 3. International experience shows that entities that previously exercised ownership
functions tend to resist change, which makes it difficult to transmit the ownership function to a centralized
body. In addition, adopting a centralized model requires significant institutional capacities, which need to
be built over time.
Box 3: Reform attempts towards a more centralized ownership and oversight model
In 2014, as response to the Presidential Taskforce Report (2013), the Government Owned Entity Bill was drafted
to address challenges stemming from fragmented ownership and oversight. It proposed a centralized ownership
and oversight model, including a reduction of the multiplicity of oversight institutions and the establishment of
an investment holding company to exercise ownership and management oversight over commercial SC[ORG] on behalf
of [ORG]. However, this Bill is yet to be enacted into law. The [ORG] faulted the Bill for being
merely a re-enactment of the existing State Corporation Act, with the addition of retrogressive provisions that
would stifle the operations of [ORG] ([ORG] 2014). But reform efforts have reportedly also been blocked due to
institutional disagreements and a lack of political will (The [ORG], 2018).
In [DATE], another reform initiative towards a more centralized model was attempted in the infrastructure
sector. An executive order by the president aimed to establish the [ORG] ([ORG])
bringing together [ORG], [ORG] and [ORG]. The [ORG] was to act as a holding company and be responsible for the management of the State’s investments
in ports, rail, and pipeline services. The new structure aimed at lowering the cost of doing business in the country
through cost effective provision of these services ([ORG] 2020). However, political resistance emerged, such as from
the [ORG] ([ORG]), which argued that the mergers would lead to job losses ([ORG]). In
[DATE], the [ORG] failed to support the initiative, citing that legislation for the merger was lacking, and
the reforms were postponed.
4.3. Performance Management and Monitoring
Monitoring and ensuring the enhancement of [ORG]’ performance is one of the core functions of the State
as owner. Regular and systematic evaluation of the performance of [ORG] is particularly important in times
of economic difficulty (such as recently due to COVID-19), when many [ORG] become financially troubled
and may attempt to negotiate support packages. It enables the state as owner to set performance
standards, put pressure on poorly performing SCs, and better manage fiscal risks emanating from SCs.
Performance Contracting
The [ORG] has used performance contracting since 2004 as a key accountability framework in its endeavor
to improve the efficiency, performance and public service delivery of [ORG] and other state entities.
Having started with 16 SCs in 2004, all SCs are currently under performance contracts.
Performance Contract Design
There are standardized performance contracts for commercial and non-commercial SCs, including
performance dimensions, indicators and reporting forms. Specific indicators and weights assigned to
each dimension are adapted to the specific state corporations. The performance contract includes a vision
statement, mission statement and strategic objectives of the contracted SC. With regards to performance
dimensions for evaluating performance, the [LOCATION] case is very comprehensive compared to many
countries. The new GoK Performance Contract Guidelines for FY2020/21 outline seven dimensions with
financial stewardship and discipline (10%), service delivery (10%), core mandate (60%) and cross-cutting
issues (13%) as the highest weighted performance dimensions.
Currently SCs identify Vision 2030 flagship projects in the performance contracts, and SCs submit
progress reports to the [ORG]. This fosters alignment of the priorities of
[ORG] with the national development strategies, and thereby addresses a key recommendation by the
Presidential Taskforce Report (2013). Furthermore, the new guidelines require [ORG] to ensure that the
identified performance indicators under the Core Mandate are aligned with post COVID-19 recovery
strategies.
The ability of management to cascade the [ORG]’ priorities throughout the enterprise depends on the
quality and number of the indicators used. The larger the number of indicators, the greater burden it
imposes on the SC[ORG], which detracts from the necessary focus on a manageable number of goals. The
number of indicators used in [LOCATION] [ORG] performance contracts is relatively high, with some having up to
38. International good practice calls for a more limited number of indicators. In addition, with COVID-19
exacerbating the financial challenges of [ORG], a greater prioritization of key performance indicators to
ensure a focus on critical financial and operational performance aspects is recommended.
The quality of the indicators used in the performance contracts is uneven. Good performance indicators
are “specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART)” (Doran 1981). There are several
of those indicators already in place, particularly those measuring financial performance. However, several
indicators used are input or activity-based and are not defined with sufficient precision to ensure the
reflection of true performance. This is most pronounced in the dimension with cross-cutting indicators,
which according to the weighting is considered the second most relevant. For example, the performance
contract of the [ORG], on Knowledge Management, outlines sub-indicators
such as “encourage the documentation of knowledge for future reference” and “set appropriate channels
of communication for storage and transfer of knowledge.” The first is not measurable, and the latter is
too vaguely defined to constitute a meaningful performance indicator. Another example is the indicator
Competence Development “Competence/Skills needs assessment”. This is a statement rather than an
indicator.
There are significant time and other costs involved in developing and evaluating a large number of
indicators. Reducing the number of indicators to the most relevant ones would save cost and time to set
high-quality key indicators that allow for a more accurate evaluation of actual performance.
Performance Contracting Process
In response to the effects of COVID-19, the government has made changes to the process of
implementing the performance contracting cycle (GoK Performance Contract Guidelines for FY2020/21).
The key players in the various processes are clearly identified, particularly the negotiations and vetting of
performance contracts. However, the agencies involved throughout the process are numerous and
fragmented, which can be particularly challenging during times of economic crisis and disruption, such as
due to COVID-19. For example, consider the development of performance contracting guidelines,
including the issuance of standardized indicators and reporting forms. This is driven by the [ORG], negotiations are undertaken by different agents such as the line ministries, [ORG] and several
specialized agencies15, while during the evaluation process additional actors like the [ORG] become involved. The newly issued [ORG] Performance Contract Guidelines for FY 2020/21
prescribe the involvement of multiple different agencies (more than 10 are outlined in total), to which [ORG]
are required to submit several different performance report forms or action plans. For example, according
to the [ORG]’s current contract of FY2020/21, the [ORG] needs to submit reports
to eight different institutions. By contrast, international good practices limit reporting to no more than
one or two institutions. Reporting agencies also have different frequency requirements regarding annual
and interim reporting. For example, [ORG] submit quarterly performance reports to the [ORG], while annual performance reports are usually submitted to the [ORG].
Such fragmentation increases coordination and logistical challenges in the process and complicates
effective follow-up and the enforcement of performance targets.
Cognizant of the need to streamline processes and the additional challenges from COVID-19, the
[ORG] has developed an online platform to fully automate the performance
contracting process. This will significantly reduce some of the coordination and logistical challenges in the
process. The automated system has already been launched and will be the basis of gradual performance
management enhancement. This notwithstanding, additional streamlining of some of the processes and
reducing reporting lines should be considered.

policymaking, however, it remains a key challenge, particularly due to manual data collection. Most of
the data currently provided by [ORG]ORG] are in hard copy and follow different reporting standards and formats,
reflecting the heterogeneous nature of [LOCATION]’s SCs. [ORG] staff need to first convert these into soft copy

4.4. Boards of Directors
The Chair of the Board is appointed by the President, with other members appointed by the Cabinet
Secretary/Minister (with some exceptions to this rule discussed below). Each Board has a representation
from the [ORG] and a responsible line Ministry (through their Principal Secretaries or other
designated persons). Boards also can include appointments from other Ministries Departments and
Agencies as well as members of the public (who have specified qualifications, expertise and experience
relevant to the mandate and operations of the [ORG]).
The State Corporation Act also empowers the President to "give directions of a general or specific
nature to a board with regard to the better exercise and performance of the functions of the state
corporation and the board shall give effect to those directions.” As per the [ORG], boards should have
the ultimate responsibility for [ORG]’ performance, for which they need the authority, autonomy, and
independence to make decisions that determine performance ([ORG] 2013). International experience
shows that strategic and operational control by the government can lead to interference with suboptimal
results. In the past, [LOCATION] has faced several challenges related to boards. For example, the Presidential
Taskforce Report 2013 stressed that patronage and undue influences in the appointment of board
members and executive management had bred impunity, which in turn affected performance. It also
highlighted that boards have not been fully in control of CEOs, and in some cases top managers were hired
directly by the ministries. This renders the board ineffective in demanding accountability from the
management especially in the era of performance contracting. This is corroborated by findings from [PERSON]
(2016) that underlined the political nature of appointment processes.
Since the weak financial performance of the majority of SC[ORG] was attributed to an inadequate
governance framework, in 2015, a uniform code of governance – “Mwongozo” (from the Swahili for
guide) – has been adopted. It is applicable to all SCs with the objective of strengthening the roles and
responsibilities of their boards. The code draws from global best practices, including the South African
King III Code and OECD Guidelines on Corporate Governance of SOEs (2005), amongst others. The
provisions in the code address many challenges found in [LOCATION]’s [ORG] boards, such as lack of proper skills
mix and bloated boards, lack of board independence, and shortcomings in the process of appointment of
boards and CEOs (see Box 4). It provides a strong framework and is an important step towards good
corporate governance practices.
Box 4: Salient Features of Mwongozo in line with international best practices
Mwongozo provides provision for, among others:
• Appointment criteria for Boards (appointee needs to have sufficient expertise to perform role)
• Gazettement of all Board members by name including Government representatives
• Composition, proper mix and size of the Boards
• Roles of the Boards, Chairpersons, Board members and CEOs
• The position of Company/Corporation Secretary in all Boards
• Tenure limit for Board members and CEOs
• Maximum number of Boards any one person can serve in
• Guidelines on Board Committees
• Board induction and Evaluation mechanisms
• Succession planning and strategies
• Regulation of ethical conduct in Boards
• Requirement for Governance audits
Source: [ORG] (2015)
Implementation of the code is on a “comply or explain” basis, recognizing that [ORG] are at different levels
of compliance with corporate governance. Thus, [ORG] boards prepare reports indicating the degree of
compliance with the code and explain reasons for non-compliance. No information is publicly available to
assess the overall compliance rate. Some recent cases show that there are still challenges related to
governance of boards in [ORG], but there is continued efforts to improve compliance with the [ORG]
guidelines. For example, [ORG], which has been facing financial difficulties, has still employed several
political appointees to the Board who reportedly did not understand operations of the utility company and
which were removed only recently ([DATE]) ([ORG] Public Notice 2020; The East African 2020).
4.5. Controls and Transparency
Ensuring high levels of transparency on [ORG]’ operational performance as well as on the overall [ORG]
portfolio improves accountability and is an important enabling factor to prioritize and contain the cost
of the government support to [ORG]. The PFM Act (2012) requires all [ORG]ORG] to prepare and submit quarterly
financial statements (within 15 days after the end of each quarter) and annual financial and non-financial
statements (within three months after the end of the FY). SCs comply with these timelines. In terms of
standards, SC[ORG] carrying out commercial activities apply the International Financial Reporting Standards
(IFRS), while the regulatory and other non-commercial entities apply the accrual basis International Public
Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS). The Financial Reporting Standards were promulgated by the Public
Sector Accounting Standard Board ([ORG]) for adoption and application with effect from [DATE]. The
use of International Standards aims for SC[ORG]’ financial reporting to: (i) improve both the quality and
comparability of financial information reported by public sector entities around the world (ii) facilitate
transparency in the financial dealings of public institutions (iii) improve consistency in preparation and
reporting of financial information (iv) improve accountability and ease the audits of public institutions (v)
result in stronger governance procedures. In terms of general compliance with the standards, commercial
SCs who use IFRSs perform better in terms of compliance and most of them have an unqualified opinion
from the [ORG] compared to the non-commercial SCs who apply the IPSAS and have
a lower compliance rate.
Public access to timely and relevant information on financial and non-financial performance is very
limited. The financial statements comprise the following: (a) Statement of comprehensive
income/financial performance (b) Statement of financial position (c) Statement of changes in equity/net
assets (d) Statement of cash flow (e) Statement of comparison of budget and actual amount (f) Notes to
the financial statements for the reporting period (e) Comparative information in respect of the preceding
reporting period. However, public access to timely and relevant information on financial and non-financial
performance remains a challenge. Most [ORG] do not upload published financial statements in a timely
manner as stipulated under Section 81 (4) (b) of the PFM Act 2012. Furthermore, while the Auditor
General publishes some audited financial statements of [ORG] on its website, this is not done in a timely
fashion, with most of the latest statements dating back to 2017.
While annual aggregated reports of [ORG] are prepared and published, they are of limited scope and do
not provide a fully transparent picture of actual developments in the portfolio. [ORG] prepares and
publishes annual aggregated reports of SC[ORG], including also [ORG] and funds. Aggregate reporting presents
the situation and performance of the [ORG] portfolio as a whole. It represents the final link in the chain of
accountability which connects the [ORG] to their ultimate owners, the country’s citizens. In [LOCATION], the
performance analysis presented in the reports is of limited scope. While it provides the key financial
performance and position indicators, such as revenue, profits, net worth, assets and liabilities, transfers
from [ORG] to [ORG], and expenditures for each SC, the level of detail could be enhanced. For example, it does
not include key information by sectors (e.g., energy, transport, agriculture) and does not distinguish
between the economic nature of the SCs. There is also a lack of contextualization and analytical clarity in
the information presented. For example, in the latest report, the large drop in commercial SCs’ profits in
FY2019/20 compared to the previous year is not presented, and since all SCs (commercial and non-
commercial), [ORG] and funds are aggregated, the report presents a profit increase of 26 percent. This
leads to a distorted picture of actual developments in the portfolio.
Fiscal Risk Reporting
Fiscal risk reporting is mainly qualitative and limited in scope and depth. While the aggregate report
does not present exposure to risk emanating from SC[ORG], the annual budget policy statement, which is
submitted to Parliament annually, has a Statement of Specific Fiscal Risks in the annex that discusses
explicit and implicit (contingent) liabilities as a potential source of fiscal risk. The budget policy statement
2021 provides information on [ORG] on-lending and guarantees to [ORG], and a discussion about the aggregate
amounts of contingent liabilities. However, the analysis is still mainly qualitative and limited in scope and
depth. A deeper analysis of high-risk SCs, including key financial risk indicators, and a clear and sufficiently
detailed outline of direct and indirect government support or guarantees to [ORG] is still lacking.
Internal Audit
The internal audit is an important tool to provide independent assurance that an [ORG]’s risk management,
governance and internal control processes are operating effectively. It can help to prevent the misuse
of funds during the expenditure process, while also flagging issues for management action. The PFM Act
2012 Section 73 requires that every national government entity complies with the Act and has appropriate
arrangements in place for conducting internal audit according to the guidelines of the Accounting
Standards Board and any applicable regulations. [ORG] are also required by [ORG] to establish an audit
committee and employ an internal audit department that reports directly to the audit committee. The
audits are carried out in accordance with the International Professional Practices Framework (IPPF) as
issued by the [ORG], as well as guidelines issued by the Public Sector Accounting
Standards Board. This ensures uniformity and consistency across national government. For most SCs the
current risk management practices support good corporate governance. However, the challenge has been
adherence to the control environment set, as there have been reported cases of misappropriation of
resources in some SCs. For example, the [ORG] ([ORG]) allegedly misused
millions of dollars of public funds meant for buying COVID-19 medical supplies (BBC 2020). The internal
audit in most SCs can hence be strengthened to become more effective in reducing cases of
misappropriation of resources in [LOCATION] and lack of accountability by management. This in effect will also
reduce the number of audit issues raised by the external auditors.
Special audits may be conducted by the Internal Auditor General from the [ORG] on [ORG] that
have received funds from the exchequer, upon request by the [ORG]. For example, [ORG] had an audit conducted in 2019 upon the request of the
[ORG], whereas it has its own internal audit
department, board and audit committee. In 2020, [ORG] had a special audit as a result of receiving
exchequer and donor support via the [ORG]. The final report of the internal auditor, which
has been deliberated on and adopted by the Audit Committee, may be copied to the auditor
general/external auditor, who may choose to use those findings for purposes of scoping their work on risk
assessment of an [ORG] in the audit process.
External Audit and Scrutiny by the Legislature
Timely completion and submission of the audits to [ORG] as well as parliamentary review of these
audits are critical for effective decision making and accountability but remain a challenge. The role of
an independent external auditor is important for reinforcing the credibility of the [ORG]’ financial
statements and compliance with regulations. The legislation governing the audit process in [LOCATION] for [ORG]
includes the Constitution of Kenya 2010, the State Corporations Act, The Public Finance Management Act
2012 and is guided by the Public Audit Act 34 of 2015, the [ORG] ([ORG]), [ORG] ([ORG]) and [ORG] ([ORG]). All [ORG] are required to submit their financial statements to the Auditor General
within three months of the end of the corresponding fiscal year. The Auditor General is required to audit
these and report within six months after the end of each financial year as specified by Article 229 of the
constitution. The auditor general will then submit the audit report and the audited financial statements
to [ORG] and the Public Investment Committee ([ORG]) for review and take appropriate action. A key
challenge over the past few decades has been the lack of timely completion of and submission of the
audits to [ORG]. This is problematic because timely and relevant information on SC[ORG] is critical for
effective decision making and accountability. The [ORG] ([ORG]) also does not submit
a consolidated audit report to [ORG] for review, as in the case of [ORG]
([ORG]) and Counties, but forwards individual audit reports for some SCs only. In addition, due to the large
number of SCs, the [ORG] has not been reviewing all the reports submitted to it. This reduces parliamentary
scrutiny, which is important to hold the government’s executive branch to account for its SC-related fiscal
and expenditure policies and implementation.
The audit reports contain a section on follow-up of auditor recommendations, which is a summary of
key issues raised by the external auditor and management comments that were provided to the auditor.
One of the challenges in some [ORG] has been the ability to track and enforce the timely resolution and
implementation of prior audit reports’ recommendations. Consequently, most [ORG] reports continually
repeat the same audit issues raised in previous years, with no recourse to the [ORG]’ accounting officers.
The [ORG], in some instances, outsources the audit services for SC[ORG], which helps reduce the backlog of
audits. This is provided for in Section 23 of the Public Audit Act, which states that for purposes of carrying
out his or her functions the Auditor General may outsource audit services from duly registered firms
whose partners and staff are not employees of the [ORG] and the public service to assist in the examination
and audit of accounts.
5. Conclusion and Recommendations
This assessment seeks to identify policy reforms and measures to help the government improve [ORG]’
performance and reduce the fiscal risks and costs associated with SC[ORG]. The net fiscal costs of commercial
[ORG] (in normal times) is fairly low, whilst the fiscal costs of non-commercial SCs are significant. Between
FY2016/17 and FY2018/19, the annual net fiscal cost of commercial SCs was equivalent to 0.08 percent of
GDP on average. While the [ORG] also received revenues from non-commercial SCs, the large volume of
subsidies and grants created average annual net fiscal costs equivalent to 3.6 percent (0.4 percent of GDP
for funds).
Many of [LOCATION]’s commercial SCs had pre-COVID-19 financial performance challenges, which in many
cases were compounded through the pandemic. Around one third of commercial SCs made losses in the
last three consecutive years. The aggregate operational performance of commercial SCs in FY2019/20
turned negative for the first time in recent years. Several sectors that showed performance improvements
in FY2018/19, such as education, trade and tourism, transport and sugar (still loss-making, but reduced),
experienced a downturn both in terms of revenue and net profits. Yet, the overall declining performance
trend is mainly driven by few large SCs some of which, despite revenue increases, showed reduced
profitability due to rising expenses, such as [ORG] and [ORG].
Fiscal Exposure for the [ORG] from commercial and non-commercial SCs has consistently and significantly
increased in the last five years. The rise in grants and subsidies is attributed to the increasing dependence
of non-commercial SCs on such transfers, which accounted for 5 percent of GDP in FY2019/20, whereas
commercial SCs have been financing their operations increasingly through government lending and debt
guarantees. Total government lending (direct and on-lent) amounted to 8.9 percent of GDP, debt
guarantees to 1.5 percent of GDP, and non-guaranteed loans to 1.6 percent of GDP in FY2019/20. The
[ORG] has already started paying some debt service for some commercial and non-commercial SCs. SCs’ low
and decreasing capacity to absorb further materialization of potential downside risks is generating
increased fiscal risks. Some SC[ORG] with the largest potential fiscal impact are high risk entities, most of them
operating in the energy and transport sector.
The deteriorating financial performance and increasing fiscal risks are compounded by corporate
governance and accountability challenges. These include challenges in SCs performance monitoring and
oversight including low transparency of SCs’ operations and relations with the government, challenges in
the internal and external audit functions, as well as fragmentation and implementation gaps of the legal
framework.
Government has partially implemented reforms outlined in the Presidential Taskforce Report (2013)
that can move SC management and monitoring toward global best practice, but the remaining agenda
is significant. The government has made some strong efforts to implement important improvements in
SC oversight, such as the creation of the “Mwongozo” governance code. However, many of the far-
reaching reforms have not been implemented. As highlighted by the [ORG] (2019), SC reforms are
particularly challenging because of their political complexity and effects on a multitude of stakeholders.
Reforms need to take into account what is politically feasible and institutionally manageable, particularly
under COVID-19 crisis and recovery conditions (which, at the same time, introduces urgency and can act
as a spur to change). [LOCATION] may thus benefit from a sequenced reform approach that allows to build
capacities and confidence over time to build towards far-reaching changes.
Following the main findings, the recommendations to strengthen the performance of [LOCATION]’s [ORG]
revolve around: 1) strengthening the legal framework and institutional structure; 2) improving
performance monitoring; and 3) enhancing controls and transparency of [ORG]’ operational performance
and relations with the government. These three priority reform areas are in line with the staged approach
to its SC[ORG] reform strategy that the NT is currently developing (GoK 2021). More specifically, this report
recommends the following measures for driving these three reform areas forward:
1) Strengthening the legal framework and institutional structure
Implement a clear and standardized classification of SCs among all oversight agencies. There is lack of a
clear and consistently applied classification among oversight institutions, departments and reports, which
complicates fiscal reporting, impedes transparency, and hampers oversight. The PFM Act and regulations
outline a relatively granular classification of national and county government entities, including SCs.
Implementing these provisions among all government institutions builds the basis for a more
differentiated and effective oversight regime that takes into account the heterogeneity of SCs, based on
their economic nature. Reducing ambiguity in the classification and terminology of SCs used by oversight
agencies when monitoring and reporting is critical to increased transparency and accountability, and
improved fiscal management.
Address proliferation of SCs and rationalize commercial and non-commercial SCs. In terms of non-
commercial SCs, reducing overlapping mandates and duplications in particular could support the [ORG]’s
fiscal consolidation efforts, particularly in light of the increasing grants and subsidies to non-commercial
SCs – with an annual average rate of 18.5 percent– and their increasing dependence on such transfers in
the last five years.. For example, measures to addressing overlapping mandates and consolidating SC[ORG] in
the education sector could improve the efficiency of public spending on higher education and reduce
spending pressures. Moreover, given the declining profitability and increasing financial risks of
commercial [ORG], exacerbated by COVID-19, and the increasing government lending and debt guarantees
to commercial SC[ORG], accelerating the commercial [ORG] rationalization agenda could help plug losses to the
exchequer while increasing overall economic efficiency. A focus could be placed on systematically poorly
performing SC[ORG] that have recorded persistent losses for an extended period (e.g., the last three
consecutive years). In doing so, the government should also take the opportunity to define the role of
commercial [ORG] and their mandate and indicate in which sector the private sector should play a greater
role.
Harmonize the legal framework. Harmonize the fragmented and at times inconsistent pieces of
legislation, including the various laws establishing [ORG], PFM Act 2012 and regulations, and State
Corporation Act to provide for a consistent and clear legal foundation for all [ORG]. A guideline for these
processes should be developed and agreed upon.
2) Improve SC performance monitoring
Improve the reliability and timeliness of data as well as analytical capacities. Having more reliable and
timely data is key to support sound policymaking, however, it remains a key challenge. Data collection,
quality and analysis challenges should be addressed in two complementary ways. First, increase the
analytical capacity of [ORG] and the [ORG], both in terms of staffing and skills.
With limited staff in these offices, analytical capacity is stretched, meaning there is insufficient time and
capacity to undertake the complex analysis required to understand large, systemically important
commercial and non-commercial SCs (which is necessary to evaluate SCs’ funding requests). In addition,
training of staff on deeper analytical methods could strengthen the government’s ability to deal with the
impact of COVID-19 on SCs and achieve better monitoring and oversight over the longer-term. Second,
adopt an IT-system to automate and systemize data collection to address the limitations of manual data
collection and related challenges, and in order to upgrade financial and fiscal risk monitoring and
management and improve the reliability and timeliness of data.
Improve the performance contracting design and processes for both commercial and non-commercial
SCs. In this regard, three main considerations should be taken into account: i) define all performance
indicators with high precision to ensure that real performance is captured; ii) reduce the number of
indicators to only the most relevant ones to ensure a focus on a manageable number of goals; and iii)
streamline performance contracting processes by reducing reporting lines and agencies involved, to
strengthen enforcement and accountability of performance targets. International good practices limit
reporting to no more than one or two institutions. Furthermore, a more coordinated approach may be
achieved through requiring reports (including off-performance contracting reports) to be submitted
through a common system that the agencies can access based on their responsibility and mandate.
3) Enhance controls and transparency of SC[ORG]’ operational performance and relations with the [ORG].
Increase transparency and comprehensiveness of SC reporting. Ensuring high levels of transparency on
SC[ORG]’ operational performance, as well as on the overall SC[ORG] portfolio, improves accountability and is an
important enabling factor to prioritize and contain the cost of the government’s support to SC[ORG]. SC[ORG] do
not publish financial statements in a timely manner, except for some few large commercial SCs. All
commercial and non-commercial SCs and the [ORG] should publish audited annual financial statements and
accompanying reports in a timely manner on their websites. Moreover, the annual aggregate [ORG] report
should provide a more comprehensive picture of the portfolio, by differentiating at least between
commercial and non-commercial SCs, and by providing more financial statistics (e.g., information on
dividends received by the government from [ORG] and standardized financial ratios), and information on
developments in key industries and the largest SCs. Subsequent annual reports could be further enriched
by including information on key issues covered in the performance contracts of major [ORG], corporate
governance information such as compliance with [ORG], and a range of other topics.16 Aggregate
reporting is not codified across the world, and actual practices vary considerably across countries, but the
OECD Guidelines on the Corporate Governance of SOEs (2015) set out general requirements relating to
aggregated reporting. Table 11 provides examples of several countries, including middle-income
countries, that produce aggregate reports providing valuable information on the portfolio of their public
enterprises.

Improve fiscal risk reporting on SCs and expand public debt statistics to include SCs. Improve the

the government’s official debt statistics to include SC’s debt, as also recommended by the [ORG], is also merited to enhance the comprehensiveness of the data and strengthen
public debt sustainability analyses.
Strengthen external audit and parliamentary scrutiny. Ensure the timely completion and submission of
audited financial statements of at least the largest, strategically most relevant, and/or most risky SCs to
[ORG]. Given the current capacity constraints, the [ORG] should consider outsourcing more external

government owned entities, including SC[ORG]. In this regard, increase traceability and the timely
implementation of prior year recommendations raised by previous audit reports. Moreover, ensure that
[ORG] reviews all key reports submitted to them, which is important to hold the government’s executive
branch to account for its SC-related fiscal and expenditure policies and implementation. Considering the
[ORG] review backlog, the Committee should adopt a structured review process, prioritizing reviewing the
largest, most strategic SCs, ideally differentiated by type of SCs (at least by commercial and non-
commercial). The [ORG] should also submit audited consolidated financial statement reports to [ORG] for
review, as in the case of [ORG] and Counties.
Enforce Mwongozo more rigorously and make compliance with it public. Mwongozo provides a strong
corporate governance framework. [ORG] compliance with Mwongozo, and thereby strengthening boards, is
crucial to ensure effective oversight, [ORG]’ effectiveness in fulfilling their mandates, and increases in their
operational efficiency. This includes the full constitution of boards of [ORG] and assurance that all board
members have the required technical and business experience to exercise the full range of responsibilities.
Implementation progress on the code should be made public.

[ORG]mmarizes the findings of the Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP)
exercise for [LOCATION] undertaken in 2010 by a joint [ORG] team.1 The first mission
(June) assessed the observance of selected international standards and codes, and initiated
discussions on a broad range of financial sector issues. The second mission (December)
completed its review and presented a draft Aide-Memoire along with draft technical and
background notes covering a range of topics relevant to [LOCATION]’s financial sector.
[LOCATION]’s financial system reform efforts have had positive results. Reforms accelerated
since 2003, with the [LOCATION] government adopting a series of policies to enhance financial
sector’s resilience and, on the structural side, strengthening a large part of domestic financial
institutions and improving market confidence. However, risks, challenges and development
opportunities remain.
This report points out near-term risks, reform challenges and development
opportunities [LOCATION] confronts as it continues to modernize its financial sector. [LOCATION]
faces potential vulnerabilities, near-term risks and policy-induced distortions common to an
evolving financial system. The challenges and opportunities are not unique, and can be
addressed. We propose that the authorities could consider carefully sequencing the following
reforms and development options: (i) further deepening the commercial orientation of the
financial system; (ii) moving to more market-based means of controlling monetary and
financial conditions; (iii) further strengthening regulation and supervision; (iv) upgrading the
framework for financial stability and crisis management; (v) revising the strategy for
financial inclusion to achieve improved access to financial services ; (vi) continuing steps to
support a broad based capital market; and (vii) continue to strengthen and deepen the
insurance and pension sectors and (viii)continue enhancement of the financial market
infrastructure.
Addressing the opportunities and challenges will require creative thinking and a
willingness to change. A gradualist and piece-meal approach to financial sector reforms
likely will fall short in meeting the increasing depth and complexity of [LOCATION]’s financial
market. Going forward it will be important to have a holistic approach and to look beyond
current laws and regulations for potential means to address market changes as well as to find
solutions to current inhibiting factors preventing the attainment of Government goals.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT AND RECOMMENDATIONS
1. [LOCATION]’s financial system reforms are progressing well. The authorities are seeking
to shift the financial sector from a centrally directed system to one that is commercially-
based and financially sound. Improvements are seen in the structure, performance, and
oversight of the financial sector. The system is becoming more transparent as it opens up.
2. [LOCATION] is confronted by a build-up of potential sources of vulnerabilities,
including greater exposure to external shocks. The inter-linkages across markets and
institutions are growing, and de-facto banks and informal credit markets, conglomerate
structures, and off-balance sheet activities are on the rise. The reform of small-and medium-
sized rural financial institutions continues. There is a need for close monitoring, better data
collection, intensive information exchange and a stronger framework for identifying and
addressing problem institutions and market practices that could impair the on-going reform
process.
3. The near term domestic risks are four-fold: (i) the impact of the recent sharp credit
expansion on banks’ asset quality; (ii) the rise of off-balance sheet exposures and lending
outside the formal banking sector; (iii) the relatively high level of real estate and commodity
prices; and (iv) the increase of imbalances due to the current economic growth pattern. Stress
tests of 17 commercial banks suggest that most major banks are resilient to risk in isolation,
but gaps and weaknesses in the informational infrastructure make it difficult to assess the
possible transmission effect through the economic and financial system. There is potential
for damage to financial stability and continued reform should the risks arise simultaneously.
4. Macroeconomic and financial policies need to be better aligned to create
incentives for a durable transformation to a more commercially oriented and effective
financial system. Emphasis should be on credit allocation processes, financial markets and
services that reduce the need for high levels of precautionary savings, and more resilient and
transparent institutional structures. To facilitate this process, the government should continue
to reorient its role and responsibilities. The state’s involvement in financial markets and
institutions—through ownership of banks and state owned enterprises, management of
interest rates, setting of priorities for the financial system, and as an implicit guarantor—is
resulting in moral hazard, weak risk management in banks, and a buildup of contingent risk
and liabilities.
5. The commercialization of the financial system needs deepening. Credit risk
strategies are dominated by loan growth targets. The use of commercial bank credit for
policy goals should be replaced by other mechanisms such as direct fiscal expenditures,
government credit programs and rationalization of policy banks. Bank risk management and
supervisory assessments focus too much on backward-looking variables and not enough on
forward-looking assessments of credit risk. The concentration of bank exposures to state
owned enterprises, the guaranteed margins, the limited ability and willingness to differentiate
loan rates, as well as the implicit guidance on credit flows, undermine the development of
effective credit risk management capabilities at banks. In this context, a move to more
market-based means of controlling monetary and financial conditions would greatly improve
credit allocation. Market interest rates should become the primary instrument for managing
credit expansion.
6. Continued advances in the regulatory and supervisory regime are required.
Efforts are needed to implement consolidated supervision and ensure timely sharing of
essential information among all relevant government bodies. The [ORG] and the primary
supervisory commissions must be empowered and have resources commensurate with their
expanding responsibilities. The mandates of the supervisory commissions should focus on
ensuring safety and soundness of regulated institutions and proper market conduct.
Approaches to supervision should be more forward looking in lieu of issuing large quantities
of regulations and using very detailed approval processes for governing the day-to-day
activities of financial institutions. In addition, customers of financial products and services
must be made aware of the underlying risks and obligations through improved market
disclosure and enhanced financial literacy. To support this, improvements in accounting
requirements, data standards, reporting requirements, and meaningful disclosure are
necessary.
7. A formalized stability framework to monitor and respond to macro-financial
vulnerabilities would benefit [LOCATION]. Building on the experience from the ad-hoc committee
in place since [DATE], a permanent Financial Stability Committee should be established
having access to relevant supervisory and other financial information.
8. A framework to resolve weak financial institutions on a timely basis is needed.
The framework should assist in resolving distressed financial institutions at least cost to the
public, and facilitate the wind up of institutions in an orderly manner. To facilitate this and to
protect the [ORG]’s balance sheet, a deposit insurance fund could be established to finance the
orderly resolution of failed institutions and to protect insured depositors. A government
entity should be vested with authority to monitor the health of the financial system and have
resolution powers for dealing with institutions declared nonviable by their supervisors.
9. Broader and more diversified financial products and services would deepen and
strengthen [LOCATION]’s financial system. Interdependencies between the government and the
corporate fixed income markets and policies relating to the interest rate regime should be
considered. This should include: (i) a more proactive government debt issuance strategy to
support the risk-free yield curve; (ii) expanding access to new non-government issuers; and
(iii) increasing the supply of different types of instruments to address the diverse needs of
issuers and investors. This should be accompanied by improvements to the repo markets;
developing risk pooling and hedging products; prudently promoting the development of
securitization, and measures to ensure regulatory consistency across all types of fixed income
products.
10. Financial infrastructure and relevant legal systems need to be further upgraded.
Progress has been seen, but more is needed to: a) enhance the legal framework and oversight
function of the payments and securities settlement system, b) improve the coverage and
quality of the Credit Reference Center, c) improve the oversight and quality of credit rating
agencies, d) upgrade and strengthen consumer protection, e) enhance the insolvency regime
and creditors rights; f) define a clear process for dealing with troubled financial institutions
and depositors and g) establish a framework and tools for effective macro prudential and
financial stability.
11. Financial Inclusion could be enhanced through a revised strategy. This should
include reforms to provide the right incentives for: provision of financial services to under-
served sectors; market competition and contestability (by adjusting entry and exit criteria);
improving the legal framework for financial inclusion; and removing policies not properly
aligned with the overall objective of improving access.
12. Sequencing reforms at the appropriate pace will be a challenge, but essential to
[LOCATION]’s sustained growth. This will be crucial to maintaining a balance between
development and financial stability while minimizing risks. To facilitate the process, a
prioritized list of key recommendations needing consideration was provided (Table 1).
I. STRUCTURE AND FUNCTIONING OF THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM
A. Context
1. [LOCATION]’s progress in reforming and developing its financial system has been considerable
(Table 2). This development has been supported by key banking sector reforms, creation of capital
markets, introduction of a prudential regulatory regime, bank recapitalizations, and a broad-based
opening of the financial system following accession to the [ORG] and reforms since 2003. Joint-stock
reforms—including initial government capital injections, and subsequent strategic investor participation
and initial public offerings (IPOs) have boosted large banks’ commercial orientation. Banks have
diversified their equity structures; enhanced corporate governance; introduced internal controls and risk
management; and increasingly adopted profit-maximizing strategies. Key securities companies were
restructured, and a securities companies’ resolution mechanism and an investor protection scheme set
up. Insurance sector reform also progressed.
2. The reform of financial policy is underway but distortions remain. These are linked to
remaining interest rate policies, quantitative credit guidance, limited investment channels, and moral
hazard related to the perception of implicit state guarantees. As a result, [LOCATION]’s system is characterized
by: (i) a low cost of capital that does not remunerate adequately domestic households; (ii) a propensity
for prices to deviate from market clearing levels; (iii) inadequate incentives to price risk in view of the
implicit guarantees on large state-[ORG] enterprise ([ORG])’ debt;2 (iv) emphasis on minimizing NPLs
on balance sheets; (v) high levels of structural liquidity; (vi) incentives to push credit off-balance sheet;
and (vii) still limited non-state ownership— including foreign shareholder participation—in the financial
system. Direct allocation and credit pricing facilitated [LOCATION]’s strong growth, when sectors with high-
growth potential were easily identified, but they also contributed to overcapacity, potential asset
bubbles, and the need for public-funded bank recapitalizations.
3. Credit is primarily channeled via the banking system, with a limited role for domestic
capital markets (Figure 1). At end-2009, commercial bank loans accounted for a larger share of total
financial system assets compared to others. [ORG] institutions ([ORG])—including trust
investment companies, financial leasing companies, and finance companies—have been growing (Table
4).

B. Macro-Financial Environment
5. [LOCATION] has maintained high growth rates over the past three decades, on the back of high
investment and rapid credit growth (Table 3). Growth has averaged double-digits since the start of
reforms in 1978, and inflation has remained relatively subdued reflecting rapid productivity growth and
additions to capacity from high levels of investment. Public debt remains low, although there are
contingent liabilities. The economy is prone to asset bubbles, notably in the stock and real estate market,
given high levels of structural liquidity, low interest rates, and lack of alternative investment vehicles.
6. The financial system plays a direct and critical role in the transmission of macroeconomic
policies. In [LOCATION] there are five key macro-financial linkages: i) The banking system directly facilitates
quasi-fiscal policy through its use as a credit channel; ii) Banking system directly facilitates monetary
policy, but the credit growth targets undermine the efficiency of credit allocation; iii) Low cost of capital
distorts the saving-investment balance of the economy; iv) Capital markets’ underdevelopment limits
alternatives for corporate funding and household investments, and represents an impediment to solving
structural problems in the financial sector: low rates of return on savings; high precautionary savings
through banks; high savings by private enterprises without access to capital markets; continued bank-
dominance of the financial system; and potential asset bubbles; v) Lack of contestability of markets or
ownership for large firms limits competition..
C. The Regulatory and Supervisory Framework
7. Progress has been made to improve financial regulation and supervision, but the challenge
is to increase its efficacy, quality, and responsiveness. The [ORG] revealed a high degree of
adherence to international standards. However, going forward, the right balance must be struck between
the degree of regulatory control and the need to enable useful innovation and development of the
financial system. Suggestions arising out of the assessment were to improve: i) the operational
autonomy of supervisory commissions, ii) skills, iii) risk monitoring capabilities, iv) resources and v)
interagency coordination.
8. Commercial Bank Regulation and Supervision
a. [ORG] has made strides in improving its framework for supervising commercial banks.
It has a clear safety and soundness mandate but its operational autonomy is challenged by the
continued use of the state dominated banking system to pursue development goals and rapid
credit growth. Going forward, it will be important to ensure its ability to act fully in pursuit
of its mandate. This should include adequate budget and supervisory resources so it can
respond to the increasing scale and complexity of the [LOCATION] banking sector.
b. Banking legal and regulatory framework has been brought in line with international
standards, but gaps remain. Identified gaps: a) absence of a requirement to be informed of
changes in indirect control and the identification of banks beneficial owners and clients; b)
inadequate rules on related parties and c) lack of a legal framework underpinning bank
resolution.
9. Securities Intermediaries and Securities Market Regulation
a. The [ORG] has overseen regulatory reforms to support a more market-based financial
system. A credible program of inspection and surveillance is in place but a stronger emphasis
is needed on illegal investment activities and monitoring of hedge funds and private equity
(PE) funds. Steps have been taken for detecting and deterring insider trades and market
manipulation, but more is needed. [ORG] should introduce a formal on-site inspection
program of the exchanges to bolster oversight and it should implement and strengthen
monitoring of risk-based net capital rules and “Know your client” rules.
b. The legal and regulatory framework for the regulation of securities markets needs to be
further improved to keep pace with market developments. Areas for improvement
include the commercial court, enforcement with respect to illegal investment activities and
detection and deterrence of unfair trading practices. [ORG] needs greater operational
autonomy to enable it to more effectively carry out its mandate without the potential for
interference. Budget flexibility is needed so it can respond to the rapid growth of markets and
the limited role played by market discipline. The accounting and auditing profession has
made strides, but there is a need to continue to develop its size and expertise to meet the
increasing size and growing complexity of the market.
10. Insurance Regulations and Supervision
a. [ORG] has a comprehensive supervisory framework, with emphasis on corporate
governance rules , consumer protection efforts and risk management systems, though
improvements are needed in: i) off-site monitoring through reinstatement of early warning
ratios; ii) the non-life liability and solvency regimes; iii) the life minimum solvency margin
to make it more risk based as investment options are expanded; iv) ensuring explicit and
clear regulation for facilitating the exit of insurance companies from the market via run off or
portfolio transfers and v) the coordination and exchange of information between [ORG] and
[ORG] in the area of AML. In addition, strict measures should be taken to prevent insurance
companies operating below the 100 percent solvency level from issuing new business.
b. The [ORG]’s mandate and operational autonomy need to be addressed. The
developmental mandate for [ORG] should be reviewed to ensure it can focus on its real
mandate. Its budget should ensure adequate organizational and industry capacity. The current
prescriptive, rules-based system should be reconsidered as the market and the risk-based
supervisory regime mature.
11. Regulation of Other Financial Institutions
a. Regulation of other financial institutions (OFIs) aims to ensure their link with the
formal banking sector remains limited. In addition to commercial and policy banks, there
are a host of other [ORG] which are part of the credit delivery system. Some trust companies,
finance companies of enterprise groups, and leasing companies, etc., are regulated by the
[ORG]. In addition, there are entities in the informal financial sector (pawn shops, financing
guarantee institutions, micro-finance companies, etc.) which are licensed by local
governments and unregulated entities (informal banks) which are surveyed or investigated by
the [ORG] occasionally.
b. Regulatory policies applied to shadow banks and their responsibilities need to be
clarified. [ORG] and [ORG] view the universe of shadow banks as comprising mainly PE
(the majority of which have not been regulated) and informal lenders and deposit takers
(monitored by the [ORG] and [ORG]). The regulatory policies applying to shadow banks and
their responsibilities need to be clarified. Interagency coordination backed by memoranda of
understanding for information sharing, needs to be strengthened to prevent episodes of build-
up of systemic risk via cross-market financial products or activities.
II. THE BANKING SECTOR
12. The banking system is dominated by [ORG] ([ORG]) and [ORG] ([ORG]). Collectively, the five [ORG] and the twelve [ORG] accounted for 83
percent of total commercial bank assets at end-2010 (Figure 3). All [ORG] and most [ORG] are owned or
partially owned by the government and thus, most are substantially controlled by the government.
Deepening the commercial orientation of the banking sector will serve to foster a general deepening of
the entire financial sector.
13. The banking sector balance sheets have expanded rapidly in part due to the
macroeconomic stimulus policies. As a result credit demand for infrastructure and transportation
increased. A large proportion of such demand came through local government financing platforms
(LGFPs) that have increased considerably as a result of the 2009 economic stimulus. The fiscal revenue
and expenditure mismatches coupled with the inability of local governments to borrow directly have
made it difficult to achieve appropriate balance between rapid economic growth and avoiding undue
financial risks.

14. Banking sector profits remained high as a result of large expansion of credit and balance
sheets, in part due to the macroeconomic stimulus policies. A large portion of the demand came
from local governments. This, together with the credit demand for property purchases and credit creation
associated with large FX inflows, led to a surge of new RMB loans. In addition, off-balance sheet
exposures have expanded rapidly since the Q2 of 2009, mostly as a result of banks’ promoting wealth-
management products.
15. Banks’ NPL ratios reflect a downward trend, reaching 1.1 percent at end-2010 (Figure 4).
This decline was driven by rapid expansion of credit and the significant decline in NPLs. The
contraction of NPLs to RMB 434 billion at end-2010 from RMB 1.3 trillion at end-2005 substantially
reflects the carve-out and resolution of RMB 816 billion (NPLs) from one large bank in 2008. The
migration of some loans to performing status and some improvements in risk management in banks also
has prevented NPL levels from rising

16. Banks’ funding appears stable, but a rise in longer-term loans adds to challenges for
banks’ maturity mismatches. The sizable and low cost deposit base contributed to stable bank
funding. The growth in domestic corporate deposits since 2008 has become a driver of total deposits.
Maturity mismatches are rising. Increasing reliance -on medium- and long-term loans for investment
project financing has lengthened asset maturities. Interest rate mismatch is balanced by the regular
repricing of loans, but the maturity mismatches pose challenges for liquidity management.
17. A stress test covering 5 [ORG] and 12 [ORG] banks was jointly conducted by the [ORG] team
and the authorities. These banks have better information disclosure and more sophisticated risk
management systems than other banks. The exercise was done in close cooperation with the [ORG] and
[ORG]. It involved single-factor shocks and macroeconomic scenario analysis, but was limited by the
lack of consistent data. The shock sizes took into account past experience in [LOCATION] and other countries,
as well as past [ORG] practice. The single-factor sensitivity calculations suggest that the system would
be able to withstand a range of sector-specific shocks occurring in isolation. The analysis suggests that
the system could be severely impacted if several major shocks materialized concurrently.
III. STRENGTHENING BOND AND EQUITY [DATE]. The capital market as an alternative funding channel to banks has grown over the last five
years (Table 6), but an enourmous potential for growth remains untapped. Although progress has
been seen in establishing a multilayer capital market addresing finanical needs of both large or state-
owned enterprises with high credit ratings and SMEs. However, there is still room for a more relevant
role of capital markets as a funding source for large enterprises with lower credit ratings (even above
investment grade) and SMEs. Bank dominance in the financial sector presents challenges in developing
the capital markets as an effective capital raising mechanism.
19. Despite prospects of banking disintermediation deepening, the banking sector is expected
to continue playing a prominent role in capital market development. As issuers, underwriters,
distributors, investors and liquidity providers, banks would influence the speed and quality of growth of
fixed income markets. The speed of development of the market also will be influenced by
Government’s plans for further interest rate reform.
20. A full-fledged Government bond market is needed for the growth of diversified and
sophisticated fixed income markets. Currently the risk-free yield curve is unevenly developed as the
Government shares it with PBC bills in the short term and the more liquid [ORG] bonds in the
medium term (Figure 5). While the active use of PBC bills has thus far played an important role in
setting up the basis and infrastructure for further development of a fully fledged bond market, going
forward the continued issuance in sizeable volumes of these bills may require further institutional
coordination with the [ORG] on its issuance policy of instruments of similar maturities. This is a common
evolution observed in many advanced emerging market economies that are confronted to large
sterilization needs related to capital inflows as they pursue development of a liquid risk free yield curve.
It is expected that as [LOCATION]’s economy continues to progress such disparities will be mitigated as large
sterilization needs diminish with reduced capital inflows.
